AI Engineering Mastery

How to build software around an AI model, whose answers can differ every time you ask. You will learn how to write a request so the answer is usable, how to let a model use tools without handing it your database, how to keep a long conversation affordable, how to fetch the right passage of text and not just a plausible one, and how to measure whether any of it works before your users find out for you. That last part is the one most people skip.

How to use this course

  • This is an engineering course, not a tour of a product. The Claude API is the concrete tool used throughout, because a course that stays vendor-neutral ends up teaching nothing you can run. But the ideas carry over to any model. You will learn what a token costs, why a cache breakpoint (the marker that says "cache everything before this point") has to sit at the end of the stable prefix, why an agent loop (a program that lets a model act, look at the result and act again) must have a stop condition, and why an LLM judge (a model that grades another model's answers) needs a rubric before it needs a model.
  • Every example runs, and the printed output is what it produced. The examples that call the model run against the real SDK (the official Python library for the API), with a scripted transport underneath standing in for the network. The request that leaves the example is genuinely serialised and the response is genuinely parsed. The examples that compute something run outright: chunkers, retrievers, token budgets, cost models, retry policies and evaluation harnesses.
  • It assumes you can read Python and have built something that talks over HTTP. If either is unfamiliar, work through the Foundations course first, then Networking and HTTP.
  • It builds on four courses and deliberately does not repeat them. Networking and HTTP covers what happens on the wire: streaming responses, retries, timeouts and TLS. Backend and API Design covers designing the service that wraps a model, including idempotency keys, rate limits and the transactional outbox. System Design covers what happens when there are many of them. Python covers the language. Where this course needs one of those, it names the course and the topic and does not re-teach it.
  • Each section follows the same order: Concept → Mechanism → Arithmetic → Practice → Exercises with solutions.

The one idea the rest of the course depends on

A language model is a function. You give it a sequence of tokens (small pieces of text, roughly word fragments), and it returns a probability for every token that could come next. Everything else you may have heard of, such as chat, agents, tool use, retrieval and structured output, is a convention that the people calling that function have layered on top. The model has no memory, no state and no session. Each request must carry the entire world the model will see.

That single fact explains most of what follows, and most of the mistakes.

It is stateless
So a conversation is a list you resend. Turn twenty costs twenty turns of input tokens, not one. Every technique in the context-engineering section — caching, editing, compaction, memory — exists because that list grows and you pay for it every time.
It is a distribution
So the same input can produce different output. You cannot test it by running it once. This is why evaluation is a section of its own rather than an afterthought, and why "it worked when I tried it" is not evidence.
It predicts, it does not know
So a fluent answer and a correct answer look identical. Grounding, citations, retrieval and structured output are all ways of making the difference visible to your code instead of leaving it to the reader.
It only emits tokens
So it cannot do anything. A tool call is the model emitting a structured request that your program chooses to execute. Every safety property of an agent comes from that sentence: the model proposes, your code disposes.

Hold on to the last one especially. "The model called the database" is never literally true. The model produced a block of JSON, and your loop decided to hand it to a function you wrote. Where that decision lives, and what it refuses, is the whole of agent security.

What you are actually learning

There are three separable skills inside "AI engineering", and mixing them up is why the field can feel like folklore.

Shaping the request
Getting the model to do the task at all. Prompt structure, examples, output format, thinking, tool definitions. This is the part that feels like the whole job at first and turns out to be the smallest.
Engineering the context
Deciding what is in the window and what it costs. Caching, retrieval, compaction, tool-result pruning, budgets. This is where production systems are won or lost, because it governs latency, price and — through the middle of a long conversation — accuracy.
Knowing whether it works
Evaluation, guardrails and operations. A test set with a grader, a judge you have validated against humans, and enough observability to notice a regression that only shows up on 2% of traffic. Almost nobody does this, which is precisely why it is worth doing.

The course is ordered so that each section can use the ones before it: - Sections 1–2 establish what the model is and the exact shape of a request. - Sections 3–5 are the ways you steer one call: prompting, structured output and thinking. - Sections 6–8 add capability: tools, server-side tools and MCP, and non-text input. - Sections 9–10 are about context, meaning what to keep, what to cache and what to retrieve. - Sections 11–12 build agents, first by hand and then on a managed runtime. - Sections 13–15 are the engineering discipline: evaluation, guardrails, and running the thing in production. - Section 16 builds one complete system end to end.

A note on versions

This course was written against the Claude API as it stood in August 2026. It names specific models, prices and parameters and does not hide behind "the latest model". That is a deliberate trade: you get concrete examples you can run, and the cost is a shorter shelf life. Two habits keep you safe as it ages.

Treat the model list as data, not as knowledge. client.models.list() returns what exists right now, with each model's context window (how much text it can read at once) and its capabilities. Section 1 uses it instead of a hard-coded table.

When something does not work, check whether the parameter still exists. The most common failure for anyone returning to this API after a year is a request field that was removed. temperature, top_p and budget_tokens were all central to writing prompts a short while ago, and the current models reject all three. The SDK tells you immediately, and §2.9 shows how to read what it says.

SECTION 1

What AI Engineering Is

Start with a puzzle. You give a small text generator the single word "the", and ask it to finish the sentence. You do that a thousand times, with exactly the same input and exactly the same program. How many different sentences come back?

Guess before reading on.

Five. The most common one came back 311 times out of 1,000, and the rarest 98 times. Nothing was broken, and nothing changed between runs. §1.1 runs exactly this and prints every sentence it got.

That generator is a cartoon of a language model, the kind of program behind Claude and every chatbot you may have used. A real model has far more than five possible answers, but it works the same way: it picks its words by weighted chance. AI engineering, in this course, means building software on top of a language model that someone else trained and runs. You send it text over the internet, and your program uses the text that comes back.

Building on a component like that is unlike anything else in this collection. The difference is not that the model is clever. It is that the component at the centre of your system is non-deterministic, priced by the word, and confidently wrong in ways that look exactly like being right. Taking those one at a time:

  • Non-deterministic means that asking twice can give two different answers. The puzzle above is that property.
  • Priced by the word means that every piece of text you send, and every piece it sends back, appears on your bill (§1.3).
  • Confidently wrong means that a made-up answer is written just as smoothly as a true one. Reading it does not tell you which one you have.

Every technique in this course is a response to one of those three properties. This section covers three things:

  1. what the model actually is (§1.1);
  2. what a token, the small piece of text you are billed in, actually costs (§1.2, §1.3);
  3. what changes about engineering when your most important dependency samples from a distribution, meaning it picks its output by weighted chance (§1.4 to §1.6).

Here is a picture to keep in mind for the whole section: a ghostwriter you can only reach by telegram. A telegram was a short message sent through a telegraph office, and the office charged by the word. Imagine a writer who has read nearly everything ever printed, and who works only that way:

  • You send the start of a text. They send back what most likely comes next, one word at a time, picking each word by feel.
  • They keep no copies. To continue a conversation, you must send the whole conversation again, every time.
  • Send the same telegram twice, and the two replies may be worded differently, or even say different things.
  • They write just as smoothly when they are guessing as when they know. Nothing in the reply tells you which.
  • The office charges for every word you send, and five times as much for every word they send back.
  • They can only send words. If a reply says "sell the shares", nothing is sold unless a clerk in your office reads it and does it.

Every idea in this section has a place in that picture:

In the telegram picture In an AI application Section
The writer, who continues whatever text arrives the language model, doing next-token prediction §1.1
Picking each word by feel, so two replies differ sampling from a probability distribution §1.1
Keeping no copies, so the whole conversation is resent statelessness §1.1
Writing just as smoothly when guessing predicting, not knowing §1.1
A reply asking your clerk to do something a tool call, which your code chooses to run §1.1
The office's own way of counting, in pieces of words tokens and the tokeniser §1.2
Charging by the piece, five times more for replies input and output prices §1.3
A long standard opening kept on file, cheaper to resend prompt caching §1.3
"The reply came back fine when I tried it" one sample from a distribution §1.4
Your own clerks: sorting, checking, filing, paying the nine components that are yours to build §1.5
"Of these 100 letters, at least 85 replies must be right" a success criterion someone else can measure §1.6

Every example in this section is plain Python. None of them calls a real model, so they need no account, and they print the same thing on every machine.

1.1 What the Model Is

A large language model, or LLM, does one thing: it reads text and predicts what text is most likely to come next. You have probably used a tiny version of this already. The keyboard on a phone suggests the next word as you type. A language model is that idea, trained on an enormous amount of text, and good enough to continue almost anything.

Here is the mechanism, step by step:

  1. The model takes a sequence of tokens: small pieces of text, roughly word fragments (§1.2 measures them).
  2. For every token that could come next, it gives back a probability, a chance between 0 and 1. Mathematicians call that list a probability distribution: every possible option, each with a chance attached.
  3. To produce an answer, you pick one token according to those chances, and add it to the text.
  4. Then you ask again, with the longer text.

Repeating that step is the whole mechanism, and it has a name: next-token prediction. In the picture, it is the writer choosing the next word of the telegram by feel, then the next, then the next.

Start with a single step. Suppose that after the word "the", the possible next words are "cat" with a 40% chance, and "dog" and "sky" with 30% each. This program picks the next word eight times, from the same input:

import random

rng = random.Random(20260825)
words = ["cat", "dog", "sky"]
chances = [0.4, 0.3, 0.3]

for _ in range(8):
    print("the", rng.choices(words, weights=chances)[0])

the cat
the dog
the cat
the cat
the dog
the cat
the cat
the cat

Line by line:

  • rng.choices(words, weights=chances) picks one word, using the chances as weights. It returns a list, so [0] takes the one word out of it.
  • The same input, "the", went in all eight times.
  • "cat" came out six times, and "dog" twice. That is what weighted chance looks like: the likeliest word wins most often, but not every time.
  • "sky" never came out at all, although it has a 30% chance. Eight picks are far too few to show the real chances.

The 20260825 is a seed: a starting number that makes Python's random choices repeat exactly, so this page and your screen show the same eight lines. §1.4 comes back to seeds.

Everything the model appears to do, such as reasoning, planning and refusing, is next-token prediction over a sequence that makes those continuations likely.

Now let the loop run to the end of a sentence. Each picked word is added to the text, and the longer text decides what can come next. A loop that feeds its own output back in as its next input like this is called autoregressive. The table DISTRIBUTIONS holds the chances for each text so far. When a text has no entry, the sentence is finished. The program builds a sentence from "the" a thousand times and counts the results:

# A toy autoregressive loop, so the shape is concrete rather than metaphorical.
import random

rng = random.Random(20260825)

DISTRIBUTIONS = {
    ("the",):            [("cat", 0.4), ("dog", 0.3), ("sky", 0.3)],
    ("the", "cat"):      [("sat", 0.7), ("ran", 0.3)],
    ("the", "cat", "sat"): [("down", 0.6), ("still", 0.4)],
}


def sample(context):
    options = DISTRIBUTIONS.get(tuple(context))
    if not options:
        return None
    roll, cumulative = rng.random(), 0.0
    for token, probability in options:
        cumulative += probability
        if roll < cumulative:
            return token
    return options[-1][0]


from collections import Counter

results = Counter()
for _ in range(1000):
    context = ["the"]
    while True:
        nxt = sample(context)
        if nxt is None:
            break
        context.append(nxt)
    results[" ".join(context)] += 1

print("1,000 runs of the SAME input:")
for sentence, count in results.most_common():
    print(f"  {count / 1000:>5.1%}  {sentence}")

print()
print(f"{len(results)} distinct outputs from one input.")
print("nothing is broken. The function returns a distribution, not an answer,")
print("which is why one run tells you almost nothing (13.1).")

1,000 runs of the SAME input:
  31.1%  the dog
  30.3%  the sky
  16.0%  the cat sat down
  12.8%  the cat ran
   9.8%  the cat sat still

5 distinct outputs from one input.
nothing is broken. The function returns a distribution, not an answer,
which is why one run tells you almost nothing (13.1).

This is the puzzle from the start of the section, answered. Read it line by line:

  • All 1,000 runs started from the same input, "the", and used the same function.
  • "the dog" and "the sky" are the most common sentences, at 31.1% and 30.3%. Each had a 30% chance at the first step, and each sentence stops right there.
  • "cat" was the likeliest first word, at 40%. But after "the cat" the sentence splits again, so its share is divided between three endings: 16.0%, 12.8% and 9.8%.
  • 5 different outputs came from one input.

Nothing is broken. The function returns a distribution, not an answer, and one run of it is one sample. That is why one run tells you almost nothing, and why §13.1 measures a prompt over many runs.

Everything layered on top of that function is a convention: an agreement about how to call it, implemented by the people calling it. That includes all of these:

  • chat, a back-and-forth conversation;
  • tools, which let the model ask your program to do something;
  • agents, loops that let the model take many steps in a row;
  • retrieval, looking up documents to put in front of the model;
  • structured output, answers in a fixed format such as JSON.

None of these lives inside the model. There is no chat inside the model. There is no memory. There is no session, nothing that remembers who you are from one request to the next.

Four consequences follow, and they are the spine of the course. In the picture, they are the four things you learn about the writer by working with them:

It is stateless
A conversation is a list you resend. Turn twenty costs twenty turns of input, not one. §2.3 shows the mechanism; §9.1 does the arithmetic, and it is a quadratic.
It is a distribution
One run is one sample. You cannot test it by trying it once, which is why §13 is a section rather than a paragraph.
It predicts, it does not know
A fluent answer and a correct answer are indistinguishable from the outside. §10's retrieval, §8.5's citations and §14.5's grounding all exist to make the difference visible to your code.
It only emits tokens
So it cannot do anything. A tool call is a structured request your program chooses to execute. §6.1 develops this and §14.4 turns it into a security model.

Two words in that list need a meaning:

  • Stateless means the model keeps nothing between requests: the writer who keeps no copies. A quadratic cost grows with the square of the length. A conversation twice as long resends about four times as much old text in total, because every turn resends all the turns before it.
  • A tool call is the model writing out a request, such as "run the function delete_record with these arguments", in a fixed format. Your program reads that request and decides whether to run it.

Hold the last one particularly firmly. "The model deleted the record" is never true. The model produced JSON, a plain-text format for structured data, naming a function. Then a loop you wrote passed it to code you wrote. In the picture, the writer wrote "sell the shares", and your own clerk sold them. An agent is exactly that arrangement running in a loop (§11). Where the decision to act lives, and what it refuses, is the entirety of agent safety.

The whole mechanism fits in one picture:

1.2 Tokens

The unit of everything, including cost, limits and latency, is the token. Latency is how long you wait for an answer. The limits are how much text one request can hold, and how much a reply may contain. All of them are counted in tokens.

A token is not a word and not a character, and the gap between intuition and reality is where budgeting goes wrong. In the picture, the telegraph office does not count words the way you do. It cuts your text into pieces by its own rule, and charges per piece. A short, common English word is often one piece. A long or unusual word, a string of digits or a word in another script can take several.

You cannot see the real pieces without asking the API (§2.8 shows how). What you can do on your own is the common estimate: divide the number of characters by four. This program applies that estimate to five kinds of text, and prints the characters, the words and the estimated tokens for each:

SAMPLES = [
    ("plain English prose",
     "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river bank."),
    ("code",
     "def get_user_by_id(user_id: int) -> User | None:\n    return DB.get(user_id)"),
    ("JSON",
     '{"order_id":"ORD-4471","total_cents":4250,"status":"shipped"}'),
    ("a UUID",
     "9f8b7c6d-5e4f-4a3b-2c1d-0e9f8a7b6c5d"),
    ("non-Latin script",
     "分散システムの設計における一貫性のトレードオフ"),
]

print(f"{'kind':<22}{'chars':>7}{'words':>7}{'chars/token at 4':>18}")
for label, text in SAMPLES:
    chars, words = len(text), len(text.split())
    print(f"{label:<22}{chars:>7}{words:>7}{round(chars / 4):>18}")

print()
print("the 'chars / 4' rule is a rule of thumb for ENGLISH PROSE only.")
print("code, JSON, identifiers and non-Latin scripts all run denser,")
print("so a budget estimated this way is optimistic exactly where it matters.")

kind                    chars  words  chars/token at 4
plain English prose        64     13                16
code                       75      9                19
JSON                       61      1                15
a UUID                     36      1                 9
non-Latin script           23      1                 6

the 'chars / 4' rule is a rule of thumb for ENGLISH PROSE only.
code, JSON, identifiers and non-Latin scripts all run denser,
so a budget estimated this way is optimistic exactly where it matters.

Line by line:

  • The English sentence has 64 characters and 13 words, and the estimate says 16 tokens. For ordinary English prose, the estimate is roughly right.
  • The code has 75 characters but only 9 "words", because text.split() cuts only at spaces.
  • The JSON, the UUID and the Japanese line each count as a single word, because none of them contains a space. (A UUID is a long random identifier, the kind databases hand out.) For text like this, a word count tells you nothing at all.
  • The last three printed lines give the catch. The estimate holds only for English prose. Code, JSON, identifiers and non-Latin scripts really produce more tokens than it predicts, so a budget built on it runs short exactly where it matters.

Use count_tokens (§2.8) for anything that must fit. count_tokens asks the real tokeniser how many tokens a request contains. It is free, it takes the same request shape (the same fields as a real request), and it includes your tools and system prompt. The system prompt is the standing instructions you send at the top of every request (§3). The chars / 4 estimate (characters divided by four) is for deciding whether to investigate, and never for deciding whether a request fits.

The tokeniser changed. The tokeniser is the part that splits text into tokens: in the picture, the office's rule for cutting text into pieces. Claude 4.7 and later use a newer one that produces roughly 30% more tokens for the same text than Sonnet 4.6 and earlier. That is not a price rise, because the per-token prices differ too. But it does mean that a token budget measured on an older model does not transfer. Any inherited "this fits in 8,000 tokens" claim should be re-measured and not trusted.

1.3 What It Costs

Two prices, and the one people ignore is the expensive one. You pay for input tokens, the text you send, and for output tokens, the text the model writes back. Prices are quoted in dollars per million tokens, written $/MTok.

This program prices one typical call, 4,000 tokens in and 600 tokens out, on the three models in this course's price list (§2.2 has the full catalogue):

CATALOGUE = [
    ("Claude Opus 5", 5.00, 25.00),
    ("Claude Sonnet 5", 2.00, 10.00),
    ("Claude Haiku 4.5", 1.00, 5.00),
]
IN_TOKENS, OUT_TOKENS = 4_000, 600

print(f"{'model':<20}{'in $/MTok':>11}{'out $/MTok':>12}{'ratio':>7}"
      f"{'per call':>11}{'input share':>13}")
for name, in_price, out_price in CATALOGUE:
    in_cost = IN_TOKENS / 1e6 * in_price
    out_cost = OUT_TOKENS / 1e6 * out_price
    total = in_cost + out_cost
    print(f"{name:<20}{in_price:>11.2f}{out_price:>12.2f}"
          f"{out_price / in_price:>7.0f}x{'$%.5f' % total:>11}"
          f"{in_cost / total:>13.0%}")

print()
out_share = 1 - (IN_TOKENS * 5.00) / (IN_TOKENS * 5.00 + OUT_TOKENS * 25.00)
print("output costs 5x input on every model.")
print(f"600 output tokens against 4,000 input is "
      f"{OUT_TOKENS / (IN_TOKENS + OUT_TOKENS):.0%} of the tokens "
      f"and {out_share:.0%} of the bill.")

model                 in $/MTok  out $/MTok  ratio   per call  input share
Claude Opus 5              5.00       25.00      5x   $0.03500          57%
Claude Sonnet 5            2.00       10.00      5x   $0.01400          57%
Claude Haiku 4.5           1.00        5.00      5x   $0.00700          57%

output costs 5x input on every model.
600 output tokens against 4,000 input is 13% of the tokens and 43% of the bill.

Line by line, for the first row:

  • Claude Opus 5 charges $5.00 per million input tokens and $25.00 per million output tokens.
  • 4,000 input tokens cost 4,000 / 1,000,000 × $5.00 = $0.020. 600 output tokens cost 600 / 1,000,000 × $25.00 = $0.015.
  • Together that is $0.035 for one call: the $0.03500 in the table.
  • The input is $0.020 of $0.035, which is the 57% in the last column.

The other two rows have different prices, but the same 5x ratio, so their input share is the same 57%. The last line puts the two halves side by side: 600 output tokens are 13% of the tokens and 43% of the bill.

Output is five times input, on every tier. A tier is one of the model sizes: Opus, Sonnet or Haiku. That ratio holds across the catalogue. It means that anything that shortens responses is working on the expensive side, such as §5.2's effort parameter (a setting for how much work the model puts into an answer) and §4's structured output.

Note also that the cost per token is the only price there is:

  • There is no per-request fee and no minimum.
  • There is no charge for a request that returns a refusal, the model declining to answer, before any output (§14.6).
  • The cost per token differs between input and output, and again for cache reads and writes (§9.3), which come up just below.

So a single blended "price per call", one average figure for every request, is always an approximation. It holds only for one particular traffic shape: one particular mix of short and long requests.

A newer model is not always more expensive. Claude Sonnet 5 costs less than the Sonnet 4.6 it succeeded (§2.2). Never assume that newer is dearer; look the price up.

The same call, split two ways:

Tokens are not the whole bill. There are three more meters that token arithmetic misses entirely, and §15.1 assembles all of them.

The first two are cache reads and writes (§9.3). A prompt cache keeps the start of a request that you send again and again, such as a long handbook, so the model does not have to work through it from scratch every time. In the picture, it is the long standard opening the office keeps on file. Reading from the cache costs 0.1× the input price, a tenth. Writing to it costs 1.25× the input price, for the standard cache that lasts five minutes. Reads and writes are two separate lines on the bill.

The third is server-tool fees (§7.1). A server tool is a tool that Anthropic runs for you, such as web search. Web search is billed per search, and not per token, so no token count will ever show it.

1.4 What Changes About Engineering

The properties in §1.1 break several habits that are correct everywhere else in this collection. Here are four sentences engineers say every day, and what each one means once a model is involved:

"It worked when I ran it"
Is one sample from a distribution. §13.1 shows that a genuinely 80%-correct prompt looks anywhere between perfect and broken across three trials — and that a 30-case eval comparing two prompts is close to a coin flip.
"The tests pass"
Requires a different kind of test. There is no assertion for "is this summary faithful". §13.4 grades what code can grade; §13.5 uses a model for the rest, and §13.6 validates that model against humans.
"The instructions say not to"
Is guidance to a component that produces text. Not a control. §14 is the whole argument, and §11.5 shows where the enforcement actually goes.
"Adding context helps"
Up to a point, then it hurts. Both cost and accuracy degrade as the window fills with material the model must sift. §9 is about deciding what is present.

A few words in that table need a meaning:

  • An eval, short for evaluation, is a fixed set of test questions with known good answers, run against your prompt and scored. A 30-case eval has thirty questions. With so few, the better of two prompts wins the comparison only a little more often than chance.
  • An assertion is a line in a test that checks one exact fact, such as "the total is 42". "This summary is faithful to the document" cannot be checked that way.
  • A control is something that makes an action impossible, such as a permission check in your code. An instruction in a prompt only makes the action less likely.
  • The window, or context window, is all the text the model is shown in one request.

In the picture, "it worked when I ran it" is one good reply from the writer. It says nothing about the next telegram.

Two habits do transfer, and they carry more weight here than usual.

Determinism where you can get it. You cannot make the model deterministic, but you can fix the test set, the ordering, the seeds and the clock. Then, when a number moves, you know it was the model.

A seed, from §1.1, is the starting number of a random-number generator. The same seed gives the same "random" numbers every time, and a different seed gives different ones:

import random

first = random.Random(7)
second = random.Random(7)
other = random.Random(8)
print([round(first.random(), 3) for _ in range(3)])
print([round(second.random(), 3) for _ in range(3)])
print([round(other.random(), 3) for _ in range(3)])

[0.324, 0.151, 0.651]
[0.324, 0.151, 0.651]
[0.227, 0.962, 0.126]

Line by line:

  • first and second both start from seed 7, so they print the same three numbers: 0.324, 0.151 and 0.651.
  • other starts from seed 8, so its numbers are different.

Every runnable example in this course does this, which is why they produce the same output every time. The toy model in §1.1 printed exactly 31.1% for "the dog" here, and it prints exactly that on your machine.

Layers that fail closed. "Fail closed" means that when a layer breaks, it blocks, and does not let things through. Think of a door lock that stays locked when its battery dies, instead of springing open. Defence in depth means several independent layers, each able to stop a bad action on its own, so that one failure does not let everything through. §14.8's argument is ordinary defence in depth, applied to a component that can be talked into things: text the model reads can contain instructions, and it may follow them (§14).

1.5 The Shape of a Real System

It is worth seeing, once, how little of a production LLM application is the model call. Production means the live system that real users depend on, as opposed to a demo on your laptop.

This program lists the ten parts that a request passes through in a typical application, who builds each one, and the section of this course that teaches it:

COMPONENTS = [
    ("input validation and screening", "yours", "§14.3"),
    ("retrieval: search, rank, assemble", "yours", "§10"),
    ("prompt construction and caching", "yours", "§3, §9.3"),
    ("THE MODEL CALL", "Anthropic", "§2"),
    ("stop-reason handling", "yours", "§2.6"),
    ("tool execution and authorisation", "yours", "§6.5, §14.4"),
    ("output validation", "yours", "§4.3"),
    ("citation and faithfulness checks", "yours", "§8.5, §10.7"),
    ("logging and cost accounting", "yours", "§15.5"),
    ("evaluation, offline and on live traffic", "yours", "§13, §15.7"),
]

yours = sum(owner == "yours" for _, owner, _ in COMPONENTS)
print(f"{'component':<42}{'owned by':<12}{'section'}")
for name, owner, section in COMPONENTS:
    print(f"{name:<42}{owner:<12}{section}")

print()
print(f"{yours} of {len(COMPONENTS)} components are yours to build.")
print("the model call is one line. Everything around it is the engineering.")

component                                 owned by    section
input validation and screening            yours       §14.3
retrieval: search, rank, assemble         yours       §10
prompt construction and caching           yours       §3, §9.3
THE MODEL CALL                            Anthropic   §2
stop-reason handling                      yours       §2.6
tool execution and authorisation          yours       §6.5, §14.4
output validation                         yours       §4.3
citation and faithfulness checks          yours       §8.5, §10.7
logging and cost accounting               yours       §15.5
evaluation, offline and on live traffic   yours       §13, §15.7

9 of 10 components are yours to build.
the model call is one line. Everything around it is the engineering.

Line by line:

  • Only one row belongs to Anthropic: the model call itself (§2). It is one line of code.
  • The other nine are yours. In order: checking what users send in, finding the documents to show the model, building the prompt, handling the stop reason (the API's note on why the model stopped writing, for example because it finished or because it reached the length limit you set), running tools and deciding whether each one is allowed, checking the reply, checking its citations, logging what each request cost, and evaluation.

In the picture, the writer is one person at the far end of the line. Your office is everyone else: the clerks who sort the post, check each reply, keep the ledger and act on the instructions.

The same ten parts, in the order a request meets them:

That list is also the shape of this course:

  • Sections 2–5 are about the model call itself: sending a request, writing the prompt, getting answers in a fixed shape, and letting the model think first.
  • §6–8 add capability: tools, tools Anthropic runs for you, and images and documents.
  • §9–10 decide what is in the window, including retrieval.
  • §11–12 build agents.
  • §13–15 are the discipline that makes it operable: measuring quality, guarding against misuse, and running it day to day.
  • §16 assembles one system out of all of it.

1.6 What Success Looks Like

A last framing before the mechanics, because it determines what you build.

The question "is the model good enough?" has no answer. The answerable version names three things:

  • a metric, the number you measure;
  • a population, the cases you measure it on;
  • a threshold, the value it must reach.

For example: "F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 tickets". A held-out set is kept aside, and never used while writing the prompt, so it cannot have been tuned to. (F1 is a single score that balances how many right answers you found against how many wrong ones you included.) In the picture, "is the writer any good?" has no answer, but "of these 100 letters, at least 85 replies must be right" does. §13.2 is about turning the first question into the second.

This program sorts six success criteria into the usable and the unusable, with the reason for each:

CRITERIA = [
    ("is the model good enough?", False, "no metric, no population, no threshold"),
    ("it should be accurate and fast", False, "two undefined words"),
    ("F1 >= 0.85 on 10,000 held-out tickets", True, "someone else can run this"),
    ("p95 time to first token < 900 ms", True, "a percentile, a metric, a bound"),
    ("< $0.012 per resolved conversation", True, "per WHAT is the load-bearing part"),
    ("0 outputs contain an email address", True, "checkable by a regex"),
]

print(f"{'criterion':<42}{'usable?':<10}{'why'}")
for text, usable, why in CRITERIA:
    print(f"{text:<42}{('yes' if usable else 'NO'):<10}{why}")

print()
usable = sum(c[1] for c in CRITERIA)
print(f"{usable} of {len(CRITERIA)} could be handed to a colleague who would "
      f"produce the same number you would.")

criterion                                 usable?   why
is the model good enough?                 NO        no metric, no population, no threshold
it should be accurate and fast            NO        two undefined words
F1 >= 0.85 on 10,000 held-out tickets     yes       someone else can run this
p95 time to first token < 900 ms          yes       a percentile, a metric, a bound
< $0.012 per resolved conversation        yes       per WHAT is the load-bearing part
0 outputs contain an email address        yes       checkable by a regex

4 of 6 could be handed to a colleague who would produce the same number you would.

Line by line:

  • The first two are NO. Neither names a number anyone could measure, so two people would argue about them forever.
  • "F1 >= 0.85 on 10,000 held-out tickets" names a metric, a population and a threshold. Someone else can run it.
  • "p95 time to first token < 900 ms" uses a percentile: p95 is the time that 95 of every 100 requests beat. Time to first token is how long you wait before the first piece of the reply arrives. And 900 ms, milliseconds, is the bound.
  • "< $0.012 per resolved conversation" stands or falls on its last words. A cost per request and a cost per resolved conversation are very different numbers, because one conversation can take many requests.
  • "0 outputs contain an email address" can be checked by a regex, a text pattern that a program searches for.

That last test is the whole definition. A criterion is usable when someone else can measure it and get your number. Everything else is a preference wearing a metric's clothes.

And a note on ordering that most projects get wrong. It is tempting to build the application first, and add evaluation once there is something to evaluate. The trouble is that without a measurement, you cannot tell whether any of your changes helped. You then spend the early weeks flying blind, which is exactly when the prompt is changing fastest and the improvements are largest. Build the smallest honest eval before the second prompt change, and not after the tenth.

Back to the puzzle at the start: one input, a thousand runs, five different sentences. A model is that, on a much larger scale. You will never make it give one answer. What you can do is measure, over many runs, how often its answers meet a criterion that someone else could check. Every section that follows is a way of moving that number.

Exercises

Exercise 1.1 — Estimate before you build. A support assistant answers from a 40,000-token handbook. 8,000 conversations a day, 3 turns each, 400-token answers. Estimate the monthly cost three ways — naive, cached, and cached on Sonnet 5 — and say what you would check before trusting any of them.

Solution 
HANDBOOK, QUESTION, ANSWER = 40_000, 60, 400
CONVERSATIONS, TURNS, DAYS = 8_000, 3, 30
OPUS_IN, OPUS_OUT = 5.00, 25.00
SONNET_IN, SONNET_OUT = 2.00, 10.00
CACHE_WRITE_MULT, CACHE_READ_MULT = 1.25, 0.10

turns = CONVERSATIONS * TURNS * DAYS
conversations = CONVERSATIONS * DAYS


def naive(in_price, out_price):
    return (HANDBOOK + QUESTION) * turns / 1e6 * in_price \
        + ANSWER * turns / 1e6 * out_price


def cached(in_price, out_price):
    """One cache write per conversation, reads on the remaining turns."""
    writes = HANDBOOK * conversations / 1e6 * in_price * CACHE_WRITE_MULT
    reads = HANDBOOK * conversations * (TURNS - 1) / 1e6 * in_price * CACHE_READ_MULT
    volatile = QUESTION * turns / 1e6 * in_price
    output = ANSWER * turns / 1e6 * out_price
    return writes + reads + volatile + output


ROWS = [("Opus 5, naive", naive(OPUS_IN, OPUS_OUT)),
        ("Opus 5, cached", cached(OPUS_IN, OPUS_OUT)),
        ("Sonnet 5, cached", cached(SONNET_IN, SONNET_OUT))]
base = ROWS[0][1]
print(f"{'configuration':<22}{'$/month':>12}{'vs naive':>11}{'per conversation':>19}")
for label, cost in ROWS:
    print(f"{label:<22}{'$' + format(cost, ',.0f'):>12}{cost / base:>10.0%}"
          f"{'$%.4f' % (cost / conversations):>19}")

print()
print(f"turns per month        : {turns:>10,}")
print(f"handbook tokens resent : {HANDBOOK * turns:>10,}")
print(f"...which is {HANDBOOK * turns / (HANDBOOK * turns + ANSWER * turns):.0%} "
      f"of all tokens, and it never changes")

configuration              $/month   vs naive   per conversation
Opus 5, naive             $151,416      100%            $0.6309
Opus 5, cached             $77,016       51%            $0.3209
Sonnet 5, cached           $30,806       20%            $0.1284

turns per month        :    720,000
handbook tokens resent : 28,800,000,000
...which is 99% of all tokens, and it never changes

Caching is the entire answer here, and the reason is structural. The handbook is the overwhelming majority of the tokens, it is byte-identical on every request, and it is resent three times per conversation. That is the textbook case from §9.3, and it is one parameter.

Sonnet on top is a further large cut, and unlike caching it is a quality decision. §13 is how you make it: run the eval on both, compare, and decide with the number in front of you. A support assistant answering from a supplied document is close to reading comprehension, which is where smaller models do well. But "close to" is a hypothesis and not a result.

Four things I would check before trusting any of this figure.

Whether the handbook actually fits and should. 40,000 tokens is a fifth of a 200k window and it fits comfortably. Per §10.1, that means retrieval is probably unnecessary. That is a useful conclusion to reach before building a pipeline, and this arithmetic is what reaches it.

Whether it changes. A handbook edited daily invalidates the cache daily. If it is edited quarterly, the 1-hour TTL (how long a cached entry lives) is worth considering (§9.4). The cost model is identical and the operational answer is not.

Whether three turns is real. The whole calculation scales with it, and the distribution matters more than the mean. If one conversation in ten runs to fifteen turns, those are a large share of the bill, and nothing above is sized for them.

The token counts themselves. count_tokens is free (§2.8), and it turns "40,000 tokens" from an assumption into a measurement. Everything here scales linearly with it.

What the estimate deliberately omits. It leaves out retries, failed requests, evaluation runs and development traffic. Evaluation in particular is a real line, because §13 argues for hundreds of cases per run, though §15.2's batch discount makes it half of what it looks like.

Exercise 1.2 — Which property is biting? Each symptom is caused by one of §1.1's four properties. Name it, and name the section that addresses it.

(a) The same question gets a good answer on Monday and a poor one on Tuesday, with no change deployed. (b) A customer is told their order will arrive Thursday. No date exists anywhere in the system. (c) The bill is four times the estimate, and request volume is unchanged. (d) An agent emailed a summary to an address that appeared in a document it read.

Solution 
DIAGNOSES = [
    ("a  good Monday, poor Tuesday", "it is a distribution", "§13",
     "not a regression — two samples. The fix is a measurement that "
     "distinguishes a real change from noise (13.9), not a code change."),
    ("b  invented delivery date", "it predicts, it does not know", "§14.5",
     "a plausible continuation of 'your order shipped' is a delivery date. "
     "Grounding and an explicit 'not in the record' escape hatch."),
    ("c  4x the bill, same volume", "it is stateless", "§9.1",
     "the conversation is resent every turn, so cost is quadratic in "
     "length. Longer conversations, not more of them."),
    ("d  emailed an address from a document", "it only emits tokens", "§14.4",
     "the model proposed; your executor disposed. The recipient must come "
     "from the session, never from an argument."),
]

for symptom, prop, section, why in DIAGNOSES:
    print(f"{symptom:<38}{prop:<32}{section}")
    print(f"{'':38}{why}")

a  good Monday, poor Tuesday          it is a distribution            §13
                                      not a regression — two samples. The fix is a measurement that distinguishes a real change from noise (13.9), not a code change.
b  invented delivery date             it predicts, it does not know   §14.5
                                      a plausible continuation of 'your order shipped' is a delivery date. Grounding and an explicit 'not in the record' escape hatch.
c  4x the bill, same volume           it is stateless                 §9.1
                                      the conversation is resent every turn, so cost is quadratic in length. Longer conversations, not more of them.
d  emailed an address from a document it only emits tokens            §14.4
                                      the model proposed; your executor disposed. The recipient must come from the session, never from an argument.

(a) is the one that wastes the most time in practice, because it presents as a regression and sends you hunting for a cause that does not exist. Two samples from the same distribution differ, and that is the mechanism and not a fault. The correct response is not to investigate Tuesday but to build the instrument that would tell you whether Tuesday is actually worse. §13.9's confidence intervals exist precisely for this, and until they exist "it got worse" is not a claim anyone can evaluate.

(b) is the most damaging, because a fluent invented date is indistinguishable from a real one, both to the customer and in your logs. Note that it is not a lie the model chose to tell: "your order shipped on the 21st" makes a delivery date a highly probable continuation. §14.5's fixes all work the same way. They narrow what the model is sampling from, by restricting it to the source and giving it somewhere to go when the answer is absent.

(c) is the most surprising and the most common. Statelessness means the conversation is resent in full on every turn. A system whose users started having longer conversations therefore has a superlinear cost increase (faster than the volume of conversations) with no change in request volume at all. §9.1's table shows ten turns costing 1.95× what ten independent requests would. The fix is caching first, then compaction.

(d) is the one to be frightened of. Nothing malfunctioned: a document contained an address, the model proposed sending to it, and an executor sent. Everything worked exactly as built. The model proposes and your code disposes. A recipient that comes from an argument and not from the session is a hole with a schema around it, and §14.4's least-privilege argument (give a component only the access it needs) is the only defence that does not depend on noticing the attack.

The pattern worth taking from this exercise. Three of the four look like bugs and are not. They are the properties of the component behaving as documented. Recognising which property is biting tells you which section to open, and, more usefully, tells you whether to look for a defect at all.

SECTION 2

The Messages API

There is one endpoint. Everything in this course, including tools, thinking, retrieval, agents and structured output, is either a parameter on POST /v1/messages or a block type in its response. Learning that request and response properly is the highest-leverage hour in the subject, because every later feature is a variation on a shape you already know.

This section is that shape: what goes in, what comes back, how it fails, and how to read the numbers on it.

2.1 The Smallest Real Request

Three parameters are required: model, max_tokens and messages. Everything else is optional.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name three primary colours."}],
)

print("id          :", response.id)
print("type        :", response.type)
print("role        :", response.role)
print("model       :", response.model)
print("stop_reason :", response.stop_reason)
print("content     :", response.content)
print("text        :", response.content[0].text)
print("usage       :", response.usage.input_tokens, "in,",
      response.usage.output_tokens, "out")

id          : msg_01Ex
type        : message
role        : assistant
model       : claude-opus-5
stop_reason : end_turn
content     : [TextBlock(citations=None, text='Red, blue and yellow.', type='text')]
text        : Red, blue and yellow.
usage       : 15 in, 9 out

Four things about that, each of which matters later.

max_tokens is required and is a hard ceiling on the response, not a target. It does not make the model verbose, and it does not reserve capacity. Set it too low and the answer is cut off mid-sentence. §2.6 shows what that looks like and how to notice.

Each entry in messages carries a message role, and only two are valid here: user and assistant. The message role alternates, and §2.3 shows what happens when it does not.

content is a list of blocks, not a string. Here there is one text block. With tools there are tool_use blocks, with thinking there are thinking blocks, and with citations the text blocks carry a citations array. Code that does response.content[0].text works until the day it does not, and that is the day you enable something. Iterate over the blocks and check block.type.

The API key comes from the environment. anthropic.Anthropic() with no arguments reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Pass it explicitly only if you have a reason, because hard-coding it in source is the first item on every security review. The SDK also sets the anthropic-version header for you, to 2023-06-01, which pins the wire format (the exact shape of requests and responses) and not the model. Raw HTTP callers must send anthropic-version themselves, and a request without it is rejected.

There is no session. This response is not stored anywhere you can refer to. The next request must carry the whole conversation, which is §2.3.

2.2 Model IDs

The model string is not a family name. It is a specific model, and the rules changed in a way that catches people returning to the API.

From the 4.6 generation onward, a dateless ID is a pinned snapshot. claude-opus-5 is not an alias that drifts to whatever is newest. It maps to one fixed model whose weights and configuration are never updated. When there is an improved version, it ships under a new ID.

Before 4.6, IDs carried a snapshot date (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001). The Claude API also accepted shorter aliases (claude-sonnet-4-5) that pointed at the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version. Those aliases do move.

CATALOGUE = [
    # (id, tier, input $/MTok, output $/MTok)
    ("claude-opus-5", "Opus", 5.00, 25.00),
    ("claude-opus-4-8", "Opus", 5.00, 25.00),
    ("claude-sonnet-5", "Sonnet", 2.00, 10.00),
    ("claude-sonnet-4-6", "Sonnet", 3.00, 15.00),
    ("claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", "Haiku", 1.00, 5.00),
    ("claude-fable-5", "Fable", 10.00, 50.00),
]

TYPICAL_IN, TYPICAL_OUT = 4_000, 600

print(f"{'model id':<28}{'tier':<9}{'in':>7}{'out':>7}{'per call':>11}")
for model_id, tier, in_price, out_price in CATALOGUE:
    per_call = TYPICAL_IN / 1e6 * in_price + TYPICAL_OUT / 1e6 * out_price
    print(f"{model_id:<28}{tier:<9}{in_price:>7.2f}{out_price:>7.2f}"
          f"{'$%.5f' % per_call:>11}")

cheapest = min(CATALOGUE, key=lambda m: m[2] * TYPICAL_IN + m[3] * TYPICAL_OUT)
dearest = max(CATALOGUE, key=lambda m: m[2] * TYPICAL_IN + m[3] * TYPICAL_OUT)
ratio = ((dearest[2] * TYPICAL_IN + dearest[3] * TYPICAL_OUT)
         / (cheapest[2] * TYPICAL_IN + cheapest[3] * TYPICAL_OUT))
print(f"\nspread across the catalogue: {ratio:.0f}x")
print("note claude-sonnet-5 is CHEAPER than claude-sonnet-4-6 — newer is not dearer")

model id                    tier          in    out   per call
claude-opus-5               Opus        5.00  25.00   $0.03500
claude-opus-4-8             Opus        5.00  25.00   $0.03500
claude-sonnet-5             Sonnet      2.00  10.00   $0.01400
claude-sonnet-4-6           Sonnet      3.00  15.00   $0.02100
claude-haiku-4-5-20251001   Haiku       1.00   5.00   $0.00700
claude-fable-5              Fable      10.00  50.00   $0.07000

spread across the catalogue: 10x
note claude-sonnet-5 is CHEAPER than claude-sonnet-4-6 — newer is not dearer

That last line is worth internalising, because the intuition it violates is strong. A newer model is not always more expensive: Sonnet 5 costs less than the Sonnet 4.6 it succeeds. Never assume a newer model costs more, and never assume an older one is cheaper.

Better still, do not hard-code the catalogue at all.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

page = client.models.list(limit=5)
for model in page.data:
    print(f"{model.id:<28} {model.display_name}")

claude-opus-5                Claude Opus 5
claude-sonnet-5              Claude Sonnet 5
claude-fable-5               Claude Fable 5
claude-opus-4-8              Claude Opus 4.8
claude-haiku-4-5-20251001    Claude Haiku 4.5

The Models API returns what exists right now, along with each model's max_input_tokens, max_tokens and a capabilities object. A model-selection routine that reads this at start-up keeps working when a new model lands. A hard-coded list quietly keeps using last year's.

The models api is the mechanism, and reading it at start-up and not hard-coding a table is the habit worth forming. A models api call costs nothing, and its answer is current.

Two companion sources are worth knowing when choosing a model. Choosing a model is a decision with three inputs: capability, price and latency (how long you wait). Only the first is hard to measure. Each model publishes a model card describing what it was trained and evaluated for. A model card is the document to read when deciding whether a model suits a domain and not whether it fits a budget, and it is the only source that describes evaluated behaviour and not mechanics. And model deprecation is a schedule you can subscribe to and not something you discover. A model deprecation notice names the retirement date and the migration path for older ids. claude-opus-4-1 and claude-sonnet-4 are retired on the Claude API and remain available on some partner platforms. That is exactly the sort of asymmetry that turns into an outage for whoever assumed otherwise.

2.3 Turns: The Conversation Is a List You Resend

The API is stateless. A multi-turn conversation is a list of alternating user and assistant messages that you own and resend in full.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "My favourite colour is teal."}]

first = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=256,
                               messages=messages)
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": first.content})
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "What did I just say?"})

second = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=256,
                                messages=messages)

print("turn 1 in/out:", first.usage.input_tokens, "/", first.usage.output_tokens)
print("turn 2 in/out:", second.usage.input_tokens, "/", second.usage.output_tokens)
print("answer       :", second.content[0].text)
print("messages sent on turn 2:", len(messages))
for message in messages:
    preview = message["content"]
    if not isinstance(preview, str):
        preview = "".join(b.text for b in preview if b.type == "text")
    print(f"  {message['role']:<10} {preview[:44]}")

turn 1 in/out: 16 / 8
turn 2 in/out: 44 / 11
answer       : You said your favourite colour is teal.
messages sent on turn 2: 3
  user       My favourite colour is teal.
  assistant  Teal is a lovely choice.
  user       What did I just say?

Append response.content, not a string. The list of blocks is what the API returns and what it expects back. Flattening it to text works for a plain conversation. It silently destroys tool calls, thinking blocks and compaction blocks (summaries the API writes to shrink a long conversation) the moment you use any of them, and §9.7 warns about exactly that mistake.

Roles must alternate, starting with user. Two consecutive user messages is a 400 (an HTTP error meaning the request itself is invalid). When you have several things to say, put them in one message as multiple content blocks.

Input tokens grow every turn, and you pay for all of them, every time. That is §9.1's quadratic growth, and it is visible right here in the two usage lines.

2.4 The System Prompt

The system prompt is a separate top-level parameter, and not a message with role: "system". It is where instructions, persona and stable context go.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# A plain string is the common form.
simple = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=256,
    system="You are a terse assistant. Answer in one sentence.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Why is the sky blue?"}],
)

# A list of blocks is the form that lets you place cache breakpoints (9.4).
structured = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=256,
    system=[
        {"type": "text", "text": "You are a terse assistant."},
        {"type": "text", "text": "House style: British spelling.",
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Why is the sky blue?"}],
)

print("string form :", simple.content[0].text)
print("block form  :", structured.content[0].text)
print("both are the same parameter, and only the block form can be cached")

string form : Sunlight scatters more strongly at short wavelengths, so we see blue.
block form  : Short wavelengths scatter most, so the sky looks blue.
both are the same parameter, and only the block form can be cached

Two practical notes. The system prompt is not a message in messages, and putting {"role": "system", ...} there is a 400. There is one exception, the mid-conversation system message covered in §9.5, which is a different mechanism for a different purpose. And the system prompt is not a security boundary, and §14 is the whole argument.

2.5 Content Blocks

The content of a user message can be a plain string or a list of blocks. The list form is what lets one turn carry an image, a document, a tool result and a question together.

BLOCK_TYPES = [
    ("text", "user + assistant", "prose", "always"),
    ("image", "user", "vision input", "§8.2"),
    ("document", "user", "PDFs and text files", "§8.3"),
    ("search_result", "user", "RAG passages with citations", "§10.7"),
    ("tool_use", "assistant", "the model asking for a call", "§6.3"),
    ("tool_result", "user", "your answer to that call", "§6.5"),
    ("server_tool_use", "assistant", "a tool Anthropic ran", "§7.1"),
    ("thinking", "assistant", "reasoning before the answer", "§5.2"),
    ("compaction", "assistant", "a server-written summary", "§9.7"),
]

print(f"{'block type':<18}{'appears in':<20}{'what it is':<32}{'where'}")
for name, where, what, section in BLOCK_TYPES:
    print(f"{name:<18}{where:<20}{what:<32}{section}")

assistant_only = [n for n, w, _, _ in BLOCK_TYPES if w == "assistant"]
print(f"\nblocks you never construct, only read: {', '.join(assistant_only)}")

block type        appears in          what it is                      where
text              user + assistant    prose                           always
image             user                vision input                    §8.2
document          user                PDFs and text files             §8.3
search_result     user                RAG passages with citations     §10.7
tool_use          assistant           the model asking for a call     §6.3
tool_result       user                your answer to that call        §6.5
server_tool_use   assistant           a tool Anthropic ran            §7.1
thinking          assistant           reasoning before the answer     §5.2
compaction        assistant           a server-written summary        §9.7

blocks you never construct, only read: tool_use, server_tool_use, thinking, compaction

The division in that last line is the one to hold on to. Assistant blocks are read, not written. You pass them back verbatim as part of the conversation, but you never build one yourself. User blocks are the ones you construct.

2.6 Stop Reasons

stop_reason says why generation ended, and handling it is the difference between an application that degrades gracefully and one that shows users half a sentence.

end_turn
Finished naturally. Use the response. The only stop reason that needs no handling.
max_tokens
Hit your ceiling. The answer is truncated, possibly mid-word. Raise max_tokens or continue the response — never present it as complete.
stop_sequence
One of your stop_sequences fired. A stop sequence is a string that ends generation the moment the model emits it; read the stop_sequence field to see which stop sequence fired. The sequence itself is not included in the output.
tool_use
The model wants a tool run. §6.4's loop. This is the one your agent keys on.
pause_turn
A server-tool loop hit its iteration limit. Append the assistant content and re-send. §7.2.
refusal
The model declined. An HTTP 200 with empty content and a stop_details object. §14.6.
model_context_window_exceeded
The response filled the window. Treat it as truncated; the conversation has outgrown the model.
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


def ask(question, max_tokens):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=max_tokens,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    )
    text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    return response.stop_reason, response.usage.output_tokens, text


for limit in (2048, 24):
    stop, out_tokens, text = ask("Explain the water cycle.", limit)
    complete = stop == "end_turn"
    print(f"max_tokens={limit:<6} stop_reason={stop:<12} "
          f"output={out_tokens:<5} complete={complete}")
    print(f"  {text[-52:]!r}")

max_tokens=2048   stop_reason=end_turn     output=31    complete=True
  'tation, and runs off or infiltrates back to the sea.'
max_tokens=24     stop_reason=max_tokens   output=24    complete=False
  'rface of the Earth. Water evaporates from oceans and'

Look at the truncated one. It ends mid-sentence, it is grammatical up to the cut, and nothing in the text says it is incomplete. A user shown that has no way to know. stop_reason is the only signal, which is why every loop in this course branches on it and not on the presence of text.

2.7 Streaming

For anything a person waits on, stream. Time to first token is what a user experiences as speed, and it is a fraction of the time to the last token.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "List three primary colours."}],
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="")
    print()
    final = stream.get_final_message()

print("stop_reason:", final.stop_reason)
print("output tokens:", final.usage.output_tokens)

Red, blue and yellow.
stop_reason: end_turn
output tokens: 9

stream.text_stream is the convenience path and covers most needs. Underneath it is a sequence of typed server-sent events (small messages the server pushes as it generates). Knowing their shape matters when you need more than text, such as a token counter, a tool-call renderer or a progress indicator.

EVENT_FLOW = [
    ("message_start", "a Message with empty content and initial usage"),
    ("content_block_start", "one per block, carrying its index"),
    ("content_block_delta", "many; text_delta, input_json_delta or thinking_delta"),
    ("content_block_stop", "one per block"),
    ("message_delta", "top-level changes: stop_reason, and CUMULATIVE usage"),
    ("message_stop", "the end"),
]
for name, what in EVENT_FLOW:
    print(f"{name:<22}{what}")

print()
print("also possible at any point:")
print(f"{'ping':<22}keep-alive; ignore it")
print(f"{'error':<22}a mid-stream failure AFTER a 200 was returned")

message_start         a Message with empty content and initial usage
content_block_start   one per block, carrying its index
content_block_delta   many; text_delta, input_json_delta or thinking_delta
content_block_stop    one per block
message_delta         top-level changes: stop_reason, and CUMULATIVE usage
message_stop          the end

also possible at any point:
ping                  keep-alive; ignore it
error                 a mid-stream failure AFTER a 200 was returned

Three traps live in that list.

Usage in message_delta is cumulative, not a delta (an increment), despite the event name. Adding successive values inflates your token counts.

Errors can arrive mid-stream, after a 200. The HTTP status was already sent, so standard error handling never sees it. An overloaded_error that would have been a 529 arrives as an error event instead. If your streaming code has no branch for that event type, an overload looks like a truncated answer.

New event types will be added. Handle unknown types by ignoring them and not by raising, or a future addition breaks your client.

Streaming is also a practical necessity and not just a nicety at large max_tokens. A long non-streaming request risks an HTTP timeout, and §11.3's task-budget example streams for exactly this reason.

2.8 Counting Tokens

Token counting has its own endpoint. count_tokens takes the same request shape and returns what it would cost in input tokens. It is free, and it is the only honest way to answer "will this fit".

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

REQUEST = {
    "model": "claude-opus-5",
    "system": "You are a concise assistant.",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise the water cycle."}],
}

count = client.messages.count_tokens(**REQUEST)
print("input tokens:", count.input_tokens)

WINDOW = 200_000
RESERVED_FOR_OUTPUT = 4_096
headroom = WINDOW - count.input_tokens - RESERVED_FOR_OUTPUT
print(f"headroom in a {WINDOW:,}-token window: {headroom:,} tokens")
print("fits:", headroom > 0)

input tokens: 26
headroom in a 200,000-token window: 195,878 tokens
fits: True

Budget for the output as well as the input. The context window holds both. A request that uses 199,000 of a 200,000-token window leaves a thousand tokens to answer in, and you will meet max_tokens or model_context_window_exceeded and not a helpful error.

Token counting includes tools and system, which is how you discover that a tool surface is larger than you assumed (§6.9).

2.9 Errors, Retries and Rate Limits

Every api error has an HTTP status and a machine-readable type, and the SDK raises a typed exception per status. Catching Exception and retrying blindly is how a 400 becomes an infinite loop.

ERRORS = [
    (400, "invalid_request_error", "malformed request, or a spend limit", False),
    (401, "authentication_error", "bad, revoked or expired key", False),
    (402, "billing_error", "payment details need attention", False),
    (403, "permission_error", "key lacks access to the resource", False),
    (404, "not_found_error", "wrong path or resource id", False),
    (413, "request_too_large", "over 32 MB on the Messages API", False),
    (429, "rate_limit_error", "rate limit or spend cap", True),
    (500, "api_error", "internal error", True),
    (504, "timeout_error", "timed out; stream instead", True),
    (529, "overloaded_error", "temporarily overloaded", True),
]

print(f"{'status':>7}  {'type':<24}{'retry?':<9}{'meaning'}")
for status, kind, meaning, retry in ERRORS:
    print(f"{status:>7}  {kind:<24}{('yes' if retry else 'NO'):<9}{meaning}")

retryable = [s for s, _, _, r in ERRORS if r]
print(f"\nretryable: {retryable}")
print("everything else is a bug in your request; retrying cannot fix it")

status  type                    retry?   meaning
    400  invalid_request_error   NO       malformed request, or a spend limit
    401  authentication_error    NO       bad, revoked or expired key
    402  billing_error           NO       payment details need attention
    403  permission_error        NO       key lacks access to the resource
    404  not_found_error         NO       wrong path or resource id
    413  request_too_large       NO       over 32 MB on the Messages API
    429  rate_limit_error        yes      rate limit or spend cap
    500  api_error               yes      internal error
    504  timeout_error           yes      timed out; stream instead
    529  overloaded_error        yes      temporarily overloaded

retryable: [429, 500, 504, 529]
everything else is a bug in your request; retrying cannot fix it

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

try:
    client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}],
    )
except anthropic.RateLimitError as exc:
    print("type       :", type(exc).__name__)
    print("status     :", exc.status_code)
    print("retry-after:", exc.response.headers.get("retry-after"), "seconds")
    print("remaining  :",
          exc.response.headers.get("anthropic-ratelimit-input-tokens-remaining"))

type       : RateLimitError
status     : 429
retry-after: 12 seconds
remaining  : 0

The type is the field to branch on and not the message, because an api error's message is prose that may be reworded while its type is stable.

The SDK already retries for you. It retries transient failures twice by default, with exponential backoff (waits that get longer each time), and it honours retry-after. Configure it with max_retries and do not write your own loop. Disable it (max_retries=0) only when you have a reason, such as an outer idempotency layer.

Honour retry-after and do not guess. It says how long to wait, and retrying earlier fails. Blind exponential backoff without it makes an overload worse for everybody.

One 429 is not like another. A rate-limit 429 carries retry-after and clears. A spend-cap 429 has no retry-after and keeps failing until access resumes, so a retry loop on it spins forever. Branch on the header's presence.

The anthropic-ratelimit-* headers are on every response, not just failures. Reading anthropic-ratelimit-input-tokens-remaining on success lets you slow down before you are throttled. That is a much better experience than discovering the limit by hitting it.

2.10 Reading usage

usage is the meter, and it grows a field every time a feature is added. Reading it properly is how cost tracking stays correct.

class Usage:
    """The shape of a usage object with everything populated at once."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.input_tokens = 42
        self.output_tokens = 380
        self.cache_creation_input_tokens = 0
        self.cache_read_input_tokens = 18_400
        self.server_tool_use = {"web_search_requests": 2}


u = Usage()
PRICES = {"input": 5.00, "output": 25.00, "cache_write": 6.25, "cache_read": 0.50}
SEARCH_FEE_PER_1000 = 10.00

total_input = (u.input_tokens + u.cache_creation_input_tokens
               + u.cache_read_input_tokens)
cost = (u.input_tokens / 1e6 * PRICES["input"]
        + u.cache_creation_input_tokens / 1e6 * PRICES["cache_write"]
        + u.cache_read_input_tokens / 1e6 * PRICES["cache_read"]
        + u.output_tokens / 1e6 * PRICES["output"]
        + u.server_tool_use["web_search_requests"] / 1000 * SEARCH_FEE_PER_1000)

print(f"input_tokens (after the last breakpoint) : {u.input_tokens:>8,}")
print(f"cache_creation_input_tokens              : "
      f"{u.cache_creation_input_tokens:>8,}")
print(f"cache_read_input_tokens                  : "
      f"{u.cache_read_input_tokens:>8,}")
print(f"TOTAL input tokens processed             : {total_input:>8,}")
print(f"output_tokens                            : {u.output_tokens:>8,}")
print(f"web searches                             : "
      f"{u.server_tool_use['web_search_requests']:>8,}")
print(f"\ncost of this one request                 : ${cost:.5f}")
print(f"of which server-tool fees                : "
      f"${u.server_tool_use['web_search_requests'] / 1000 * SEARCH_FEE_PER_1000:.5f}"
      f"  ({u.server_tool_use['web_search_requests'] / 1000 * SEARCH_FEE_PER_1000 / cost:.0%})")

input_tokens (after the last breakpoint) :       42
cache_creation_input_tokens              :        0
cache_read_input_tokens                  :   18,400
TOTAL input tokens processed             :   18,442
output_tokens                            :      380
web searches                             :        2

cost of this one request                 : $0.03891
of which server-tool fees                : $0.02000  (51%)

input_tokens is not the total input. It counts only what came after the last cache breakpoint. The total is the sum of the three input fields, and a cost dashboard reading input_tokens alone will report a collapse the day caching is switched on.

Server-tool fees are a separate meter and, as that percentage shows, can be most of the bill on a search-heavy request. §15 assembles all of it into one model.

usage.iterations appears when compaction is enabled (§9.7), and the top-level fields then exclude the compaction pass. Any cost tracking has to sum the iterations instead.

Exercises

Exercise 2.1 — Fix five bugs. This helper has five distinct defects. Find them all.

def chat(client, history, question):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": question})
    try:
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-3-opus",
            max_tokens=100,
            temperature=0.7,
            messages=history,
        )
    except Exception:
        return chat(client, history, question)
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content[0].text})
    return response.content[0].text
Solution 
import anthropic


class Truncated(Exception):
    pass


def chat(client, history, question, *, model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=2048):
    """Five fixes, each addressing a distinct failure."""
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": question})

    # 2. Retry only what is retryable, and let the SDK do the backoff.
    try:
        response = client.messages.create(
            model=model,               # 1. a model that exists, and pinned
            max_tokens=max_tokens,     # 4. room to answer
            messages=history,
        )                              # 3. no temperature: it was removed
    except anthropic.APIStatusError as exc:
        history.pop()                  # do not leave a dangling user turn
        raise

    # 5. append the BLOCKS, and branch on stop_reason
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
        raise Truncated(f"answer cut off after {response.usage.output_tokens} tokens")
    return text


FIXES = [
    ("model", "claude-3-opus (retired, 404)", "a pinned, current id"),
    ("retries", "except Exception: recurse forever", "let the SDK retry; re-raise"),
    ("sampling", "temperature=0.7 (removed; TypeError)", "omitted entirely"),
    ("max_tokens", "100 — about two sentences", "2048, and a parameter"),
    ("history", "appends content[0].text", "appends the whole block list"),
    ("truncation", "not checked at all", "raises on stop_reason=max_tokens"),
]
print(f"{'aspect':<12}{'was':<38}{'now'}")
for aspect, was, now in FIXES:
    print(f"{aspect:<12}{was:<38}{now}")
print(f"\n{len(FIXES)} changes for 5 defects: the missing stop_reason check and the")
print("string append are two halves of the same bug, and both had to be fixed")

aspect      was                                   now
model       claude-3-opus (retired, 404)          a pinned, current id
retries     except Exception: recurse forever     let the SDK retry; re-raise
sampling    temperature=0.7 (removed; TypeError)  omitted entirely
max_tokens  100 — about two sentences             2048, and a parameter
history     appends content[0].text               appends the whole block list
truncation  not checked at all                    raises on stop_reason=max_tokens

6 changes for 5 defects: the missing stop_reason check and the
string append are two halves of the same bug, and both had to be fixed

1. claude-3-opus is not a model ID. The Claude 3 generation is retired, and even when it existed the ID carried a snapshot date. This request fails with a 404 every time. It is worth noting why this bug is so common: model IDs are the part of an integration most likely to be copied from an old blog post.

2. except Exception: return chat(...) is an unbounded retry on every failure. That line has three separate problems. It retries a 400, which can never succeed, so a malformed request becomes an infinite loop. It uses recursion, so a persistent failure ends in a RecursionError and not a useful message. And it retries after appending the user turn, so each attempt appends the question again, and the history grows on every retry, making the request larger and more expensive as it fails. The SDK already retries transient failures twice with exponential backoff, honouring retry-after, so the right amount of retry logic here is none.

3. temperature=0.7 is rejected outright. Sampling parameters were removed from the current models' request surface, and Messages.create() raises TypeError on an unexpected keyword. This is the single most likely defect in any code written against an older version of this API, and it is the reason to write examples against the SDK and not from memory.

4. max_tokens=100 truncates nearly every real answer. It is a ceiling and not a target, so raising it costs nothing unless the model actually uses the tokens. A hundred is roughly two sentences.

5. response.content[0].text twice over. Appending the extracted string and not the block list means the history loses everything that is not text. Index zero is also not reliably the text block once the model narrates or thinks. Combined with the missing stop_reason check, a truncated answer is appended to history as though complete, and the model then continues a conversation in which it appears to have said something it did not finish.

One judgement call. Raising on max_tokens is deliberate and not obviously right, because some applications would rather return the partial text with a flag. What is not defensible is returning it as though it were complete, which is what the original does.

Exercise 2.2 — Budget a request. You have a 200,000-token window, a 3,200-token system prompt, 34 tool definitions totalling 3,230 tokens, and a conversation that grows by about 1,100 tokens per turn. You need 4,000 tokens of output. How many turns before you have a problem, and what do you do about it?

Solution 
WINDOW = 200_000
SYSTEM, TOOLS, PER_TURN, OUTPUT = 3_200, 3_230, 1_100, 4_000

fixed = SYSTEM + TOOLS
budget = WINDOW - fixed - OUTPUT
turns_available = budget // PER_TURN

print(f"window                    : {WINDOW:>8,}")
print(f"fixed (system + tools)    : {fixed:>8,}")
print(f"reserved for output       : {OUTPUT:>8,}")
print(f"left for conversation     : {budget:>8,}")
print(f"turns before it overflows : {turns_available:>8,}")
print()

# Where the pain actually starts: cost, long before capacity.
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00
cumulative = 0
print(f"{'turn':>6}{'context':>10}{'cost so far':>14}")
for turn in (1, 20, 50, 100, 175):
    context = fixed + turn * PER_TURN
    cumulative = sum(fixed + t * PER_TURN for t in range(1, turn + 1))
    print(f"{turn:>6}{context:>10,}{'$%.2f' % (cumulative / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>14}")

print()
# Caching the fixed prefix bills it at 0.10x. What that saves depends entirely on
# how much of the request the fixed part still is — which shrinks every turn.
print(f"{'turn':>6}{'context':>10}{'cached cost':>13}{'saving':>9}")
for turn in (1, 20, 100):
    conversation = turn * PER_TURN
    plain = fixed + conversation
    cached = fixed * 0.10 + conversation
    print(f"{turn:>6}{plain:>10,}{cached:>13,.0f}{1 - cached / plain:>9.0%}")
print("caching the fixed part matters most early; by turn 100 the conversation")
