print("itself is the bill, which is what compaction (9.7) is for")

window                    :  200,000
fixed (system + tools)    :    6,430
reserved for output       :    4,000
left for conversation     :  189,570
turns before it overflows :      172

  turn   context   cost so far
     1     7,530         $0.04
    20    28,430         $1.80
    50    61,430         $8.62
   100   116,430        $30.99
   175   198,930        $90.33

  turn   context  cached cost   saving
     1     7,530        1,743      77%
    20    28,430       22,643      20%
   100   116,430      110,643       5%
caching the fixed part matters most early; by turn 100 the conversation
itself is the bill, which is what compaction (9.7) is for

Capacity is not the binding constraint, and that is the answer. The window holds around 175 turns, which almost no conversation reaches. Long before that, two other things bite.

Cost. By turn 100 the conversation has cost $31 in input tokens alone, and by turn 175 it is $90, for a single conversation. It is still growing quadratically (§9.1), so the last 75 turns cost twice what the first 100 did. This is where the pain is felt, and it is felt as a bill and not as an error.

Quality. A context of 100,000 tokens of accumulated conversation is one in which the relevant part is a small fraction of the whole. Response quality degrades before capacity runs out, which is why §9.7 recommends compaction on a trigger well below the window and not at it.

What I would do, in order. Cache the fixed 6,430 tokens (§9.3). That is one parameter, and it removes most of the cost of the part that never changes. But read the second table before assuming that is the answer: it saves 77% of a turn-1 request and only 5% by turn 100, because by then the conversation dwarfs the prefix. So also enable compaction with a trigger around 150,000 (§9.7), which is what actually bounds the growth. And reserve output explicitly, so you do not discover the limit through a model_context_window_exceeded.

And measure rather than model. This whole calculation rests on "about 1,100 tokens per turn", which is an estimate. count_tokens is free and gives the real figure for a real conversation. The arithmetic above is for deciding whether to bother, not for setting the trigger.

Exercise 2.3 — Write the retry policy. Given §2.9's error table, write a should_retry(exc) and say what you deliberately left out.

Solution 
RETRYABLE_STATUSES = {429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 529}


class FakeResponse:
    def __init__(self, headers):
        self.headers = headers


class FakeError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, status, headers=None):
        self.status_code = status
        self.response = FakeResponse(headers or {})


def should_retry(exc, attempt, max_attempts=3):
    """Returns (retry, seconds_to_wait, why)."""
    status = getattr(exc, "status_code", None)
    if status not in RETRYABLE_STATUSES:
        return False, 0, f"{status} is not transient; retrying cannot fix it"
    if attempt >= max_attempts:
        return False, 0, f"attempt {attempt} of {max_attempts} exhausted"

    headers = getattr(getattr(exc, "response", None), "headers", {}) or {}
    retry_after = headers.get("retry-after")

    # A 429 with no retry-after is the spend-cap case: it does NOT clear.
    if status == 429 and retry_after is None:
        return False, 0, "429 without retry-after: spend cap, not a rate limit"

    if retry_after is not None:
        return True, float(retry_after), "honouring retry-after"
    return True, min(2 ** attempt, 30), "exponential backoff"


CASES = [
    ("400 bad request", FakeError(400), 1),
    ("401 bad key", FakeError(401), 1),
    ("429 rate limited", FakeError(429, {"retry-after": "12"}), 1),
    ("429 spend cap", FakeError(429), 1),
    ("529 overloaded", FakeError(529), 1),
    ("529 overloaded", FakeError(529), 2),
    ("529 overloaded", FakeError(529), 3),
]
for label, exc, attempt in CASES:
    retry, wait, why = should_retry(exc, attempt)
    print(f"{label:<20} attempt {attempt}  "
          f"{'RETRY in %5.1fs' % wait if retry else 'give up      ':<16}  {why}")

400 bad request      attempt 1  give up           400 is not transient; retrying cannot fix it
401 bad key          attempt 1  give up           401 is not transient; retrying cannot fix it
429 rate limited     attempt 1  RETRY in  12.0s   honouring retry-after
429 spend cap        attempt 1  give up           429 without retry-after: spend cap, not a rate limit
529 overloaded       attempt 1  RETRY in   2.0s   exponential backoff
529 overloaded       attempt 2  RETRY in   4.0s   exponential backoff
529 overloaded       attempt 3  give up           attempt 3 of 3 exhausted

The spend-cap 429 is the case that makes this exercise worth doing. Two 429s that look identical to any status-code check behave completely differently. One carries retry-after and clears in seconds, and the other has no such header and keeps failing until access resumes. A policy that treats them the same either spins forever on the spend cap or gives up needlessly on the rate limit. Branching on the header's presence is the whole distinction.

retry-after overrides your backoff, always. It is the server telling you when it will accept the request. An exponential curve that fires earlier fails and adds load.

What I deliberately left out, and why each matters.

Jitter. Every client backing off on the same curve retries in the same instant, so real backoff adds randomness (jitter). It is omitted here only to keep the output deterministic, following §11.3's determinism rule, and any production version needs it.

Idempotency. This policy retries a request that may have already been processed. For a plain completion that is harmless. For anything with a side effect it is not, and the fix lives above this function: an idempotency key (a unique token that makes a repeated request safe), which the Backend and API Design course develops properly.

A circuit breaker. Retrying into a sustained outage is how a client turns a degraded service into a down one. After a threshold of consecutive failures the right move is to stop calling and fail fast. Networking and HTTP covers the pattern.

And the honest conclusion: you probably should not write this at all. The SDK retries transient failures twice by default, with exponential backoff, honouring retry-after, and max_retries configures it. The reason to build your own is a requirement the default does not meet, such as a circuit breaker, an idempotency layer or per-endpoint policy. The reason to understand it is that you still have to handle what the SDK gives up on.

SECTION 3

Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering has an unfortunate reputation, and half of it is earned. There is a version that is superstition: magic phrases, threats, offers of tips. And there is a version that is ordinary technical writing under an unusual constraint. Your reader is extremely capable, has no context about your organisation, cannot ask a clarifying question, and will do exactly what you asked and not what you meant.

The second version is what this section teaches, and it has one governing test.

Show your prompt to a colleague with no context on the task and ask them to follow it. If they would be confused, so is the model.

That test resolves most prompting questions without any theory. It also explains why the techniques below are unglamorous: they are the things that make a specification unambiguous.

One prerequisite, from §13. Prompt engineering assumes you have success criteria and a way to test against them. Without an eval (a repeatable test of how well the system does its job), you are not engineering. You are guessing, and remembering the guesses that felt good. If you have not read §13, the honest order is to build the eval first.

3.1 Be Clear and Direct

The most common defect in a real prompt is not a missing technique. The prompt simply does not say what it wants, and no amount of prompt engineering compensates for an instruction that never named its target.

PROMPTS = [
    ("Create an analytics dashboard.", "vague"),
    ("Create an analytics dashboard. Include as many relevant features and "
     "interactions as possible. Go beyond the basics to create a "
     "fully-featured implementation.", "explicit"),
    ("NEVER use ellipses.", "unmotivated"),
    ("Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, so never "
     "use ellipses — the engine does not know how to pronounce them.",
     "motivated"),
]

for text, label in PROMPTS:
    words = len(text.split())
    print(f"{label:<14}{words:>3} words  {text[:62]}")

vague, explicit = (len(PROMPTS[0][0].split()), len(PROMPTS[1][0].split()))
print()
print(f"the explicit version is {explicit / vague:.1f}x longer and removes a whole")
print("class of under-delivery; the motivated version generalises to en-dashes,")
print("emoji and anything else the engine cannot pronounce")

vague           4 words  Create an analytics dashboard.
explicit       22 words  Create an analytics dashboard. Include as many relevant featur
unmotivated     3 words  NEVER use ellipses.
motivated      24 words  Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, s

the explicit version is 5.5x longer and removes a whole
class of under-delivery; the motivated version generalises to en-dashes,
emoji and anything else the engine cannot pronounce

Two principles are doing the work there.

Ask for what you want, including "above and beyond". A model given a vague brief produces a reasonable minimum. If you want a thorough implementation, say so. The model will not infer it from your tone.

Give the reason, not just the rule. "Never use ellipses" is a rule the model follows literally. "…because a text-to-speech engine cannot pronounce them" is a rule the model can generalise from. It will also avoid the em-dash, the emoji and the ASCII table that would have had the same problem. Explaining why is the single highest-leverage habit in this section, and it costs one clause.

Use numbered steps when order or completeness matters. A list makes omission visible, both to you when you write it and to the model when it works through it. Most of prompt engineering is this unglamorous. The techniques in the rest of this section are ways of being unambiguous, and not ways of being persuasive.

3.2 XML Tags

Once a prompt mixes instructions, context, examples and variable input, the model has to work out which is which. XML tags (labels like <document> wrapped around each part) remove the ambiguity, and they are the closest thing this subject has to a universally applicable technique.

CONTEXT = "Acme refunds within 30 days. Perishables excluded."
QUESTION = "Can I return the cheese I bought last week?"

flat = f"""You are a support agent. Here is the policy: {CONTEXT}
Answer this question: {QUESTION}
Be concise."""

tagged = f"""<instructions>
You are a support agent. Answer the question using only the policy.
Be concise.
</instructions>

<policy>
{CONTEXT}
</policy>

<question>
{QUESTION}
</question>"""

for label, prompt in (("flat", flat), ("tagged", tagged)):
    print(f"--- {label} ---")
    print(prompt)
    print()

print("in the flat version, where does the policy end and the question begin?")
print("a policy containing the words 'answer this question' would merge them")

--- flat ---
You are a support agent. Here is the policy: Acme refunds within 30 days. Perishables excluded.
Answer this question: Can I return the cheese I bought last week?
Be concise.

--- tagged ---
<instructions>
You are a support agent. Answer the question using only the policy.
Be concise.
</instructions>

<policy>
Acme refunds within 30 days. Perishables excluded.
</policy>

<question>
Can I return the cheese I bought last week?
</question>

in the flat version, where does the policy end and the question begin?
a policy containing the words 'answer this question' would merge them

Delimiters are a correctness property, not tidiness. A delimiter is a marker that separates one part of the prompt from another. The flat prompt works until a document contains a sentence that looks like an instruction. §14.2 shows that this is not merely an accident waiting to happen but an attack. Tagging your own prompt is the same discipline that makes untrusted content safe to include.

Two conventions are worth adopting. Use the same tag names across your prompts, so a change of wording never changes structure. And nest when the content has a hierarchy: documents go inside <documents>, each in <document index="n"> with <source> and <document_content> subtags.

3.3 Examples

Examples are the most reliable way to steer format, tone and structure. The technique is usually called few-shot prompting (showing the model a few worked examples). It is also where people over-invest in quantity and under-invest in coverage.

EXAMPLES = [
    ("refund request", "refund"),
    ("where is my parcel", "order_status"),
    ("cancel please", "cancel_order"),
]
EDGE_EXAMPLES = EXAMPLES + [
    ("", "clarify"),
    ("late AND wrong address", "ambiguous"),
]


def render(examples):
    body = "\n".join(
        f"  <example>\n    <input>{text or '(empty)'}</input>\n"
        f"    <label>{label}</label>\n  </example>"
        for text, label in examples)
    return f"<examples>\n{body}\n</examples>"


for label, examples in (("happy path only", EXAMPLES),
                        ("with edge cases", EDGE_EXAMPLES)):
    covered = {lab for _, lab in examples}
    print(f"{label:<18}{len(examples)} examples, labels covered: {sorted(covered)}")

print()
print(render(EDGE_EXAMPLES))

happy path only   3 examples, labels covered: ['cancel_order', 'order_status', 'refund']
with edge cases   5 examples, labels covered: ['ambiguous', 'cancel_order', 'clarify', 'order_status', 'refund']

<examples>
  <example>
    <input>refund request</input>
    <label>refund</label>
  </example>
  <example>
    <input>where is my parcel</input>
    <label>order_status</label>
  </example>
  <example>
    <input>cancel please</input>
    <label>cancel_order</label>
  </example>
  <example>
    <input>(empty)</input>
    <label>clarify</label>
  </example>
  <example>
    <input>late AND wrong address</input>
    <label>ambiguous</label>
  </example>
</examples>

Three to five examples is the useful range for few-shot prompting. Beyond that, the return falls off sharply and the token cost does not.

Diversity matters more than count. Three examples that all look like the happy path teach the model that the happy path is the whole task, and it will then confidently classify an empty string as a refund request. The two edge cases added above are worth more than three more ordinary ones.

Wrap them in tags. Use <example> for each one and <examples> for the group, so they are distinguishable from instructions. Without that, a model reading an example of bad input may follow it.

Two tricks are worth knowing. You can ask the model to evaluate your examples for relevance and diversity, or to generate more from your initial set. That is a good use of a cheap model, and it surfaces gaps you did not see. And if you have no first draft at all, the metaprompt recipe in the Claude Cookbook generates one from a task description. A metaprompt is simply a prompt whose output is another prompt. It is a starting point to edit and not an output to ship, and it is most useful for getting past the blank page on an unfamiliar task.

3.4 Roles

Role prompting, which means setting a role in the system prompt, focuses behaviour and tone. One sentence is often enough, and the gain is largest where the task has domain conventions.

ROLES = [
    (None, "generic assistant behaviour"),
    ("You are a support agent for Acme.",
     "adopts your product's vocabulary and tone"),
    ("You are a data protection officer reviewing a policy for GDPR "
     "compliance.", "applies the conventions of that discipline"),
]

for role, effect in ROLES:
    words = len(role.split()) if role else 0
    print(f"{words:>3} words  {effect}")
    if role:
        print(f"           {role}")

print()
print("a role sets defaults; it does not grant permissions or enforce policy")

0 words  generic assistant behaviour
  7 words  adopts your product's vocabulary and tone
           You are a support agent for Acme.
 12 words  applies the conventions of that discipline
           You are a data protection officer reviewing a policy for GDPR compliance.

a role sets defaults; it does not grant permissions or enforce policy

The gain from role prompting comes from the domain conventions a role carries and not from the words themselves. That is why "data protection officer" outperforms "expert assistant".

A role is a default, not a control. "You are a support agent who never discloses internal data" shapes ordinary behaviour, and it is not a security boundary. §14.4 is the whole argument. Use roles for tone and domain conventions, and use code for anything that must not happen.

3.5 Controlling the Format

Four techniques, in descending order of how well they work.

Say what to do, not what to avoid. "Do not use markdown" leaves the model guessing at the alternative. "Write in smoothly flowing prose paragraphs" names the target, which is an output format stated positively. A negative output format instruction excludes one option out of many, while a positive one names the single option you want.

Use XML format indicators. "Put the prose sections in <prose> tags" is unambiguous and trivially parseable.

Match your prompt's style to the output you want. This one is unintuitive and real: a prompt written in heavy markdown tends to produce heavy markdown. Removing bullets from your prompt reduces bullets in the response.

Be detailed when the preference is specific. A paragraph of formatting guidance, in its own tag, works better than a sentence.

INSTRUCTIONS = [
    ("Do not use markdown.", "negative", "no target named"),
    ("Write in smoothly flowing prose paragraphs, using standard paragraph "
     "breaks for organisation.", "positive", "names the target"),
    ("Write the prose sections inside <prose> tags.", "structural",
     "parseable, and unambiguous"),
]
for text, kind, why in INSTRUCTIONS:
    print(f"{kind:<12}{why:<28}{text[:52]}")

print()
print("and the strongest option of all, when the output feeds code:")
print("  output_config.format — a grammar, not a request (see 4.2)")

negative    no target named             Do not use markdown.
positive    names the target            Write in smoothly flowing prose paragraphs, using st
structural  parseable, and unambiguous  Write the prose sections inside <prose> tags.

and the strongest option of all, when the output feeds code:
  output_config.format — a grammar, not a request (see 4.2)

That last line is the honest summary of this subsection. If the output feeds code, stop prompting for format and constrain it (§4). Format instructions are for output a person reads.

Two notes on current models. Verbosity has shifted, and verbosity is now something you ask for and no longer something you suppress. The latest models are less verbose by default. They are direct, grounded, and inclined to skip elaborate summaries unless asked, so if you want a detailed write-up, request one. And they default to LaTeX for mathematics (a typesetting notation full of backslashes). If you need plain text, say so explicitly, naming the notations to avoid.

3.6 Prefill Is Gone

For years the standard trick for controlling output was to prefill the assistant turn: you supplied the start of the assistant's reply and let the model continue from it. It is worth knowing this existed, because a great deal of published prompting advice still assumes it.

From Claude 4.6 onwards, a prefilled final assistant turn is a 400 error. It is not degraded. It is rejected.

MIGRATIONS = [
    ("force a JSON shape", 'prefill "{"',
     "structured outputs (4.2) — a grammar rather than a nudge"),
    ("skip the preamble", 'prefill "Here is the summary:"',
     "instruct directly: 'respond without preamble'; strip stragglers"),
    ("steer past a refusal", "prefill an agreeable opening",
     "clear prompting in the user turn; models refuse better now"),
    ("continue a cut-off answer", "prefill the partial text",
     "put it in a USER turn: 'your previous response ended with X, continue'"),
    ("re-inject context", "prefill a reminder",
     "inject into the user turn, a tool, or compaction (9.7)"),
]

print(f"{'what it was for':<28}{'the old trick':<34}{'what to do now'}")
for purpose, old, new in MIGRATIONS:
    print(f"{purpose:<28}{old:<34}{new}")

print()
print("adding assistant messages ELSEWHERE in the conversation is unaffected;")
print("only a prefilled FINAL assistant turn is rejected")

what it was for             the old trick                     what to do now
force a JSON shape          prefill "{"                       structured outputs (4.2) — a grammar rather than a nudge
skip the preamble           prefill "Here is the summary:"    instruct directly: 'respond without preamble'; strip stragglers
steer past a refusal        prefill an agreeable opening      clear prompting in the user turn; models refuse better now
continue a cut-off answer   prefill the partial text          put it in a USER turn: 'your previous response ended with X, continue'
re-inject context           prefill a reminder                inject into the user turn, a tool, or compaction (9.7)

adding assistant messages ELSEWHERE in the conversation is unaffected;
only a prefilled FINAL assistant turn is rejected

The first row is the important one. Prefill was a probabilistic way to get a shape, and structured outputs is a guaranteed one. The feature that replaced it is strictly better, which is why the removal is not a loss.

Note also that prefill is incompatible with thinking (§5), so on any model where thinking is on by default the technique was already unavailable.

3.7 Long Context

Long context prompting is a distinct skill. Above roughly 20,000 tokens of input, where things sit in the prompt starts to matter as much as what it says.

DOCUMENT_TOKENS, QUERY_TOKENS = 42_000, 120

query_first = ["<query>", "<documents> (42,000 tokens)"]
documents_first = ["<documents> (42,000 tokens)", "<query>"]

print(f"{'query first':<16}", " -> ".join(query_first))
print(f"{'documents first':<16}", " -> ".join(documents_first))
print()
print("put longform data at the TOP, above the query, instructions and examples.")
print("On complex multi-document inputs, queries at the end have been measured")
print("to improve response quality by up to 30% in Anthropic's testing.")
print()

DOCS = [("annual_report_2023.pdf", "{{ANNUAL_REPORT}}"),
        ("competitor_analysis_q2.xlsx", "{{COMPETITOR_ANALYSIS}}")]
parts = ["<documents>"]
for i, (source, content) in enumerate(DOCS, start=1):
    parts += [f'  <document index="{i}">',
              f"    <source>{source}</source>",
              "    <document_content>",
              f"      {content}",
              "    </document_content>",
              "  </document>"]
parts.append("</documents>")
print("\n".join(parts))

query first      <query> -> <documents> (42,000 tokens)
documents first  <documents> (42,000 tokens) -> <query>

put longform data at the TOP, above the query, instructions and examples.
On complex multi-document inputs, queries at the end have been measured
to improve response quality by up to 30% in Anthropic's testing.

<documents>
  <document index="1">
    <source>annual_report_2023.pdf</source>
    <document_content>
      {{ANNUAL_REPORT}}
    </document_content>
  </document>
  <document index="2">
    <source>competitor_analysis_q2.xlsx</source>
    <document_content>
      {{COMPETITOR_ANALYSIS}}
    </document_content>
  </document>
</documents>

Longform data at the top; the query at the bottom. This is the single most useful long context prompting rule, and it costs nothing to follow. It also works with §9.3: the documents are the stable prefix, so putting them first is exactly where a cache breakpoint wants them.

Structure multiple documents with metadata. <source> alongside <document_content> lets the model say which document a claim came from. If you want that mechanically and not in prose, §10.7's search results and §8.5's citations do it properly.

3.8 Prompt Chaining

With adaptive thinking and subagents, the model handles most multi-step reasoning internally, so explicit chaining (splitting a task into several calls, each feeding the next) is less necessary than it once was. It still earns its place when you need to inspect intermediate output or enforce a pipeline shape.

The most useful pattern is self-correction: draft, review against criteria, refine.

def draft(brief):
    return f"[draft for {brief}]"


def review(text, criteria):
    """A separate call, so its output can be logged, evaluated or branched on."""
    failures = [c for c in criteria if c not in text]
    return {"passes": not failures, "failures": failures}


def refine(text, review_result):
    return text + " + " + ", ".join(review_result["failures"])


CRITERIA = ["cites the policy", "names the deadline", "offers a next step"]
text = draft("a refund decline")
result = review(text, CRITERIA)
print("step 1 draft :", text)
print("step 2 review:", result)

if not result["passes"]:
    text = refine(text, result)
    print("step 3 refine:", text)
    print("step 4 review:", review(text, CRITERIA))

print()
print("three calls instead of one. The value is that step 2's verdict is a")
print("value your code can log, threshold, or route on — 13.8's harness")
print("plugs straight into it")

step 1 draft : [draft for a refund decline]
step 2 review: {'passes': False, 'failures': ['cites the policy', 'names the deadline', 'offers a next step']}
step 3 refine: [draft for a refund decline] + cites the policy, names the deadline, offers a next step
step 4 review: {'passes': True, 'failures': []}

three calls instead of one. The value is that step 2's verdict is a
value your code can log, threshold, or route on — 13.8's harness
plugs straight into it

A related pattern is worth naming here because it is often confused with chaining. A subagent is a separate model call with its own context, whose summary returns to a coordinator (§11.8). A chain keeps one context and inspects it between steps. Reach for a subagent when the intermediate material is large and disposable. Reach for a chain when the intermediate value is what you need.

Chain when you need the intermediate value, and do not chain to simulate reasoning. Asking the model to "think step by step" across three API calls is a worse version of thinking (§5), which does the same work in one request with the reasoning kept out of your context. Chain when the intermediate result is something your program needs.

3.9 Steering Agentic Behaviour

Three behaviours come up repeatedly once a model has tools, and each has a prompt-shaped fix. The caveat from §11.2 applies: a prompt is a default and not a control.

Under-acting. "Can you suggest some changes" gets suggestions and not changes. The current models follow instructions precisely, so if you want the edit made, ask for the edit.

Over-engineering. This means extra files, unnecessary abstractions, and flexibility nobody asked for. The fix is explicit scope: "Only make changes that are directly requested or clearly necessary. Keep solutions simple and focused."

File litter. Models use temporary scripts as a scratchpad, which improves outcomes in agentic coding and leaves debris. The fix is to ask: "If you create any temporary files or helper scripts for iteration, remove them at the end of the task."

GUIDANCE = [
    ("under-acting", "suggests instead of doing",
     "ask for the action explicitly"),
    ("over-engineering", "extra files and abstractions",
     "state the scope: only what is requested"),
    ("file litter", "temporary scratchpad files remain",
     "ask it to clean up at the end"),
    ("over-eager tool use", "calls tools that were not needed",
     "lower `effort` (5.2) — it reduces tool calls, not just thinking"),
]
print(f"{'behaviour':<22}{'symptom':<36}{'fix'}")
for name, symptom, fix in GUIDANCE:
    print(f"{name:<22}{symptom:<36}{fix}")

print()
print("the last row is not a prompt fix at all, and is usually the better lever")

behaviour             symptom                             fix
under-acting          suggests instead of doing           ask for the action explicitly
over-engineering      extra files and abstractions        state the scope: only what is requested
file litter           temporary scratchpad files remain   ask it to clean up at the end
over-eager tool use   calls tools that were not needed    lower `effort` (5.2) — it reduces tool calls, not just thinking

the last row is not a prompt fix at all, and is usually the better lever

3.10 A Prompt Template

Now we put the section together: a shape that works with caching, structured output and untrusted content.

def build(system_role, policy, examples, documents, question):
    """Stable content first, volatile content last — 9.3's ordering, exactly."""
    system = [
        {"type": "text", "text": f"<role>\n{system_role}\n</role>"},
        {"type": "text",
         "text": f"<policy>\n{policy}\n</policy>",
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "<examples>\n" + "\n".join(examples)
                                 + "\n</examples>",
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}},
    ]
    user = []
    if documents:
        user.append({"type": "text",
                     "text": "<documents>\n" + "\n".join(documents)
                             + "\n</documents>"})
    user.append({"type": "text", "text": f"<question>\n{question}\n</question>"})
    return {"system": system, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": user}]}


request = build(
    system_role="You are a support agent for Acme.",
    policy="Refunds within 30 days. Perishables excluded.",
    examples=["  <example><input>where is my parcel</input>"
              "<label>order_status</label></example>"],
    documents=["  <document index=\"1\"><source>ticket-4471</source>"
               "<document_content>My cheese arrived warm.</document_content>"
               "</document>"],
    question="Is this refundable?",
)

for i, block in enumerate(request["system"]):
    ttl = block.get("cache_control", {}).get("ttl", "—")
    print(f"system[{i}]  cache ttl={ttl:<4} {block['text'].splitlines()[0]}")
for i, block in enumerate(request["messages"][0]["content"]):
    print(f"user[{i}]    {block['text'].splitlines()[0]}")

print()
print("order: role -> policy -> examples -> documents -> question")
print("breakpoints sit at the boundary between stable and volatile")

system[0]  cache ttl=—    <role>
system[1]  cache ttl=1h   <policy>
system[2]  cache ttl=1h   <examples>
user[0]    <documents>
user[1]    <question>

order: role -> policy -> examples -> documents -> question
breakpoints sit at the boundary between stable and volatile

Four properties of that shape, each earned in a different section.

Stable content is first and cached. Role, policy and examples change rarely, while the question changes every request (§9.3).

Everything is tagged, so nothing in a document can be mistaken for an instruction (§3.2, §14.2).

Documents sit above the question, per §3.7.

Nothing here constrains the output, because that is output_config.format's job and not a sentence's (§4).

Exercises

Exercise 3.1 — Rewrite this prompt. It works about 70% of the time. Find every problem and rewrite it.

You are a helpful assistant. Read the ticket below and figure out what the
customer wants. Don't be too verbose. Output JSON.

TICKET: {{ticket}}

Also if it's urgent flag it. Never make things up.
Solution 
SYSTEM = """<role>
You are a support triage assistant for Acme, an online grocery retailer.
</role>

<task>
Classify the customer's ticket into exactly one intent and assess urgency.
Work only from the ticket text. If the ticket does not contain enough
information to classify it, use the intent "needs_clarification" rather than
guessing — a wrong route costs the customer a day, an honest one costs a
follow-up question.
</task>

<urgency_definition>
Urgent means the customer is blocked right now or money is at risk:
a failed payment, a missing perishable delivery, or a duplicate charge.
A late non-perishable parcel is NOT urgent.
</urgency_definition>

<examples>
  <example>
    <input>where is my parcel, ordered tuesday</input>
    <output>order_status, urgent=false</output>
  </example>
  <example>
    <input>charged twice for the same order</input>
    <output>billing_dispute, urgent=true</output>
  </example>
  <example>
    <input>my milk arrived warm and it's 30 degrees out</input>
    <output>refund, urgent=true</output>
  </example>
  <example>
    <input>hi</input>
    <output>needs_clarification, urgent=false</output>
  </example>
</examples>"""

SCHEMA = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "intent": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["order_status", "refund", "billing_dispute",
                                "cancel_order", "needs_clarification"]},
            "urgent": {"type": "boolean"},
            "evidence": {"type": "string",
                         "description": "The phrase from the ticket that "
                                        "decided the urgency call."},
        },
        "required": ["intent", "urgent", "evidence"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}

print("system prompt sections:",
      [line.strip("<>") for line in SYSTEM.splitlines()
       if line.startswith("<") and not line.startswith("</")])
print("examples                :", SYSTEM.count("<example>"))
print("includes an edge case   :", "<input>hi</input>" in SYSTEM)
print("enum members            :", SCHEMA["schema"]["properties"]["intent"]["enum"])
print("output constrained      :", SCHEMA["type"] == "json_schema")
print("ticket goes in          : a tagged USER turn, not the system prompt")

system prompt sections: ['role', 'task', 'urgency_definition', 'examples']
examples                : 4
includes an edge case   : True
enum members            : ['order_status', 'refund', 'billing_dispute', 'cancel_order', 'needs_clarification']
output constrained      : True
ticket goes in          : a tagged USER turn, not the system prompt

Seven problems, roughly in order of how much they cost.

"Output JSON" is a request, not a constraint. This is the single largest defect, and it explains a good share of the 30% failure rate. §4.1's table lists every shape a model can return when asked politely for JSON. Replace it with output_config.format, and the whole class of failure disappears.

"Figure out what the customer wants" names no output space. There is no enum (a fixed list of allowed values), so there is no way for the model to know that order_status and cancel_order are the categories and not a free-text description. An enum in the schema fixes it, and the schema is now the specification.

"If it's urgent flag it" defines nothing. Urgency is exactly the sort of judgement two humans disagree about, so the model's disagreement with you is not a model failure. It is a missing definition. The rewrite defines it, gives the negative case, and requires evidence, which makes the call auditable.

No examples at all, and the four added carry more weight than any instruction in the prompt. Note that the fourth is deliberately degenerate: a bare "hi". Without it, the model has no demonstration that declining to classify is allowed.

"Never make things up" is unactionable as written. The model does not experience itself as making things up. The actionable form is an escape hatch, an explicit needs_clarification value, plus the reason it exists (§3.1's motivation rule). That is why the task section explains the cost of a wrong route.

"Don't be too verbose" is a negative with no target. With structured output it becomes irrelevant, which is the tidiest kind of fix.

The ticket is interpolated into the system prompt. It is untrusted customer text sitting in the most trusted position in the request. §14.2 covers the general form. Here it is enough to say the ticket belongs in a tagged user turn.

One judgement call worth defending. I added a required evidence field that is not part of the original spec. It costs a few tokens per call, and it turns every urgency decision into something a human can check at a glance, which is what makes the eval in §13 possible at all. If a field makes a decision auditable, it usually pays for itself.

Exercise 3.2 — Which technique? For each symptom, name the technique and say why the obvious alternative is worse: (a) the model answers in bullet points and you want prose; (b) it invents a delivery date; (c) it summarises a 60,000-token document poorly; (d) it suggests code changes instead of making them; (e) its JSON sometimes has an extra field.

Solution 
ANSWERS = [
    ("a  bullets instead of prose", "positive format instruction",
     "'do not use markdown' names no target; say what prose looks like, "
     "and match your prompt's own style to it"),
    ("b  invents a delivery date", "grounding + an escape hatch",
     "a format rule cannot help; give permission to say 'the record does "
     "not contain that' and restrict it to the source (14.5)"),
    ("c  poor 60k-token summary", "put the document first",
     "the reflex is a better instruction; the measured fix is ordering — "
     "data at the top, query at the bottom (3.7)"),
    ("d  suggests instead of doing", "ask for the action",
     "the models follow instructions precisely; 'can you suggest' got "
     "exactly what it asked for"),
    ("e  extra field in the JSON", "structured outputs, not prompting",
     "no wording makes this impossible; additionalProperties:false does"),
]

print(f"{'symptom':<30}{'technique':<32}{'why not the obvious thing'}")
for symptom, technique, why in ANSWERS:
    print(f"{symptom:<30}{technique:<32}")
    print(f"{'':62}{why}")

symptom                       technique                       why not the obvious thing
a  bullets instead of prose   positive format instruction     
                                                              'do not use markdown' names no target; say what prose looks like, and match your prompt's own style to it
b  invents a delivery date    grounding + an escape hatch     
                                                              a format rule cannot help; give permission to say 'the record does not contain that' and restrict it to the source (14.5)
c  poor 60k-token summary     put the document first          
                                                              the reflex is a better instruction; the measured fix is ordering — data at the top, query at the bottom (3.7)
d  suggests instead of doing  ask for the action              
                                                              the models follow instructions precisely; 'can you suggest' got exactly what it asked for
e  extra field in the JSON    structured outputs, not prompting
                                                              no wording makes this impossible; additionalProperties:false does

(a) and (e) look similar and are not. Both are format complaints, but (a) is about prose a person reads and (e) is about a field your code consumes. Prompting is the right tool for the first and cannot solve the second. No phrasing makes an extra field impossible, and additionalProperties: false does. The test is who reads the output.

(b) is the one where prompt engineering is genuinely the answer, and the technique is unobvious. The fix is not "be more accurate" but giving the model somewhere to go when the source lacks the fact. A model with no way to express "not in the record" produces something anyway. Adding the escape hatch and restricting it to the provided source removes the pressure that caused the invention.

(c) is the most surprising, and it is why the section includes an ordering rule at all. The instinct on a bad summary is to rewrite the instruction. The measured intervention is to move the document above the query. That change has no wording in it, and it is worth up to 30% on complex multi-document inputs in Anthropic's testing. It also happens to be where a cache breakpoint wants the document anyway (§9.3), so it is free twice.

(d) is not a defect. "Can you suggest some changes" is a request for suggestions, and it got them. The current models follow instructions precisely, which means imprecise instructions are followed precisely too. This is the clearest case of the section's governing test: a colleague handed that sentence would also have sent suggestions.

The pattern across all five. Three of the five are not prompting problems: (e) is a constraint problem, (c) is a layout problem, and (d) is a specification problem. Reaching for better wording first is the reflex worth unlearning. The question to ask before rewording is which layer can make this impossible and not just unlikely.

SECTION 4

Structured Outputs

Most of the time you do not want prose. You want a record: a classification, an extracted field, or a decision your code can branch on. Getting one out of a language model used to mean asking politely for JSON, parsing it, and handling the cases where the model wrapped it in a sentence, used single quotes, or invented a field.

Structured outputs remove that entire category of failure. They do it not by asking more firmly but by constraining what the model is allowed to emit. The output is generated against a compiled grammar derived from your schema (the description of the shape you want), so a response that violates the schema is not merely unlikely. It is unreachable.

There are two features, and you can use them independently or together. JSON outputs (output_config.format) constrain the response. Strict tool use (strict: true, from §6.8) constrains tool inputs. This section covers both and, more importantly, where the guarantee stops.

4.1 The Problem, Stated Honestly

Before the mechanism, it is worth seeing precisely what goes wrong without it, because the failure modes are not the ones people expect.

import json

# Six real shapes a model can produce when you ask for JSON in the prompt.
RESPONSES = [
    ('{"intent": "refund", "confidence": 0.9}', "clean"),
    ('Sure! Here is the JSON:\n{"intent": "refund"}', "prose wrapper"),
    ('```json\n{"intent": "refund"}\n```', "markdown fence"),
    ("{'intent': 'refund'}", "single quotes"),
    ('{"intent": "refund", "urgency": "high"}', "extra field"),
    ('{"intent": "money back"}', "value outside the enum"),
]

VALID_INTENTS = {"refund", "order_status", "cancel_order"}
EXPECTED_FIELDS = {"intent", "confidence", "order_id"}

print(f"{'shape':<24}{'parses?':<10}{'valid enum?':<14}{'no stray fields?'}")
for raw, label in RESPONSES:
    try:
        parsed = json.loads(raw)
        parses = True
        good_enum = parsed.get("intent") in VALID_INTENTS
        no_stray = set(parsed) <= EXPECTED_FIELDS
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        parses = good_enum = no_stray = False
    print(f"{label:<24}{str(parses):<10}{str(good_enum):<14}{no_stray}")

print()
print("the last two parse perfectly and are still wrong, in different ways")

shape                   parses?   valid enum?   no stray fields?
clean                   True      True          True
prose wrapper           False     False         False
markdown fence          False     False         False
single quotes           False     False         False
extra field             True      True          False
value outside the enum  True      False         True

the last two parse perfectly and are still wrong, in different ways

The parse failures are the easy half. A wrapper or a fence around the JSON is annoying and detectable. You write a regex, you feel dirty, and it works. The dangerous rows are the last two: valid JSON with an extra field, and valid JSON with a value outside your enum. Both parse. Both flow into your code. Neither raises anything, and the second one silently routes a refund request to no handler at all.

Every one of these becomes impossible under a constrained grammar.

4.2 JSON Outputs

output_config.format takes a json schema and guarantees the response conforms to it. A JSON schema is a description of the shape you want. The json schema is the specification: the properties, their types, which ones are required, and the enum values a string may take.

import anthropic
import json

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

SCHEMA = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "intent": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["refund", "order_status", "cancel_order"]},
            "order_id": {"type": "string"},
            "confidence": {"type": "number"},
        },
        "required": ["intent", "confidence"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    output_config={"format": SCHEMA},
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Where has my order ORD-4471 got to?"}],
)

raw = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
print("raw text  :", raw)

record = json.loads(raw)
print("intent    :", record["intent"])
print("order_id  :", record["order_id"])
print("confidence:", record["confidence"])
print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)

raw text  : {"intent":"order_status","confidence":0.94,"order_id":"ORD-4471"}
intent    : order_status
order_id  : ORD-4471
confidence: 0.94
stop_reason: end_turn

Three things to notice.

The JSON arrives in an ordinary text block. There is no new block type, and content[0].text is a JSON string. You still call json.loads, and it cannot fail.

additionalProperties: false is required for objects. This is not optional styling, because the API rejects a schema without it. It is also what makes the "extra field" row from §4.1 impossible.

Changing the format invalidates your prompt cache for that conversation. Structured outputs inject an additional system prompt describing the expected format, so output_config.format is part of the cached prefix (§9.5). Alternating between two schemas on the same conversation means alternating between two prefixes.

The SDK also offers messages.parse, a helper that validates the response for you and works with schema libraries such as Pydantic. The value you get back is then a typed object and not a string. Use it where it fits. The manual form above is shown because it makes the mechanism visible.

Reach for messages.parse when you already have a schema library in the project. The manual json.loads is fine when you do not.

One note on what "guaranteed" means precisely: schema conformance covers structure and types. Schema conformance is not validation, and §4.3 is the whole of that distinction. The response will be an object with your required properties at your declared types. It will not necessarily be an object whose values are in range, and that is §4.3's subject.

4.3 What the Schema May Contain

The grammar is compiled, and compilation constrains what can be expressed. The supported subset is generous and the gaps are specific, so it is worth knowing them and not discovering them as 400s.

Supported
Not supported
All basic types; enum (scalars only); const; anyOf and allOf; $ref, $def and definitions (internal only); default; required; additionalProperties: false; string formats date-time, date, time, duration, email, hostname, uri, ipv4, ipv6, uuid; array minItems of 0 or 1.
Recursive schemas; complex types inside enum; external $ref; numeric constraints (minimum, maximum, multipleOf); string constraints (minLength, maxLength); array constraints beyond minItems 0 or 1; additionalProperties set to anything but false.

The omission that surprises people most is numeric and string constraints. You cannot say "confidence between 0 and 1" or "at most 200 characters" in the schema. Those still have to be validated in your code. The grammar guarantees a number, and not a number in range.

SCHEMA_PROPS = {
    "confidence": {"type": "number"},
    "summary": {"type": "string"},
    "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
}
GUARANTEED = {"confidence": "is a number",
              "summary": "is a string",
              "tags": "is an array of strings"}
NOT_GUARANTEED = {"confidence": "is between 0 and 1",
                  "summary": "is under 200 characters",
                  "tags": "has at most 5 entries"}

print(f"{'field':<12}{'the grammar guarantees':<28}{'you must still check'}")
for field in SCHEMA_PROPS:
    print(f"{field:<12}{GUARANTEED[field]:<28}{NOT_GUARANTEED[field]}")

print()
print("the schema removes parse errors and type errors, not validation")

field       the grammar guarantees      you must still check
confidence  is a number                 is between 0 and 1
summary     is a string                 is under 200 characters
tags        is an array of strings      has at most 5 entries

the schema removes parse errors and type errors, not validation

Regex pattern is supported for the common cases: anchored and partial matching, *, +, ?, simple {n,m}, character classes and groups. It does not support backreferences, lookahead or lookbehind, or \b. A complex pattern is a 400 and not a silent degradation.

There are also complexity limits, and they are shared across the whole request and not per schema. You get at most 20 strict tools, 24 optional parameters in total, and 16 parameters using union types. That last one is low because anyOf makes compilation cost grow exponentially. Four strict tools with six optional parameters each already reach the 24 limit, which is the kind of thing that fails on the day you add the fourth tool.

4.4 Where the Guarantee Stops

This is the part to read twice, because "guaranteed schema-compliant" is stated in the documentation with three exceptions, and each one produces output your parser will choke on.

import json

CASES = [
    ("end_turn", '{"intent": "refund", "confidence": 0.9}',
     "conforms"),
    ("max_tokens", '{"intent": "refund", "confi',
     "cut off mid-token; not valid JSON at all"),
    ("refusal", "",
     "empty content; the refusal takes precedence over the schema"),
]

print(f"{'stop_reason':<14}{'parses?':<10}{'what happened'}")
for stop, raw, note in CASES:
    try:
        json.loads(raw)
        parses = True
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError):
        parses = False
    print(f"{stop:<14}{str(parses):<10}{note}")

print()
print("guaranteed conformance applies to a COMPLETED, non-refused response")

stop_reason   parses?   what happened
end_turn      True      conforms
max_tokens    False     cut off mid-token; not valid JSON at all
refusal       False     empty content; the refusal takes precedence over the schema

guaranteed conformance applies to a COMPLETED, non-refused response

max_tokens truncation produces invalid JSON. The grammar constrains which tokens may be emitted, but it cannot make the response finish. Cut it off and you get a fragment. So a structured-output call still needs stop_reason checked before parsing. That is the same rule as §2.6, and the one most likely to be skipped precisely because the output is "guaranteed".

A refusal takes precedence over the schema. You get stop_reason: "refusal", a 200, and content that does not match. Note that, unlike the pre-output refusals in §14.6, you are billed for tokens generated here.

Enum capitalisation is not guaranteed. This one is genuinely surprising. The model may return a value that differs from your enum only in capitalisation, typically the first letter of a word after a space. The response completes normally with no error and no special stop reason. Given ["Conversation topic 3"] you may receive "Conversation Topic 3".

ENUM = ["Conversation Topic 1", "Conversation Topic 2", "Conversation topic 3"]
RETURNED = "Conversation Topic 3"          # note the capital T

print("declared in the schema:", repr(ENUM[2]))
print("actually returned     :", repr(RETURNED))
print("exact match           :", RETURNED in ENUM)
print("case-insensitive match:", RETURNED.lower() in {v.lower() for v in ENUM})
print()

# A separate hazard: an enum whose own members collide when case is ignored.
# Then NO comparison strategy can recover the intended member.
COLLIDING = ["Draft", "draft", "DRAFT"]
lowered = [v.lower() for v in COLLIDING]
print("an enum that cannot be repaired:", COLLIDING)
print("distinct members            :", len(set(COLLIDING)))
print("distinct once lowercased    :", len(set(lowered)))
print("case-insensitive comparison is ambiguous:",
      len(set(lowered)) < len(set(COLLIDING)))

declared in the schema: 'Conversation topic 3'
actually returned     : 'Conversation Topic 3'
exact match           : False
case-insensitive match: True

an enum that cannot be repaired: ['Draft', 'draft', 'DRAFT']
distinct members            : 3
distinct once lowercased    : 1
case-insensitive comparison is ambiguous: True

These are two separate rules, and the block shows why they are separate. Compare enum values case-insensitively. That repairs the first case, where the returned value differs from a schema member only in capitalisation. And never define two enum values that differ only in capitalisation. That is the second block, where case-insensitive comparison collapses three distinct members into one and no strategy recovers the intended value. The first rule saves you, and the second is a hole the first rule cannot patch.

4.5 Property Ordering

Here is a small behaviour with a large capacity to confuse: required properties are emitted first, then optional ones, each group in schema order.

SCHEMA_ORDER = ["notes", "name", "email", "age"]
REQUIRED = ["name", "email"]

emitted = ([p for p in SCHEMA_ORDER if p in REQUIRED]
           + [p for p in SCHEMA_ORDER if p not in REQUIRED])

print("declared in the schema :", SCHEMA_ORDER)
print("required               :", REQUIRED)
print("emitted in this order  :", emitted)
print()
print("if order matters to you, mark everything required —")
print("or stop depending on the order of keys in a JSON object")

declared in the schema : ['notes', 'name', 'email', 'age']
required               : ['name', 'email']
emitted in this order  : ['name', 'email', 'notes', 'age']

if order matters to you, mark everything required —
or stop depending on the order of keys in a JSON object

This matters in exactly two situations: when you are diffing JSON as text, and when a downstream consumer is order-sensitive. Both are worth avoiding on their own merits. If you cannot avoid them, marking every property required restores schema order.

4.6 Strict Tool Use, and Using Both Together

§6.8 introduced strict: true. It is the same constrained-decoding machinery applied to tool inputs and not to the response, and the two work together.

import anthropic
import json

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "lookup_order",
    "description": "Look up an order by id.",
    "strict": True,
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string",
                                    "pattern": "^ORD-[0-9]{4}$"}},
        "required": ["order_id"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}]

RESPONSE_SCHEMA = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "status": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["shipped", "delivered", "cancelled"]},
            "eta_days": {"type": "integer"},
        },
        "required": ["status"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    tools=TOOLS,
    output_config={"format": RESPONSE_SCHEMA},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Where is ORD-4471?"}],
)

call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
print("tool input :", call.input)
print("matches the pattern:",
      bool(__import__("re").fullmatch(r"ORD-[0-9]{4}", call.input["order_id"])))

tool input : {'order_id': 'ORD-4471'}
matches the pattern: True

The tool input is constrained on the way in, and the final response is constrained on the way out. A pattern on the tool's order_id means the model cannot even propose a malformed id. That is stronger than validating it in your executor, though §14.4's argument still stands: validate anyway, because the executor is reachable by other callers.

There are two incompatibilities to remember. Strict tools cannot be used with programmatic tool calling (§7.6), so a tool that needs to be callable from inside code execution cannot also be schema-guaranteed. And the 20-strict-tool limit is a limit on the request, so a large tool surface has to choose which tools get the guarantee.

4.7 What It Costs

Constrained decoding is not free, and the costs are unusual enough to be worth naming.

SCHEMA_SIZES = [("a 3-field classification", 180, 40),
                ("a 12-field extraction", 640, 140),
                ("a nested report schema", 2_100, 460)]
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00
REQUESTS_PER_DAY, DAYS = 50_000, 30

print(f"{'schema':<26}{'chars':>8}{'injected tokens':>17}{'$/month':>10}")
for name, chars, injected in SCHEMA_SIZES:
    monthly = injected * REQUESTS_PER_DAY * DAYS / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK
    print(f"{name:<26}{chars:>8,}{injected:>17,}{'$%.0f' % monthly:>10}")

print()
FIRST_MS, CACHED_MS = 340, 0
print(f"grammar compilation on first use : ~{FIRST_MS} ms of extra latency")
print(f"on every subsequent use          :  {CACHED_MS} ms — cached for 24 hours")
print()
print("the cache is invalidated by:")
for cause in ("changing the schema structure",
              "changing the SET of tools in the request",
              "(but NOT by changing only a name or description)"):
    print(f"  - {cause}")

schema                       chars  injected tokens   $/month
a 3-field classification       180               40      $300
a 12-field extraction          640              140     $1050
a nested report schema       2,100              460     $3450

grammar compilation on first use : ~340 ms of extra latency
on every subsequent use          :  0 ms — cached for 24 hours

the cache is invalidated by:
  - changing the schema structure
  - changing the SET of tools in the request
  - (but NOT by changing only a name or description)

A system prompt describing the format is injected on your behalf, so your input token count rises. It is small per request and real at volume.

The grammar is compiled and cached for 24 hours from last use. The first request with a new schema pays compilation latency, and the rest do not. This is a separate cache from prompt caching, with separate invalidation rules. Note that changing only a name or description does not invalidate it, while changing the set of tools does.

The practical consequence is this: do not generate schemas dynamically per request. A schema assembled from user input is a new grammar every time, so you pay compilation on every call and never hit the cache. Define a fixed set of schemas and choose between them.

4.8 When Not to Use It

Structured outputs are so clearly better than prompting for JSON that the failure mode becomes using them where prose was the right choice.

Use it
Whenever the output feeds code. Classification, extraction, routing, scoring, anything with an enum. This is the large majority of production LLM traffic and it should all be constrained.
Consider a forced tool
When you also want the model to choose whether to answer. §6.7's tool_choice pattern predates this feature and remains useful when structure is one option among several.
Do not use it
When a person reads the output. Constraining generation to a grammar is a constraint on how the model can express itself; for an explanation or a draft, that is a cost with no benefit.
Do not use it
To smuggle prose into a field. A schema whose only property is {"answer": {"type": "string"}} has bought you a pair of braces and paid an injected system prompt for them.

That last row is a real pattern and worth naming. Wrapping a free-text answer in a one-field object gives the appearance of structure with none of its properties. Nothing is validated, nothing is enumerated, and the parse could not have failed anyway. If the schema has no enum, no required numeric field and no branching, ask whether you wanted structure at all.

Exercises

Exercise 4.1 — Fix this schema. It fails with a 400. Find every reason, then write the version that works and say what you still have to validate yourself.

SCHEMA = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "score": {"type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 10},
            "summary": {"type": "string", "maxLength": 200},
            "category": {"type": "string",
                         "enum": ["Bug Report", "Feature request",
                                  "bug report"]},
            "related": {"$ref": "https://example.com/schemas/ticket.json"},
            "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"},
                     "maxItems": 5},
        },
        "required": ["score"],
    },
}
Solution 
FIXED = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            # 1. numeric constraints are not supported: state the range in the
            #    description, and check it in code.
            "score": {"type": "number",
                      "description": "Severity from 0 to 10 inclusive."},
            # 2. string constraints are not supported either.
            "summary": {"type": "string",
                        "description": "One sentence, at most 200 characters."},
            # 3. two enum values differing only in capitalisation are
            #    unresolvable; and casing is not guaranteed anyway.
            "category": {"type": "string",
                         "enum": ["bug_report", "feature_request"]},
            # 4. external $ref is not supported; inline it or drop it.
            "related_ticket": {"type": "string",
                               "pattern": "^TICKET-[0-9]{4}$"},
            # 5. maxItems is not supported (only minItems, and only 0 or 1).
            "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"},
                     "description": "At most 5 tags."},
        },
        "required": ["score", "summary", "category"],
        # 6. required for every object, and missing from the original.
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}


def validate(record):
    """What the grammar cannot express, and therefore what you still own."""
    problems = []
    if not 0 <= record["score"] <= 10:
        problems.append(f"score {record['score']} outside 0-10")
    if len(record["summary"]) > 200:
        problems.append(f"summary is {len(record['summary'])} chars")
    if len(record.get("tags", [])) > 5:
        problems.append(f"{len(record['tags'])} tags, max 5")
    return problems


SAMPLES = [
    {"score": 7.5, "summary": "Login fails on Safari.",
     "category": "bug_report", "tags": ["auth", "safari"]},
    {"score": 12, "summary": "x" * 240, "category": "bug_report",
     "tags": ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"]},
]
for record in SAMPLES:
    problems = validate(record)
    print(f"score={record['score']:<5} -> {problems or 'ok'}")

print()
print("enum after the fix:", FIXED["schema"]["properties"]["category"]["enum"])
print("required          :", FIXED["schema"]["required"])
print("additionalProperties:", FIXED["schema"]["additionalProperties"])

score=7.5   -> ok
score=12    -> ['score 12 outside 0-10', 'summary is 240 chars', '6 tags, max 5']

enum after the fix: ['bug_report', 'feature_request']
required          : ['score', 'summary', 'category']
additionalProperties: False

Six defects, and they fall into two kinds.

Four are unsupported features and produce a 400 immediately: minimum/maximum, maxLength, an external $ref, and maxItems. Each is easy to fix once you know the list, and each has the same replacement. Say it in the description so the model still knows the intent, and enforce it in code.

One is the missing additionalProperties: false, which objects must set. This is the most common single cause of a rejected schema.

And one is not a 400 at all, which makes it the interesting one. ["Bug Report", "Feature request", "bug report"] contains two values that differ only in capitalisation. §4.4's rule says enum casing is not guaranteed, so receiving "Bug report" is possible, and there is no comparison, case-sensitive or insensitive, that maps it to the right member. The fix is not clever matching. It is choosing enum values that are distinguishable. Lowercase identifiers with underscores are a good default because they have no capitalisation to get wrong.

What you still validate yourself. That is range, length and cardinality (how many items), which is everything the grammar cannot express. That is why the solution ships a validate() alongside the schema and does not treat "structured" as "checked". The schema is a type system, not a validator, and the distinction is exactly the one between int and "an integer between 0 and 10".

One judgement call. I made summary and category required. The original required only score, which permits a response that is technically conformant and useless. If a field is needed for the record to mean anything, requiring it is free and removes a branch from every consumer.

Exercise 4.2 — Should these be structured? For each, decide and justify: (a) classify a support ticket into one of six queues; (b) draft a reply to a customer; (c) extract line items from an invoice image; (d) explain why a deploy failed; (e) decide whether to escalate, with a reason.

Solution 
DECISIONS = [
    ("a  classify into 6 queues", "YES — JSON outputs",
     "The output is an enum that routes code. Constrain it, and the whole "
     "class of unroutable values disappears."),
    ("b  draft a customer reply", "no",
     "A person reads it. Constraining generation to a grammar buys nothing "
     "and costs expressiveness plus an injected system prompt."),
    ("c  extract invoice line items", "YES — JSON outputs",
     "An array of typed objects feeding an accounting system. The canonical "
     "case, and the arrays are where hand-parsing hurts most."),
    ("d  explain a deploy failure", "no",
     "Prose is the deliverable. A one-field {\"explanation\": string} schema "
     "is 4.8's anti-pattern in its purest form."),
    ("e  escalate, with a reason", "YES — mixed",
     "The decision is an enum the code branches on; the reason is prose for "
     "a human. One schema holds both, and only the enum is load-bearing."),
]

for task, verdict, why in DECISIONS:
    print(f"{task:<30} -> {verdict}")
    print(f"{'':30}    {why}")

ESCALATION = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "escalate": {"type": "boolean"},
        "tier": {"type": "string", "enum": ["none", "l2", "l3", "oncall"]},
        "reason": {"type": "string",
                   "description": "One sentence, for the receiving engineer."},
    },
    "required": ["escalate", "tier", "reason"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}
print()
print("(e) the schema that gets both halves right:")
for field, spec in ESCALATION["properties"].items():
    kind = spec.get("enum") or spec["type"]
    print(f"  {field:<10} {kind}")

a  classify into 6 queues      -> YES — JSON outputs
                                  The output is an enum that routes code. Constrain it, and the whole class of unroutable values disappears.
b  draft a customer reply      -> no
                                  A person reads it. Constraining generation to a grammar buys nothing and costs expressiveness plus an injected system prompt.
c  extract invoice line items  -> YES — JSON outputs
                                  An array of typed objects feeding an accounting system. The canonical case, and the arrays are where hand-parsing hurts most.
d  explain a deploy failure    -> no
                                  Prose is the deliverable. A one-field {"explanation": string} schema is 4.8's anti-pattern in its purest form.
e  escalate, with a reason     -> YES — mixed
                                  The decision is an enum the code branches on; the reason is prose for a human. One schema holds both, and only the enum is load-bearing.

(e) the schema that gets both halves right:
  escalate   boolean
  tier       ['none', 'l2', 'l3', 'oncall']
  reason     string

(a) and (c) are unambiguous yeses, and they are most of what structured outputs exist for. In (a) the enum means an unroutable value is unreachable and not merely rare, which is a failure your code no longer needs a branch for. In (c) the win is arrays of typed objects, which is where prompt-and-parse is at its worst: a single malformed row in a twelve-row invoice used to poison the whole extraction.

(b) and (d) are noes for the same reason. A human reads the output, so the only thing a grammar can do is constrain how the model expresses itself. That is a real cost, because constrained decoding changes phrasing around the constrained region. And it is bought for a parse that was never going to happen, because nobody is parsing.

(e) is the interesting one, and it is the shape most production decisions take. There is a machine-readable decision and a human-readable justification, and it is tempting to treat that as two different problems. One schema handles both: escalate and tier are constrained and load-bearing, and reason is a free string with guidance in its description. The grammar does nothing useful for reason, and that is fine. It is along for the ride, and putting it in the same response means the reason is guaranteed to accompany the decision and does not need a second call.

The general test. Ask what would happen if the model returned something unexpected. If the answer is "my code takes a wrong branch or throws", constrain it. If the answer is "a person reads a slightly odd sentence", do not.

SECTION 5

Thinking and Effort

A model answering in one pass has to be right immediately. It has no scratch work, no checking, and no way to change course halfway. For a proof, a subtle bug or a long agentic task, the first approach is often not the best one, and a model with no room to discover that produces a confident wrong answer.

Thinking removes that constraint. With thinking active, the model first works through the problem in its own words: restating it, trying approaches, checking intermediate results, and abandoning paths that do not hold up. That reasoning arrives in thinking content blocks ahead of the response.

It is not free, and the cost is not where people expect. Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, at output prices, and they count against max_tokens alongside the answer. So the question is never "should I enable thinking" but "how much reasoning is this task worth". The API gives you two separate controls for that.

5.1 Two Controls, and Which One You Want

thinking decides whether the model reasons in thinking blocks. effort decides how much work goes into the whole response, meaning text, tool calls and thinking together.

thinking
A mode. {"type": "adaptive"} lets the model decide when and how deeply to think. {"type": "disabled"} turns it off where the model allows that. It is not a dial.
output_config.effort
The dial, and the one to reach for. Five levels from low to max. It scales everything the model spends tokens on, including how many tool calls it makes.

That second property is what makes effort the better control in agentic systems: lower effort means fewer tool calls, and not merely shorter thinking. No thinking-specific parameter can do that.

On Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, thinking is already on. No configuration is needed. What you usually want first on these models is to see it, because display defaults to "omitted" there.

On Opus 4.8, 4.7, 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, thinking is off until you set thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}. There is also an older mode you will meet in inherited code: manual extended thinking, written {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}, where budget_tokens reserves a fixed allowance for reasoning. Adaptive thinking replaced it, and the two differ in more than syntax. A budget_tokens allowance is a number you must tune per task, while adaptive thinking decides per request. Note also that a top-level budget_tokens argument is not a thing at all. It belongs inside thinking, and passing it at the top level is the TypeError that §2's exercise plants.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    thinking={"type": "adaptive", "display": "summarized"},
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "A train leaves at 14:05 and arrives at 17:40, "
                          "stopping twice for 8 minutes each. What was its "
                          "moving time?"}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "thinking":
        print("thinking  :", block.thinking[:90])
        print("signature :", block.signature[:24] + "…")
    elif block.type == "text":
        print("answer    :", block.text)

print("output tokens (thinking INCLUDED):", response.usage.output_tokens)

thinking  : The train runs 14:05 to 17:40, which is 3 hours 35 minutes, or 215 minutes. Two stops of 8
signature : WaUjzkypQ2mUEVM36O2TxuHt…
answer    : 3 hours and 19 minutes of moving time.
output tokens (thinking INCLUDED): 312

Two fields on that block matter later. thinking holds a summary of the reasoning, and never the raw chain of thought, on any setting. signature holds the full reasoning, encrypted, and it is what you pass back so the model can continue from where it left off (§5.4).

5.2 Effort Levels

There are five levels. high is the default, and setting it explicitly is identical to omitting the parameter.

max
No constraint on token spend. The deepest reasoning available. For problems where getting it right dominates everything else — and where overthinking is an acceptable price, because at this level the model will keep exploring a problem that a lower level would have closed.
xhigh
Extended, for long-horizon work — agentic and coding tasks running over thirty minutes with token budgets in the millions. Newer than max, and some models that support max do not support it.
high
The default. Complex reasoning, difficult coding, agentic tasks. Identical to omitting effort entirely.
medium
Balanced. Moderate token savings for agentic work that has to weigh speed and cost against quality.
low
Most efficient. Significant savings with some capability reduction. The right default for subagents (§11.8) and for graders (§13.5).

Effort is a behavioural signal, not a token budget. At low the model still thinks on a genuinely hard problem. It simply thinks less than it would at high for the same problem. If you need a hard ceiling, that is max_tokens, which is strict.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

QUESTION = ("Given a list of 1,000,000 integers, find the two that sum to a "
            "target. Explain the approach you would choose and why.")

for level in ("low", "high"):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=4096,
        output_config={"effort": level},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": QUESTION}],
    )
    text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    print(f"effort={level:<6} output_tokens={response.usage.output_tokens:>5}"
          f"  answer starts: {text[:44]!r}")

effort=low    output_tokens=  198  answer starts: 'Use a hash set: one pass, O(n) time and O(n)'
effort=high   output_tokens= 1364  answer starts: 'The choice is between sorting with two point'

Two operational notes that will save you a debugging session.

Do not pass adaptive as an effort value. adaptive is a thinking mode, and the effort levels are the five above. Mixing them up produces a 400 that reads confusingly.

If the model is overthinking, lower the effort and do not instruct it not to. Overthinking means long deliberation on a problem that did not need it. It is a spend problem with a spend dial, and asking the model in prose to think less is a far weaker lever than the parameter that governs how many tokens it may use.

Changing effort invalidates prompt cache. It is rendered into the prompt, so it always invalidates message blocks and, on some models, tools and system too (§9.5). There is one exception: setting effort explicitly to the model's default is equivalent to omitting it and does not invalidate. So a request that alternates between low and high on the same conversation is two prefixes and not one.

5.3 Reading Thinking Output

Thinking display is controlled by the display field, which decides whether the summary text comes back at all.

BEHAVIOUR = [
    ("summarized", "a readable summary of the reasoning", "yes", "yes",
     "Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 and earlier"),
    ("omitted", "an EMPTY thinking field", "no", "yes",
     "Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Fable 5, Mythos 5"),
]

print(f"{'display':<13}{'thinking field':<38}{'text?':<7}{'signature?':<12}"
      f"{'default on'}")
for value, what, text, sig, default_on in BEHAVIOUR:
    print(f"{value:<13}{what:<38}{text:<7}{sig:<12}{default_on}")

print()
print("BILLED THE SAME in both cases: omitting reduces latency, not cost")
print("the signature is IDENTICAL either way, and can be switched between turns")

display      thinking field                        text?  signature?  default on
summarized   a readable summary of the reasoning   yes    yes         Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 and earlier
omitted      an EMPTY thinking field               no     yes         Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Fable 5, Mythos 5

BILLED THE SAME in both cases: omitting reduces latency, not cost
the signature is IDENTICAL either way, and can be switched between turns

display: "omitted" buys latency, not money. Thinking display is therefore an interface decision and not a cost one: set it to "summarized" when you show reasoning to a user, and "omitted" when you do not. You are charged for every thinking token generated regardless. What it saves is time to first text token when streaming. The server skips streaming thinking tokens and delivers only the signature, so the answer starts sooner. If your interface does not show reasoning to users, this is a straightforward win.

Three further facts about summarised thinking change how you should read it:

It is never the raw chain of thought. No setting returns that. The summary is produced by a different model from the one you targeted, and the thinking model never sees the summary.

You are billed for the full thinking, not the summary. The billed output-token count will not match the tokens visible in the response, and that is expected and not a discrepancy to investigate.

Summarisation behaviour is subject to change. Do not build parsing on its shape.

There is also a distinct block type worth knowing about, because it breaks naive filtering.

# What a response's content list can hold when thinking is active.
BLOCKS = [
