    {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "Let me work through this…",
     "signature": "WaUjzkypQ2mUEVM36O2Txu…"},
    {"type": "redacted_thinking", "data": "EncRypTedOpAqUeBlOb…"},
    {"type": "text", "text": "The moving time was 3 hours 19 minutes."},
]

naive = [b for b in BLOCKS if b["type"] == "thinking"]
correct = [b for b in BLOCKS if b["type"] in ("thinking", "redacted_thinking")]

print("blocks in the response      :", [b["type"] for b in BLOCKS])
print("kept by `type == 'thinking'`:", [b["type"] for b in naive])
print("kept by the correct filter  :", [b["type"] for b in correct])
print()
print("the naive filter silently drops redacted_thinking, which breaks the")
print("multi-turn protocol with a 400 on the NEXT request, not this one")

blocks in the response      : ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'text']
kept by `type == 'thinking'`: ['thinking']
kept by the correct filter  : ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking']

the naive filter silently drops redacted_thinking, which breaks the
multi-turn protocol with a 400 on the NEXT request, not this one

redacted_thinking blocks appear when part of the reasoning is safety-redacted. The data field is opaque and encrypted, and the block must be passed back unchanged like any other. Filtering on block.type == "thinking" alone drops it, and the failure surfaces one request later as a rejected message sequence. That is exactly the kind of bug that is hard to attribute.

5.4 Thinking With Tools

Thinking and tool use work together, with one rule that is absolute: within a tool-use turn, every thinking block must go back to the API complete and unmodified.

The reason is that a tool-use loop is one assistant turn. From the model's point of view it has not finished responding. It paused to wait for information. The reasoning that led to the tool call is part of the response it is still constructing.

def round_trip(assistant_content, tool_result):
    """Preserve the assistant turn exactly, then append the result."""
    return [
        {"role": "assistant", "content": assistant_content},
        {"role": "user", "content": [tool_result]},
    ]


ASSISTANT = [
    {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "I need the current weather first.",
     "signature": "sig_abc…"},
    {"type": "redacted_thinking", "data": "opaque…"},
    {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "get_weather",
     "input": {"city": "Paris"}},
]
RESULT = {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01", "content": "20C"}

good = round_trip(ASSISTANT, RESULT)
stripped = round_trip([b for b in ASSISTANT if b["type"] == "tool_use"], RESULT)
edited = round_trip(
    [{**b, "thinking": "shortened"} if b["type"] == "thinking" else b
     for b in ASSISTANT], RESULT)

for label, turn in (("preserved", good), ("thinking stripped", stripped),
                    ("thinking edited", edited)):
    blocks = [b["type"] for b in turn[0]["content"]]
    ok = blocks == [b["type"] for b in ASSISTANT] and turn[0]["content"] == ASSISTANT
    print(f"{label:<20}{str(blocks):<58}{'accepted' if ok else 'REJECTED (400)'}")

preserved           ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'tool_use']             accepted
thinking stripped   ['tool_use']                                              REJECTED (400)
thinking edited     ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'tool_use']             REJECTED (400)

Modified thinking blocks are rejected with a 400. They are not silently ignored. Within the latest assistant message, the sequence of consecutive thinking blocks must match what the model generated: you cannot rearrange them, edit them, or drop some of them. The single exception is text placed in the empty thinking field of an omitted block, which is ignored and not rejected.

Across turns the rule relaxes:

Required
Within a tool-use turn, pass thinking blocks back.
Recommended
Across turns, pass everything back. The API filters automatically, keeps what it needs, and bills input tokens only for the blocks actually shown to the model.
Allowed
Outside tool use, omit prior turns' thinking entirely.

Do not prune old thinking yourself. Pass it all back, and the API decides what to keep. Which prior-turn blocks survive depends on the model. Opus 4.5 and later, Sonnet 4.6 and later, Fable 5 and Mythos 5 keep all prior turns. Earlier Opus and Sonnet models and every Haiku through 4.5 keep only the last turn and strip the rest for you.

One case demands manual stripping: switching models mid-conversation. Thinking blocks are tied to the model that produced them. After a fallback to a different model (§14.6), strip thinking and redacted_thinking from prior assistant turns. Other models will not reject them, because they silently ignore them, but ignored blocks still cost input tokens.

Interleaved thinking means reasoning between tool calls and not only before the first one. It is automatic with adaptive thinking on every model that supports it, and needs no beta header (a request header that opts in to a feature still in testing). That is worth stating because interleaved thinking used to require one, and under manual extended thinking it still does, and it changes how the thinking budget is counted. Any guide that tells you to set a beta header for interleaved thinking is describing the manual mode. On Fable 5, Mythos 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 4.7, reasoning between tool calls always appears in thinking blocks. Haiku 4.5 does not support it. Note that consecutive tool calls do not require interleaving. It changes where thinking appears, and not whether calls can chain.

There is one incompatibility to know: forced tool use works with adaptive thinking and not with manual extended thinking. Under thinking: {"type": "enabled"}, only a tool_choice of auto or none is accepted, and any and a named tool are errors. Adaptive thinking, including where it is on by default, supports forced tool use.

5.5 Thinking and the Context Window

Thinking occupies the window, and how much depends on when it was generated.

TURNS = 12
THINKING_PER_TURN = 900
TEXT_PER_TURN = 260
QUESTION = 60
SYSTEM = 1_200

keep_all, last_only = SYSTEM, SYSTEM
print(f"{'turn':>5}{'keep-all context':>19}{'last-turn-only':>17}{'gap':>9}")
for turn in range(1, TURNS + 1):
    keep_all += QUESTION + THINKING_PER_TURN + TEXT_PER_TURN
    last_only += QUESTION + TEXT_PER_TURN
    if turn in (1, 4, 8, 12):
        print(f"{turn:>5}{keep_all:>19,}{last_only + THINKING_PER_TURN:>17,}"
              f"{keep_all - last_only - THINKING_PER_TURN:>9,}")

print()
print(f"after {TURNS} turns, retained thinking accounts for "
      f"{TURNS * THINKING_PER_TURN:,} input tokens")
print("on keep-all models that is ordinary conversation history, billed as input")

turn   keep-all context   last-turn-only      gap
    1              2,420            2,420        0
    4              6,080            3,380    2,700
    8             10,960            4,660    6,300
   12             15,840            5,940    9,900

after 12 turns, retained thinking accounts for 10,800 input tokens
on keep-all models that is ordinary conversation history, billed as input

On keep-all models, budget for thinking as if it were conversation history, because it is. Long agentic sessions accumulate it. The lever is clear_thinking_20251015 (§9.6), and note that its cache interaction runs opposite to tool-result clearing: keeping thinking blocks preserves the cache, and clearing them invalidates it at the clearing point.

Two hard limits worth having in mind:

max_tokens includes thinking and is strict. On Claude 4.5 and newer, if input plus max_tokens exceeds the window, the request is accepted, and generation stops with stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded" if it actually reaches the limit. On earlier models it is a validation error up front.

Output caps are per model. Fable 5, Mythos 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 support up to 128k output tokens, and Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5 support 64k. The message batches API raises it further: a beta header there lifts the cap to 300k for several models, which is one of several reasons message batches suit thinking-heavy work (§15.2).

And here is a client-side rule that trips people: the SDKs require streaming when max_tokens exceeds 21,333, to avoid HTTP timeouts. That is validation in the SDK and not an API restriction, and it is why §11.3's task-budget example uses .stream() with get_final_message().

5.6 Choosing an Effort Level

The decision is economic, and it is worth doing with numbers and not instinct.

OUT_PER_MTOK, IN_PER_MTOK = 25.00, 5.00
INPUT_TOKENS = 3_500
REQUESTS_PER_DAY, DAYS = 40_000, 30

# Output token counts observed for one workload at each level.
PROFILE = [("low", 210, 0.71), ("medium", 640, 0.83),
           ("high", 1_450, 0.89), ("max", 3_900, 0.91)]

print(f"{'effort':<9}{'out tokens':>12}{'accuracy':>10}{'$/month':>12}"
      f"{'$ per accuracy point':>22}")
previous = None
for level, out_tokens, accuracy in PROFILE:
    monthly = ((INPUT_TOKENS / 1e6 * IN_PER_MTOK
                + out_tokens / 1e6 * OUT_PER_MTOK)
               * REQUESTS_PER_DAY * DAYS)
    if previous is None:
        marginal = "—"
    else:
        prev_cost, prev_acc = previous
        marginal = "$" + format((monthly - prev_cost)
                                / ((accuracy - prev_acc) * 100), ",.0f")
    previous = (monthly, accuracy)
    print(f"{level:<9}{out_tokens:>12,}{accuracy:>10.0%}"
          f"{'$' + format(monthly, ',.0f'):>12}{marginal:>22}")

print()
print("the last column is the cost of ONE more accuracy point at that step,")
print("not the average since `low` — the two tell very different stories")

effort     out tokens  accuracy     $/month  $ per accuracy point
low               210       71%     $27,300                     —
medium            640       83%     $40,200                $1,075
high            1,450       89%     $64,500                $4,050
max             3,900       91%    $138,000               $36,750

the last column is the cost of ONE more accuracy point at that step,
not the average since `low` — the two tell very different stories

Read the last column, not the third. Accuracy rises steadily with effort, and so does cost. What decides the level is the marginal cost of each additional point, and that column climbs from $1,075 to $36,750 across three steps. The last step buys two accuracy points for $73,500, which is nearly twice what the first eighteen points cost in total. "Diminishing returns" is too gentle a phrase for a 34-fold change in marginal price, and this shape is typical and not pathological.

That does not make max wrong. It makes it a choice you should make deliberately, and usually a per-request one. Using max on the 3% of requests a router judges hard, and low on the rest, is a far better system than either level applied uniformly.

Three defaults worth adopting:

low for graders and subagents. A judge applying an explicit rubric (§13.5) and a worker summarising a document (§11.8) are not the tasks that need deep reasoning, and both run at high volume.

high, which means doing nothing, for the main path. It is the default because it is the right default.

xhigh for long-horizon agentic work, where the token budget is in the millions and the run takes half an hour. It exists for that shape specifically.

And measure it. The accuracy column above is a profile of one workload, and yours will differ. §13's eval harness (the program that runs your test cases and scores the results) is how you produce your own version of that table and do not inherit someone else's. Running an eval harness across two effort levels is an afternoon's work, and it replaces every guess in this subsection with your own numbers.

Exercises

Exercise 5.1 — Find the bug in this loop. An agent using thinking and tools works for one turn and then fails with a 400 saying thinking blocks cannot be modified. Find it.

while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    thinking = [b for b in response.content if b.type == "thinking"]
    calls = [b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": thinking + calls})
    results = [run(c) for c in calls]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    response = client.messages.create(**kwargs, messages=messages)
Solution 
ORIGINAL = [
    {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "First I should check the order.",
     "signature": "sig_a…"},
    {"type": "redacted_thinking", "data": "opaque…"},
    {"type": "text", "text": "Let me look that up."},
    {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_1", "name": "get_order",
     "input": {"id": "ord_1"}},
]


def buggy(content):
    thinking = [b for b in content if b["type"] == "thinking"]
    calls = [b for b in content if b["type"] == "tool_use"]
    return thinking + calls


def fixed(content):
    """Pass the assistant turn back exactly as it arrived."""
    return list(content)


for label, rebuilt in (("filtered", buggy(ORIGINAL)), ("verbatim", fixed(ORIGINAL))):
    types = [b["type"] for b in rebuilt]
    print(f"{label:<10}{str(types):<70}")
    print(f"{'':10}identical to what the model produced: {rebuilt == ORIGINAL}")
    dropped = [b["type"] for b in ORIGINAL if b not in rebuilt]
    print(f"{'':10}dropped: {dropped or 'nothing'}")
    print()

filtered  ['thinking', 'tool_use']                                              
          identical to what the model produced: False
          dropped: ['redacted_thinking', 'text']

verbatim  ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'text', 'tool_use']                 
          identical to what the model produced: True
          dropped: nothing

The filter drops redacted_thinking. That is the bug, and it is the specific trap §5.3 named. block.type == "thinking" looks exhaustive and is not. When part of the reasoning is safety-redacted, it arrives as a redacted_thinking block, which must be passed back unchanged like any other. The rebuilt turn no longer matches what the model generated, and the API rejects it.

It also drops the text block, which is a second, quieter defect. The model often narrates before calling, with something like "Let me look that up.", and reconstructing the turn from thinking plus tool calls discards that. Here it happens not to be the thing that triggers the 400, but it does mean the conversation history no longer reflects what the assistant actually said.

The fix is not a better filter. It is not filtering. response.content is exactly what the API expects back. Every rule in §5.4 (do not rearrange, do not edit, do not partially drop) is satisfied for free by appending the list you were given. Any code that rebuilds an assistant turn from selected blocks will break the next time a block type is added, and block types keep being added.

Why it worked for one turn. The first request has no prior assistant turn to preserve, so the bug cannot fire. It fires on the second. That makes it look like a problem with the loop and not with the append, which is a good example of why the §13.10 trajectory tests matter: a single-turn test passes.

Exercise 5.2 — Choose the effort level. Three workloads. Pick a level for each and say what you would measure to confirm it: (a) a customer-facing chat assistant, 200,000 requests a day; (b) an LLM judge grading 5,000 eval cases per run; (c) an agent that refactors a module and opens a pull request, a few dozen runs a day.

Solution 
WORKLOADS = [
    ("a  customer chat", 200_000, "low or medium", 3_200, 240,
     "latency and cost dominate; answers are short and mostly routine"),
    ("b  LLM judge", 5_000, "low", 900, 60,
     "an explicit rubric is not a reasoning task; volume is what matters"),
    ("c  refactor + PR", 40, "xhigh", 28_000, 9_000,
     "long-horizon, high value per run, and a human gate catches errors"),
]
IN_PER_MTOK, OUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 25.00

print(f"{'workload':<20}{'runs/day':>10}  {'effort':<16}{'$/day':>10}{'$/run':>11}")
for name, runs, effort, in_tokens, out_tokens, _ in WORKLOADS:
    per_run = in_tokens / 1e6 * IN_PER_MTOK + out_tokens / 1e6 * OUT_PER_MTOK
    print(f"{name:<20}{runs:>10,}  {effort:<16}"
          f"{'$' + format(per_run * runs, ',.0f'):>10}{'$%.4f' % per_run:>11}")

print()
for name, _, _, _, _, reason in WORKLOADS:
    print(f"{name:<20}{reason}")

workload              runs/day  effort               $/day      $/run
a  customer chat       200,000  low or medium       $4,400    $0.0220
b  LLM judge             5,000  low                    $30    $0.0060
c  refactor + PR            40  xhigh                  $15    $0.3650

a  customer chat    latency and cost dominate; answers are short and mostly routine
b  LLM judge        an explicit rubric is not a reasoning task; volume is what matters
c  refactor + PR    long-horizon, high value per run, and a human gate catches errors

(a) Customer chat: low, moving to medium only if an eval says so. At 200,000 requests a day, this is the workload where effort is worth the most money, and it is also the one where deep reasoning helps least, because most turns are routine. The thing to measure is not cost, which is obvious, but quality on the tail. Run §13's suite at low and medium and look specifically at the hard cases, because the mean will barely move while the difficult 5% may move a lot. If it does, the answer is not a higher global effort. It is a router that escalates those cases.

(b) The judge: low, and I would not consider anything else. §13.5 makes the argument: grading against an explicit rubric is a classification and not a reasoning problem, and the rubric is doing the work that thinking would otherwise have to do. What to measure is Cohen's kappa against human labels (§13.6) at low. If it clears the bar, higher effort is spending money to agree with humans slightly more confidently.

(c) The refactor agent: xhigh, and this is what it exists for. Long-horizon coding over half an hour with a token budget in the millions is the documented shape for that level. At forty runs a day, the cost per run is what matters, and it is small against an engineer's time. The gate matters too. The pull request is a human review (§11.6), so an error is caught and not shipped, which is what makes spending on capability rational here and not in (a).

What I would measure in all three, and it is the same thing. Effort is a behavioural signal and not a budget, so the only way to know what a level costs you is to run your own workload at two levels and compare output tokens and quality. The profile in §5.6 is one workload's curve. The shape generalises, and the numbers do not.

And one thing I would not do: set effort globally and forget it. The largest gain available in (a) is not choosing between low and medium. It is routing, so that most requests run at low and the hard ones run at high. A single global level leaves most of the value on the table.

SECTION 6

Tool Use

Everything so far has been one request and one answer. This section is where a language model stops being a text generator and becomes something you can build a system out of. The mechanism is smaller than its reputation suggests. There is no new endpoint, no agent runtime and no framework. You add a tools array to the same request, and the model gains the ability to emit a structured request instead of prose. Your program decides what to do with it.

Hold that sentence, because every safety property in the rest of this course descends from it. The model never executes anything. It produces a block of JSON that names a function and supplies arguments. A loop you wrote decides whether to run it, what to run it against, and what to say happened. "The model deleted the row" is never true. What always happened is that "my loop passed the model's proposal to a function that deleted the row".

6.1 The Contract: The Model Proposes, Your Code Disposes

Tool use is a contract with three parties, and it is worth naming them because two of the three are yours.

You, declaring
The schema. A name, a description written for a reader who has never seen your system, and a JSON Schema for the arguments. This is the entire interface — the model never sees your implementation, your database, or your error messages except the ones you choose to hand back.
The model, choosing
Whether to call, which to call, and with what arguments. It decides from the conversation and your descriptions. This is the only part you do not control, and improving it is almost entirely a matter of improving the description.
You, executing
The call, the authorisation, and the result. Your loop runs the function — or refuses to. Every check that matters (is this user allowed to read that row? is this amount above the approval threshold?) lives here, because it is the only place that has the request context the model does not.

There is a second axis, and it decides how much of the loop you write at all: where the code runs. There are three cases, and they behave differently enough that mixing them up is a genuine source of confusion.

User-defined tools are the ordinary case and most of this section. You write the schema and the code. The response contains a tool_use block, and you execute it and send back a tool_result.

Anthropic-schema tools are also executed by you, but the schema is published and not invented by you. The set is bash, the text editor tool for creating and editing files, the memory tool for state that outlives a conversation (§9.8), computer use for screenshot-and-keyboard control of a desktop, and browser use for navigating and interacting with pages in your own browser. Note that computer use and browser use are toolsets and not single tools, meaning one entry declares a fixed set of member tools. The text editor tool and the memory tool are ordinary single entries. You declare them by a date-versioned type and no input_schema. The reason to prefer one over a custom tool that does the same job is not convenience. These signatures are trained-in, so the model calls them more reliably and recovers from their errors more gracefully than it does with a bespoke equivalent. §6.10 returns to when that matters.

Server-executed tools (web_search, web_fetch, code_execution and tool_search) run on Anthropic's infrastructure. You enable them and read the answer, and you never build a tool_result for them. §7 is entirely about these, including the one case where the server loop hands control back to you mid-flight.

The distinction that matters for this section: client tools require a loop, server tools do not.

6.2 Defining a Tool

A user-defined tool is a dict with three required keys and one optional one that earns its place surprisingly often.

get_weather = {
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": (
        "Get the current weather for a city. Returns temperature in Celsius, "
        "a one-word condition, and the observation time in UTC. Use this when the "
        "user asks about current conditions; it does not provide forecasts, "
        "historical weather, or air quality. If the city is ambiguous, ask the "
        "user to disambiguate rather than guessing a country."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "city": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "City name, optionally with country: 'Lisbon, PT'.",
            },
            "unit": {
                "type": "string",
                "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                "description": "Temperature unit. Defaults to celsius.",
            },
        },
        "required": ["city"],
    },
}

print("name       :", get_weather["name"])
print("required   :", get_weather["input_schema"]["required"])
print("optional   :", sorted(set(get_weather["input_schema"]["properties"])
                             - set(get_weather["input_schema"]["required"])))
print("desc words :", len(get_weather["description"].split()))

name       : get_weather
required   : ['city']
optional   : ['unit']
desc words : 54

name must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$. input_schema is ordinary JSON Schema. Neither is where the difficulty lives.

The tool description is the tool. It is by a wide margin the largest lever on whether the model calls the right thing with the right arguments. It is also the part engineers under-write, because to the person who built the function its purpose is obvious. It is not obvious to a reader who has only this paragraph. Aim for three or four sentences at minimum, and cover four things: what it does, when to use it, when not to, and what it does not return. A tool description written to that shape is longer than feels necessary and is still the cheapest accuracy improvement available.

That last one is worth dwelling on. A tool called get_weather that silently returns no forecast will be called for forecasts, the result will not contain one, and the model will do something unhelpful with the gap, most often inventing a forecast. Saying "it does not provide forecasts" costs a handful of tokens and removes an entire failure mode.

The optional fourth key is input_examples. It is an array of example input objects, schema-validated, for tools whose arguments are complex, nested or format-sensitive. Descriptions come first, and you reach for examples when a sentence cannot convey the shape.

search_orders = {
    "name": "search_orders",
    "description": (
        "Search orders by any combination of customer, status and date range. "
        "Omitted filters are not applied. Returns at most 50 orders, newest first."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "customer_id": {"type": "string"},
            "status": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["placed", "shipped", "cancelled"]},
            "placed_between": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {"from": {"type": "string", "format": "date"},
                               "to": {"type": "string", "format": "date"}},
                "required": ["from", "to"],
            },
        },
    },
    "input_examples": [
        {"customer_id": "c_8814"},
        {"status": "shipped",
         "placed_between": {"from": "2026-08-01", "to": "2026-08-25"}},
    ],
}

for i, ex in enumerate(search_orders["input_examples"], 1):
    print(f"example {i}: {ex}")

example 1: {'customer_id': 'c_8814'}
example 2: {'status': 'shipped', 'placed_between': {'from': '2026-08-01', 'to': '2026-08-25'}}

One more thing happens when you pass tools, and it is invisible unless you know to look: the API builds a system prompt out of your tool definitions and prepends it to whatever system prompt you supplied. Your descriptions are not metadata sitting beside the conversation. They are text in the context window, they cost input tokens on every single request, and they compete for the model's attention with everything else. §6.9 does the arithmetic. It is the reason "just add all forty tools" stops working.

6.3 The Shape of a Tool-Use Turn

Send a request with tools, and the model may answer with prose as usual, or it may stop and ask for a call. The signal is stop_reason.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

tools = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Current weather for a city. Returns Celsius and a condition.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["city"],
    },
}]

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Lisbon?"}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
for block in response.content:
    print("block type :", block.type)
    if block.type == "text":
        print("  text     :", block.text)
    elif block.type == "tool_use":
        print("  id       :", block.id)
        print("  name     :", block.name)
        print("  input    :", block.input)

stop_reason: tool_use
block type : text
  text     : Let me look that up.
block type : tool_use
  id       : toolu_01Wx9Kq
  name     : get_weather
  input    : {'city': 'Lisbon'}

Four things in that output are load-bearing.

stop_reason is "tool_use", and not "end_turn". This is the flag your loop keys on, and it is the only reliable one. The presence of a tool_use block and this stop reason always agree, but reading the stop reason keeps the loop readable and handles the other reasons in the same if.

The turn can contain both text and a tool call. Models often narrate before calling. Your loop must iterate over response.content and not assume content[0] is the call. Assuming index zero is a real bug that appears the first time the model says "Let me check that for you." before calling.

block.input is already a dict. The SDK parsed it. Never string-match on the serialised form, because escaping of Unicode and forward slashes varies, and a regex over it will break on a customer whose name contains an apostrophe.

block.id is the correlation key. It is how the result you send back gets matched to the call. Losing it is how you end up with a 400 that says your tool_result has no corresponding tool_use.

6.4 The Agent Loop

The whole of client-side tool use is one while. Here it is with a real, if small, tool behind it.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

WEATHER = {"Lisbon": (19, "clear"), "Reykjavik": (4, "sleet")}


def get_weather(city):
    if city not in WEATHER:
        raise KeyError(f"no station for {city!r}")
    degrees, condition = WEATHER[city]
    return f"{degrees}C, {condition}"


TOOLS = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Current weather for a city. Returns Celsius and a condition.",
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
                     "required": ["city"]},
}]
IMPLEMENTATIONS = {"get_weather": get_weather}

messages = [{"role": "user",
             "content": "Compare the weather in Lisbon and Reykjavik."}]

turns = 0
while True:
    turns += 1
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    print(f"turn {turns}: stop_reason={response.stop_reason}")

    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break

    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

    results = []
    for block in response.content:
        if block.type != "tool_use":
            continue
        print(f"  calling {block.name}({block.input})")
        try:
            output = IMPLEMENTATIONS[block.name](**block.input)
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": output})
        except Exception as exc:
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
                            "is_error": True})

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

final = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
print("final:", final)
print("messages in the conversation:", len(messages))

turn 1: stop_reason=tool_use
  calling get_weather({'city': 'Lisbon'})
  calling get_weather({'city': 'Reykjavik'})
turn 2: stop_reason=end_turn
final: Lisbon is 19C and clear; Reykjavik is 4C with sleet. Lisbon is 15 degrees warmer.
messages in the conversation: 3

Read the structure rather than the weather.

The assistant turn is appended verbatim. response.content goes back as the assistant message, meaning the SDK objects and not a string you reconstructed. Rebuilding it by hand drops the tool call, and the next request is then a conversation in which the model asked for nothing and you answered anyway.

All results go back in a single user message. That means one message with all of them, and not one message per result. This matters more than it looks. Splitting them is accepted by the API but teaches the model, turn after turn, that its parallel calls are being serialised, and it stops making them. §6.6 measures what that costs.

The loop exits on any stop reason that is not tool_use. end_turn is the happy path. max_tokens, stop_sequence and refusal all also land here, and all need handling, which §2.9 and §14.6 cover. A loop written as while response.stop_reason == "tool_use" with no other branch will silently treat a truncated answer as a final one.

There is no stop condition. That is the loop's one real defect, and it is deliberate here so you see it plainly. A model that keeps calling tools keeps this loop running until your bill or your patience ends. §11.3 fixes it properly with an iteration cap, a token budget, and a rule for what to do when either is hit.

Here is one shortcut worth knowing before you write this loop a second time. The SDK ships a tool runner, client.beta.messages.tool_runner, which drives exactly this loop for you given your tools and their implementations, with a max_iterations cap built in. It is the right default for a straightforward loop. Write the loop by hand when you need a gate, a budget beyond iterations, or a trace. §11 does that, and it is why the loop is worth understanding and not merely calling. The tool runner is the right shortcut once you understand what it is doing on your behalf, and the wrong one before.

The conversation grows by two messages per tool round trip, and you resend all of it every time. That is the arithmetic that makes §9 necessary.

6.5 Returning Results, and Returning Failures

A tool_result block has three fields that matter: tool_use_id, content, and is_error. The last one separates a robust agent from a fragile one.

The instinct when a tool throws is to catch it, log it, and drop out of the loop. That is almost always wrong. The model is capable of recovering from a failure it is told about. It can retry with a corrected argument, try a different tool, or tell the user what went wrong. It can do none of those if the failure never reaches it.

def render(result):
    """The three shapes a tool result takes, and what each tells the model."""
    return {k: v for k, v in result.items() if v is not None}


ok = render({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01",
             "content": "19C, clear", "is_error": None})

vague = render({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_02",
                "content": "failed", "is_error": True})

useful = render({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_02",
                 "content": "RateLimitError: weather service allows 10 requests "
                            "per minute. Retry after 42 seconds, or call "
                            "get_cached_weather for a reading up to 1 hour old.",
                 "is_error": True})

for label, block in (("success", ok), ("useless error", vague),
                     ("instructive error", useful)):
    print(f"{label:<18} {len(str(block)):>4} chars  is_error={block.get('is_error', False)}")
    print(f"{'':18} {block['content'][:70]}")

success              75 chars  is_error=False
                   19C, clear
useless error        89 chars  is_error=True
                   failed
instructive error   228 chars  is_error=True
                   RateLimitError: weather service allows 10 requests per minute. Retry a

Write errors as instructions, not as status. "failed" tells the model nothing it can act on, so it apologises to the user. The third form names the constraint, gives a number, and offers an alternative, and the model will take the alternative. This is the single cheapest reliability improvement available in tool use, and it costs a sentence.

Three rules follow from the same principle:

Return a result for every call, including ones you chose not to run. If you executed a batch sequentially and stopped after a failure, the skipped calls still need tool_result blocks with is_error: true and a line saying why ("Not executed: the preceding write_file call failed."). A missing result is a protocol error, and an explained non-execution is information.

Do not leak internals into the error. The content goes into the context window and, through the model's reply, potentially to the user. A stack trace with your table names in it is both a token cost and a disclosure. §14.4 treats this as the injection surface it is.

An invalid tool call is a description bug first. If the model omits a required parameter, the honest fix is a clearer schema and description. Returning "Error: missing required 'city'" does work, because the model retries two or three times with corrections. But you are paying a round trip to compensate for a sentence you did not write. §6.8 removes the failure mode entirely for the cases where that is worth doing.

6.6 Parallel Tool Use

A single assistant turn can contain several tool_use blocks. This is on by default, and it is the difference between an agent that feels responsive and one that does not. The comparison is not subtle, because the cost is a model round trip per serialised call and not a function call.

LATENCY_MS = {"model_turn": 1400, "search_orders": 220,
              "get_customer": 180, "get_shipment": 260}
CALLS = ["search_orders", "get_customer", "get_shipment"]

# Serial: the model asks for one tool, gets the answer, asks for the next.
serial = 0
for call in CALLS:
    serial += LATENCY_MS["model_turn"] + LATENCY_MS[call]
serial += LATENCY_MS["model_turn"]          # the final answer

# Parallel: one turn proposes all three, you run them concurrently, one turn answers.
parallel = LATENCY_MS["model_turn"] + max(LATENCY_MS[c] for c in CALLS) \
    + LATENCY_MS["model_turn"]

# Parallel calls, but executed one after another by your loop.
parallel_serial_exec = LATENCY_MS["model_turn"] + sum(LATENCY_MS[c] for c in CALLS) \
    + LATENCY_MS["model_turn"]

for name, ms in (("serial (one call per turn)", serial),
                 ("parallel calls, serial execution", parallel_serial_exec),
                 ("parallel calls, concurrent execution", parallel)):
    print(f"{name:<38} {ms:>5} ms  {ms / parallel:>4.1f}x")

serial (one call per turn)              6260 ms   2.0x
parallel calls, serial execution        3460 ms   1.1x
parallel calls, concurrent execution    3060 ms   1.0x

The saving comes from collapsing model turns and not from the tools being fast. Even executing the three calls one after another inside your loop captures most of it, because the model round trip dominates. Concurrency in your executor is the last increment.

The API does not prescribe an execution order. Running the calls concurrently is your choice, and it is usually right for independent, read-only operations. It is the wrong choice for tools with side effects, shared state or ordering requirements, and you should run those sequentially and stop at the first failure. Two of the Anthropic-schema toolsets, computer and browser, are stricter still. When several of their member calls arrive in one turn, they must be run sequentially in the order given and abandoned at the first failure, because a click that lands after a page has changed means something different from the click that was requested.

The formatting rules are absolute, and they produce clear errors when broken. There must be one tool_result per tool_use, matched by tool_use_id, all in the same user message, with every tool_result block placed before any text content in that message.

def build_user_turn(calls, outcomes, note=None):
    """tool_result blocks first, then any text. The order is required."""
    blocks = [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call_id,
               "content": outcomes[call_id]} for call_id in calls]
    if note:
        blocks.append({"type": "text", "text": note})
    return {"role": "user", "content": blocks}


turn = build_user_turn(
    ["toolu_a", "toolu_b"],
    {"toolu_a": "3 orders", "toolu_b": "customer c_8814, gold tier"},
    note="Prioritise the oldest unshipped order.",
)
for block in turn["content"]:
    print(block["type"], "->", block.get("content", block.get("text")))

tool_result -> 3 orders
tool_result -> customer c_8814, gold tier
text -> Prioritise the oldest unshipped order.

If the model has stopped calling tools in parallel, the first thing to check is whether your loop has been splitting results across messages. The second is disable_parallel_tool_use, which lives inside tool_choice and is discussed next.

6.7 Steering the Choice with tool_choice

By default the model decides whether to call anything at all. tool_choice overrides that, and it has four forms.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "record_sentiment",
    "description": "Record the sentiment of a customer message.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "sentiment": {"type": "string",
                          "enum": ["positive", "neutral", "negative"]},
            "confidence": {"type": "number"},
        },
        "required": ["sentiment", "confidence"],
    },
}]

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    tools=TOOLS,
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "record_sentiment"},
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "The delivery was three days late and nobody replied."}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
print("sentiment  :", call.input["sentiment"])
print("confidence :", call.input["confidence"])

stop_reason: tool_use
sentiment  : negative
confidence : 0.92
{"type": "auto"}
The default. The model calls a tool if it judges one useful, otherwise it answers in prose. Right for anything conversational.
{"type": "any"}
Some tool must be called, the model picks which. Useful when every path through the turn should end in a structured action, such as a router that must dispatch to one of several handlers.
{"type": "tool", "name": …}
This exact tool must be called. This is the classifier-and-extractor pattern above: the "tool" is not an action at all, it is a schema, and forcing it turns the model into a typed function. §4 shows the modern alternative and when to prefer it.
{"type": "none"}
No tool may be called on this turn, though the definitions stay in context. Useful for a final "now summarise what you found" turn that must not start new work.

tool_choice also carries disable_parallel_tool_use. Setting it with auto or any limits the turn to at most one call, and setting it with a forced tool gives you exactly one. Reach for it when your executor genuinely cannot handle concurrent calls, and be aware you are paying §6.6's arithmetic to get there.

One trap is worth naming: forcing a tool suppresses the model's ability to say "I cannot". A forced record_sentiment on an empty message still records a sentiment. If "no answer" is a legitimate outcome, it has to be representable inside the schema, such as an enum value of "insufficient_evidence", because the forced call removes the model's other way of telling you.

6.8 Strict Tool Use

An ordinary tool schema is guidance. The model usually produces conforming arguments, but occasionally it omits a required field that looked optional, passes "3" where you asked for a number, or invents a property. Your code then has to validate, and your loop has to round-trip an error.

strict: true on the tool definition removes that class of failure, because inputs are guaranteed to validate against the schema.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "create_refund",
    "description": "Issue a refund against an order.",
    "strict": True,
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "order_id": {"type": "string"},
            "amount_cents": {"type": "integer"},
            "reason": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["damaged", "late", "duplicate"]},
        },
        "required": ["order_id", "amount_cents", "reason"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}]

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    tools=TOOLS,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Refund order ord_5512 in full — it arrived damaged. "
                          "The order was 42.50 EUR."}],
)

call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
print("input      :", call.input)
print("amount type:", type(call.input["amount_cents"]).__name__)
print("reason ok  :", call.input["reason"] in {"damaged", "late", "duplicate"})

input      : {'order_id': 'ord_5512', 'amount_cents': 4250, 'reason': 'damaged'}
amount type: int
reason ok  : True

There are two requirements, and they are the ones people miss. strict is a top-level field on the tool definition, alongside name and description, and not something you put inside tool_choice. And the schema must set additionalProperties: false and list its required fields, because a schema that permits anything cannot guarantee anything.

Use it wherever a bad argument is expensive. Examples are a refund, a write, a deletion and an outbound message. Skip it where the tool is a search whose arguments are advisory and a slightly odd query is harmless.

It is not free of consequences. Strict tools are incompatible with programmatic tool calling (§7.6), and constraining generation has a measurable effect on how the model phrases things around the call. Neither is a reason to avoid it on the tools that change state.

6.9 What a Tool Surface Costs

Tool definitions are context. Every request carries all of them, they are billed as input tokens every time, and they occupy the window that your conversation, your retrieved documents and your system prompt also want. Managing tool context means deciding which definitions are present and what their results leave behind, and it is the constraint that decides how big a tool surface can get. Tool context is also the part of the window you control most directly, which is why it is the first place to look when a request is larger than expected.

# Rough but honest sizing: a serialised tool definition costs about a token per
# four characters. Real counts come from count_tokens (see 2.8); this is the
# back-of-envelope that tells you whether to bother.
def approx_tokens(chars):
    return round(chars / 4)


SMALL = 320     # a two-parameter tool with a four-sentence description
LARGE = 1150    # a nested schema, an enum of 20, three input_examples

for n_tools, size, label in ((5, SMALL, "5 simple tools"),
                             (20, SMALL, "20 simple tools"),
                             (20, LARGE, "20 complex tools"),
                             (120, SMALL, "120 simple tools")):
    per_request = approx_tokens(n_tools * size)
    # 500 requests a day, 30 days, at Opus input pricing of $5 per million tokens.
    monthly = per_request * 500 * 30 / 1_000_000 * 5
    share = per_request / 200_000 * 100
    print(f"{label:<18} {per_request:>7,} tokens/request  "
          f"{share:>5.1f}% of a 200k window  ${monthly:>7,.2f}/month")

5 simple tools         400 tokens/request    0.2% of a 200k window  $  30.00/month
20 simple tools      1,600 tokens/request    0.8% of a 200k window  $ 120.00/month
20 complex tools     5,750 tokens/request    2.9% of a 200k window  $ 431.25/month
120 simple tools     9,600 tokens/request    4.8% of a 200k window  $ 720.00/month

The pricing here is ordinary input-token pricing. There is no separate charge for declaring a tool, so this table is entirely a question of size. Read the two middle rows together: twenty complex definitions cost more than a hundred simple ones, so "how many tools" is the wrong question and "how much schema" is the right one. And note what the table does not show. Even the 120-tool row is under five per cent of a 200k window. Context pressure is rarely the reason a large tool surface fails.

The reason it fails is selection accuracy. The model is choosing from a longer list of similar-sounding options, and a wrong choice costs a whole round trip plus whatever the wrong tool did. That cost does not appear in any of these columns, which is exactly why sizing a surface by tokens alone is reassuring and misleading.

There are four ways out, and they compose.

Fewer, better tools
Consolidate. Six tools with an action parameter beat eighteen near-identical ones. Always try this first; it is free and it improves selection accuracy rather than merely paying for it.
Tool search
Load definitions on demand. Mark tools defer_loading: true and add a search tool; the model discovers what it needs by regex or BM25 instead of carrying everything. §7.5 builds it. Scales to thousands.
Prompt caching
Stop paying repeatedly for the same definitions. Tools render first in the request, before system and messages, which makes them the ideal stable prefix. §9.3 does this properly, including the trap that a changing tool list invalidates everything after it.
Fine-grained tool streaming
For one large argument. Fine-grained tool streaming sends tool inputs without buffering or JSON validation, so a tool taking a long string starts arriving sooner. It trades the guarantee that the JSON is well formed for latency, so validate what arrives.
Context editing
Clear old tool results, which in a long agent run outweigh the definitions many times over. §9.6.

Note that the second and third options pull in opposite directions, and you should know which you are choosing. Deferred loading keeps tokens out of the request, and caching makes their presence cheap. For a stable surface of twenty tools used every turn, caching wins. For a surface of four hundred where any given conversation touches three, search wins.

6.10 Designing a Tool Surface

The mechanics above are quickly learned. What separates an agent that works from one that thrashes is the design of the surface, and the guidance is unglamorous.

Consolidate related operations. create_pr, review_pr, merge_pr and close_pr should be one pull_request tool with an action enum. Four similar names is four opportunities to pick the wrong one, while one tool with an enum is a choice the schema itself constrains.

Namespace by service. Use github_list_prs and slack_send_message and not list_prs and send_message. This matters immediately when two services both have a search, and it matters enormously once tool search is involved, because the prefix is what makes a query selective.

Return high-signal results, not payloads. A tool that hands back the whole database row when the model needs six fields has spent most of its tokens on internal identifiers the model cannot use. Worse, it buries the useful part. Return stable, semantic identifiers, such as a slug or a UUID, and not opaque internal handles, and return only the fields the model needs to decide what to do next.

FULL_RECORD = {
    "id": 88213, "uuid": "c1f2...", "created_at": "2026-08-21T09:14:02.113Z",
    "updated_at": "2026-08-25T11:02:44.882Z", "customer_id": 4471,
    "customer_uuid": "9ab3...", "billing_address_id": 20114,
    "shipping_address_id": 20115, "currency": "EUR", "subtotal_cents": 4250,
    "tax_cents": 978, "shipping_cents": 499, "total_cents": 5727,
    "status": "shipped", "carrier_code": "DHL_EXPRESS",
    "tracking_number": "JJD0099887766", "warehouse_id": 7, "channel": "web",
    "internal_notes": None, "risk_score": 0.02, "fraud_review": False,
}

SHAPED = {
    "order": "ord_88213", "customer": "cus_4471", "status": "shipped",
    "total": "57.27 EUR", "carrier": "DHL_EXPRESS",
    "tracking": "JJD0099887766",
}

for label, payload in (("raw record", FULL_RECORD), ("shaped result", SHAPED)):
    chars = len(str(payload))
    print(f"{label:<15} {len(payload):>2} fields  {chars:>4} chars  "
          f"~{round(chars / 4):>3} tokens")

saved = round((len(str(FULL_RECORD)) - len(str(SHAPED))) / 4)
print(f"\nsaved per call: ~{saved} tokens")
print(f"over a 12-call agent run: ~{saved * 12} tokens")

raw record      21 fields   521 chars  ~130 tokens
shaped result    6 fields   144 chars  ~ 36 tokens

saved per call: ~94 tokens
over a 12-call agent run: ~1128 tokens

Prefer the trained-in schema when one exists. If your tool is "run a shell command", use the bash tool and do not invent execute_command. The bash tool's signature is one the model has seen thousands of successful trajectories through. If it is "edit this file", use text_editor. The model has seen thousands of successful trajectories through those exact signatures, while a custom equivalent starts from nothing. §11 uses both.

Put the authorisation in the executor, never in the description. A description that says "only use this for orders belonging to the current user" is a request and not a control. The check belongs in the function, where the session is in scope:

class Forbidden(Exception):
    pass


ORDERS = {"ord_1": {"customer": "cus_A", "total": 4250},
          "ord_2": {"customer": "cus_B", "total": 1195}}


def get_order(order_id, *, session_customer):
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        raise KeyError(f"no order {order_id!r}")
    if order["customer"] != session_customer:
        raise Forbidden(f"order {order_id} does not belong to this account")
    return order


for requested in ("ord_1", "ord_2", "ord_9"):
    try:
        print(f"{requested}: {get_order(requested, session_customer='cus_A')}")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"{requested}: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")

ord_1: {'customer': 'cus_A', 'total': 4250}
ord_2: Forbidden: order ord_2 does not belong to this account
ord_9: KeyError: "no order 'ord_9'"

The model is free to ask for ord_2, and the executor is what makes asking pointless. Treat every argument as untrusted input from a component that has read your users' text, because that is exactly what it is. §14.4 develops this into the full injection model.

Exercises

Exercise 6.1 — Fix a tool definition. The definition below is what a working engineer's first draft usually looks like. Rewrite it, and list the specific failures each change prevents.

tool = {
    "name": "lookup",
    "description": "Looks up a user.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"q": {"type": "string"}},
    },
}
Solution

There are five separate defects, and each maps to a failure you would see in production.

fixed = {
    "name": "directory_find_user",
    "description": (
        "Find a user in the staff directory by email address, employee ID, or "
        "full name. Use this when you need a user's team, manager or office "
        "before taking any other action on their behalf. Returns at most 10 "
        "matches, each with employee ID, full name, team and office. It does "
        "NOT return contact details, salary, or employment history, and it does "
        "not search customers — use crm_find_customer for those. If more than "
        "10 users match, narrow the query rather than paginating."
    ),
    "strict": True,
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "query": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "Email, employee ID (E-prefixed, e.g. E-4471), "
                               "or full name. Partial names are matched.",
            },
            "field": {
                "type": "string",
                "enum": ["email", "employee_id", "name", "any"],
                "description": "Which field to search. Use 'any' when unsure.",
            },
        },
        "required": ["query", "field"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
    "input_examples": [
        {"query": "ana.silva@example.com", "field": "email"},
        {"query": "E-4471", "field": "employee_id"},
    ],
}

print("name    :", fixed["name"])
print("required:", fixed["input_schema"]["required"])
print("desc has 'does NOT':", "does NOT" in fixed["description"])
print("strict  :", fixed["strict"])

name    : directory_find_user
required: ['query', 'field']
desc has 'does NOT': True
strict  : True

lookup → directory_find_user. "Lookup" is a verb with no object. In a surface with a customer directory, a DNS tool and a price table, the model has to guess which "lookup" this is. The service prefix makes the choice unambiguous and survives the surface growing.

A one-line description → a paragraph that says what it does not do. The original leaves four questions open: look up by what, returning what, how many, and is this customers or staff? The rewrite closes all four. The "does NOT return contact details… use crm_find_customer" sentence is the one that prevents the specific failure of the model calling this tool for a customer and then inventing the answer from the empty result.

q → query, plus a description. A single-letter parameter with no description tells the model nothing about accepted formats. The description naming the E- prefix is what stops 4471 being sent when E-4471 is required.

No required → required with additionalProperties: false and strict: true. As written, a call with no arguments at all satisfies the schema. Adding field as required also removes an ambiguity the original had no way to express.

input_examples. Two examples cost about forty tokens, and they demonstrate the two formats that a sentence describes less precisely.

The one judgement call: adding a required field parameter makes the model commit to a search mode, which is better than a magic string but does force a decision. Making it required with an "any" member is the compromise, because the model can decline to choose without omitting the field.

Exercise 6.2 — Find the four bugs in this loop. This agent loop looks reasonable and has four distinct defects, at least two of which will only appear in production.

response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)

while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    call = response.content[0]
    output = IMPLEMENTATIONS[call.name](**call.input)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id, "content": output}]})
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
Solution 
class ToolFailed(Exception):
    pass


def run_agent(client, messages, tools, implementations, *, max_turns=12):
    """The same loop with the four defects fixed."""
    for turn in range(1, max_turns + 1):
        response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                          tools=tools, messages=messages)

        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            # 2. every other stop reason is handled, not treated as success
            return response, turn, response.stop_reason

        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

        results = []
        for block in response.content:          # 1. all tool_use blocks, not [0]
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            try:
                output = implementations[block.name](**block.input)
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                "content": str(output)})
            except Exception as exc:            # 3. failures go back to the model
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                "content": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
                                "is_error": True})

        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

    return None, max_turns, "max_turns_exhausted"   # 4. a stop condition


FIXES = [
    "1. iterate every content block, never content[0]",
    "2. branch on every stop reason, not just tool_use",
    "3. return tool failures with is_error instead of raising",
    "4. bound the loop with max_turns",
]
print(run_agent.__doc__)
for fix in FIXES:
    print(" ", fix)

The same loop with the four defects fixed.
  1. iterate every content block, never content[0]
  2. branch on every stop reason, not just tool_use
  3. return tool failures with is_error instead of raising
  4. bound the loop with max_turns

1. response.content[0] assumes the tool call is the first block. It frequently is not, because the model often emits a short text block first ("Let me look that up."), and it is never the whole story when the model makes parallel calls. This bug is invisible in testing with a terse model and appears the moment the model narrates. At that point content[0] is a TextBlock and .name raises AttributeError. It also silently drops the second and third of three parallel calls, producing a 400 on the next request because those tool_use blocks have no matching results.

2. while stop_reason == "tool_use" treats every other stop reason as success. max_tokens means the answer was truncated mid-sentence, and the loop returns it as final. refusal means the model declined. pause_turn means a server-side tool has not finished. All three exit the loop into code that assumes a complete answer.

3. An exception in the tool escapes the loop. The model is never told the call failed, so it cannot retry with a corrected argument or route around the failure. The conversation is also left with an assistant turn containing a tool_use and no corresponding result, which means it cannot even be resumed. Catching the exception and returning is_error: true keeps both the model and the conversation recoverable.

4. There is no stop condition. Nothing bounds the number of turns. A model that keeps calling a tool that keeps failing will loop until something else breaks. max_turns is the minimum, and §11.3 adds a token budget alongside it, because twelve turns of a large tool result is a very different bill from twelve turns of a small one.

There is arguably a fifth issue: the request is duplicated above and inside the loop, which is what let the two calls drift apart in the first place. The for form has exactly one call site.

Exercise 6.3 — Size a tool surface. Your agent has 34 tools averaging 380 characters of serialised definition. It runs 2,000 conversations a day, averaging 6 model turns each, on Claude Opus 5 at $5 per million input tokens. Compute the monthly cost of the tool definitions alone, then compute what prompt caching at a cache-hit rate of $0.50 per million tokens would change, and say what you would do.

Solution 
N_TOOLS, CHARS_EACH = 34, 380
CONVERSATIONS_PER_DAY, TURNS_EACH, DAYS = 2000, 6, 30
INPUT_PER_MTOK, CACHE_HIT_PER_MTOK, CACHE_WRITE_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 0.50, 6.25

defs_tokens = round(N_TOOLS * CHARS_EACH / 4)
turns_per_month = CONVERSATIONS_PER_DAY * TURNS_EACH * DAYS
tokens_per_month = defs_tokens * turns_per_month

uncached = tokens_per_month / 1_000_000 * INPUT_PER_MTOK

# Caching: the first turn of each conversation writes the cache, the rest read it.
writes = defs_tokens * CONVERSATIONS_PER_DAY * DAYS
reads = defs_tokens * CONVERSATIONS_PER_DAY * (TURNS_EACH - 1) * DAYS
cached = (writes / 1_000_000 * CACHE_WRITE_PER_MTOK
          + reads / 1_000_000 * CACHE_HIT_PER_MTOK)

print(f"definitions           : {defs_tokens:,} tokens per request")
print(f"share of a 200k window: {defs_tokens / 200_000 * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"model turns per month : {turns_per_month:,}")
print(f"tokens per month      : {tokens_per_month:,}")
print()
print(f"uncached              : ${uncached:,.2f}/month")
print(f"cached                : ${cached:,.2f}/month")
print(f"saving                : ${uncached - cached:,.2f} "
      f"({(1 - cached / uncached) * 100:.0f}%)")

definitions           : 3,230 tokens per request
share of a 200k window: 1.6%
model turns per month : 360,000
tokens per month      : 1,162,800,000

uncached              : $5,814.00/month
cached                : $1,695.75/month
saving                : $4,118.25 (71%)

The money is larger than it feels, and that is the first lesson. 3,230 tokens looks trivial. Multiplied by 360,000 model turns a month, it is 1.16 billion input tokens and $5,814, for text that never changes. Nobody arrives at that figure by intuition, which is the argument for spending two minutes on the arithmetic before spending a sprint on anything.

Caching removes 71% of it, taking $5,814 to $1,696. That is the highest-value change available, and it is roughly twenty minutes of work, because tools render first in the request, before system and before messages, and are therefore already the natural stable prefix (§9.3). Note that the saving is 71% and not 90%, because one turn in six is a cache write at $6.25 per million, which is more expensive than an ordinary input token. Conversations with more turns each would do better.

The context window is not the problem here. 3,230 tokens is 1.6% of a 200k window and negligible against 1M, so context pressure is not the argument for restructuring. This is exactly the sort of conclusion this arithmetic exists to reach before someone builds tool search that nothing needed.

What I would actually do, in order. Add caching. Then look at the 34 tools for consolidation, not to save tokens but because 34 similar-sounding names is where selection accuracy degrades, and a wrong tool call costs a full round trip plus whatever the wrong tool did. Leave tool search alone, because it earns its complexity in the hundreds and not the thirties.

The number this calculation does not contain, and which dominates all of it, is tool results. Six turns of a search tool returning even 800 tokens each is 4,800 tokens per conversation, against 3,200 for the definitions. Unlike the definitions, results are different every time and therefore uncacheable. That is what §9.6's context editing is for, and it is why sizing a tool surface by its definitions alone always looks reassuring.

SECTION 7

Server Tools, Skills and MCP

Section 6 built the client-side loop: the model asks, you execute, and you report back. This section is about the capabilities where you do not write that loop. Either the tool runs on Anthropic's infrastructure, or its schema comes from a server you did not build, or the "tool" is a folder of instructions that the model reads when it decides it needs them.

There are four mechanisms, and they are easy to mix up because they all end up as entries in tools. Two questions keep them straight: who executes and who supplies the definition.

Server tools
Anthropic executes; Anthropic defines. web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, tool_search. You enable them and read the answer. No tool_result, no loop.
MCP connector
A third party executes; a third party defines. A remote MCP server's tools become callable from the Messages API with no MCP client of your own. Anthropic's servers do the calling.
Agent Skills
Not a tool at all. A folder of instructions, reference files and scripts that the model reads from a filesystem when its description matches your request. Runs inside code execution.
Programmatic tool calling
You execute; the model orchestrates in code. Your client tools become callable from inside the code execution sandbox, so a loop over 400 rows costs one turn instead of 400.

7.1 The server_tool_use Block

A server-side tool changes the shape of a turn in one specific way. A call and its result both appear in the same assistant message, and there is nothing for you to send back. That is the defining property of a server-side tool, and it is what removes the loop.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "max_uses": 5}],
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "What did the ECB decide at its last meeting?"}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "server_tool_use":
        print(f"  server_tool_use  id={block.id}  name={block.name}")
        print(f"                   input={block.input}")
    elif block.type == "web_search_tool_result":
        print(f"  result for       {block.tool_use_id}: "
              f"{len(block.content)} results")
    elif block.type == "text":
        print(f"  text             {block.text[:60]}")

print("searches billed:", response.usage.server_tool_use.web_search_requests)

stop_reason: end_turn
  server_tool_use  id=srvtoolu_01A2B3C4D5  name=web_search
                   input={'query': 'ECB latest monetary policy decision'}
  result for       srvtoolu_01A2B3C4D5: 3 results
  text             At its most recent meeting the ECB held the deposit facility
searches billed: 1

Three details in that output are worth naming.

The id prefix is srvtoolu_, not toolu_. That is how you tell a server call from a client call when reading a trace. It is worth keying on the prefix and not on the block type, because new server tools keep arriving.

The result block follows the call in the same turn, paired by tool_use_id. You never construct one. A loop written to answer every *_tool_use block with a tool_result will send something the API did not ask for.

usage.server_tool_use is a separate meter. Web search is billed at $10 per 1,000 searches on top of tokens, and failed searches are not billed. Web fetch is free beyond tokens, and so is code execution when it is paired with search or fetch. §15 puts these in one cost model.

7.2 pause_turn: The Server Loop Handing Control Back

The server runs its own agentic loop entirely inside one request: it searches, reads, and decides whether to search again. That loop has an iteration cap, and when it hits the cap you get a stop reason you must handle.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "max_uses": 10}]
messages = [{"role": "user",
             "content": "Compare the last three ECB and Fed rate decisions."}]

for attempt in range(1, 5):
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=2048,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    print(f"request {attempt}: stop_reason={response.stop_reason}")
    if response.stop_reason != "pause_turn":
        break
    # Send the paused turn straight back, unmodified, and it continues.
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
else:
    raise RuntimeError("still pausing after 4 continuations")

print("final:", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

request 1: stop_reason=pause_turn
request 2: stop_reason=end_turn
final: The ECB cut once and held twice; the Fed held across all three meetings.

A paused turn is resumed by appending it and re-sending. You do not start over, and you do not summarise what happened. The assistant content carries the partial work, and stripping it throws away every search already paid for.

Bound the continuations. The loop above gives up after four. Without a bound, you have re-created §6.4's unbounded loop in a place where each iteration is more expensive, because every continuation resends a conversation that now contains search results.

One further server tool is worth knowing about even though it is used differently from the rest. The advisor tool pairs a fast executor model with a higher-intelligence advisor that supplies strategic guidance mid-generation. The advisor tool is aimed at long-horizon agentic workloads, where the executor benefits from a second opinion without paying the larger model's price for every token.

There is a second way control comes back, and it is easy to miss. If the model calls a server tool and one of your client tools in the same turn, you get stop_reason: "tool_use" and a server_tool_use block without its result. Return your client tool_result blocks as usual, and the API runs the server tool afterwards. So a turn can contain a server call you must not answer and a client call you must.

7.3 Web Search

Web search is the most-used server tool and the one whose configuration matters most, because its defaults are permissive by design.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[{
        "type": "web_search_20250305",
        "name": "web_search",
        "max_uses": 3,
        "allowed_domains": ["ecb.europa.eu", "federalreserve.gov"],
        "user_location": {"type": "approximate", "city": "Lisbon",
                          "country": "PT", "timezone": "Europe/Lisbon"},
    }],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the current ECB deposit rate?"}],
)

print("stop_reason :", response.stop_reason)
print("searches    :", response.usage.server_tool_use.web_search_requests)
print("answer      :", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

stop_reason : end_turn
searches    : 1
answer      : According to the ECB press release, the deposit facility rate was left unchanged at this meeting.

max_uses is the only hard constraint on how much searching happens. Everything else, such as "search more readily" or "prefer answering directly", is steering through the system prompt, which is guidance. A simple factual question uses one to three searches, and a comparative research question can use ten or more, each billed. Exceeding max_uses produces a max_uses_exceeded error in the result block and not a failed request.

allowed_domains and blocked_domains are mutually exclusive. Sending both is a 400. Entries are bare domains with an optional path (example.com, example.com/blog) and no scheme, so a value of https://example.com is not what the API expects.

Search results enter the context window and stay there. They are input tokens on this turn and on every later turn of the conversation, which is §9's arithmetic applied to content you did not write. This is the strongest argument for max_uses, because it bounds tokens and not just search fees.

That last problem has a purpose-built answer. Dynamic filtering, available on web_search_20260209 and later, has the model write and run code that filters results before they reach the context window, so only the relevant part is loaded. It is the same idea as §7.6's programmatic tool calling, and it uses the same machinery.

7.4 Web Fetch, and the Exfiltration Problem

Web fetch retrieves a specific URL. It costs nothing beyond tokens, which makes its real cost easy to underestimate. A research paper PDF is around 125,000 tokens, and it lands in your context window.

CONTENT_SIZES = [("average web page", 10, 2_500),
                 ("large documentation page", 100, 25_000),
                 ("research paper PDF", 500, 125_000)]
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00

print(f"{'content':<26}{'size':>8}{'tokens':>10}{'cost once':>11}"
      f"{'over 10 turns':>15}")
for label, kilobytes, tokens in CONTENT_SIZES:
    once = tokens / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK
    print(f"{label:<26}{str(kilobytes) + ' kB':>8}{tokens:>10,}"
          f"{'$%.3f' % once:>11}{'$%.2f' % (once * 10):>15}")

print("\nthe fetch itself is free; the context it fills is not")

content                       size    tokens  cost once  over 10 turns
average web page             10 kB     2,500     $0.013          $0.12
large documentation page    100 kB    25,000     $0.125          $1.25
research paper PDF          500 kB   125,000     $0.625          $6.25

the fetch itself is free; the context it fills is not

max_content_tokens caps this, and on anything user-facing it should be set.

The other consideration is security, and it is not hypothetical. Web fetch in an environment where the model reads untrusted input alongside sensitive data is a data-exfiltration channel. The attack is simple. Text the model reads contains an instruction to fetch https://attacker.example/?data=<the secret>, and the fetch itself is the leak.

The platform mitigates the worst version, because the model may not construct URLs dynamically. It may only fetch ones the user supplied or that came from a previous search or fetch result. But that is a mitigation and not a fix, since a search result is itself content the model did not verify. Three controls are yours:

Do not enable it
The only complete answer when the same conversation holds untrusted text and data that must not leave. Consider whether fetch is doing enough work to justify the channel.
allowed_domains
Restrict to hosts you trust. An allowlist turns the exfiltration channel into one that only reaches places you chose, which for most internal tools is sufficient.
max_uses
Bound the number of requests. Limits both the token bill and how much can be exfiltrated per conversation.

§14.4 develops the general form of this argument. The point to carry here is that a tool that makes outbound network requests is an exfiltration primitive, whoever executes it, and it should be reasoned about as one.

7.5 Tool Search: Scaling Past a Few Dozen Tools

§6.9 established that tool definitions are context you pay for on every request, and that selection accuracy degrades as the surface grows. Tool search fixes both by not loading most of them.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[
        {"type": "tool_search_tool_regex_20251119", "name": "tool_search_tool_regex"},
        {"name": "github_list_prs",
         "description": "List open pull requests for a repository.",
         "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                          "properties": {"repo": {"type": "string"}},
                          "required": ["repo"]},
         "defer_loading": True},
        {"name": "slack_send_message",
         "description": "Post a message to a Slack channel.",
         "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                          "properties": {"channel": {"type": "string"},
                                         "text": {"type": "string"}},
                          "required": ["channel", "text"]},
         "defer_loading": True},
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What PRs are open on acme/api?"}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "server_tool_use":
        print("  searched for:", block.input)
    elif block.type == "tool_search_tool_result":
        for ref in block.content:
            print("  discovered  :", ref.name)
    elif block.type == "tool_use":
        print("  called      :", block.name, block.input)

stop_reason: tool_use
  searched for: {'pattern': 'github_.*pr'}
  discovered  : github_list_prs
  called      : github_list_prs {'repo': 'acme/api'}

The mechanism is this: you send every tool definition, marking with defer_loading: true the ones that should not be loaded up front. The model's context initially holds only the search tool and any non-deferred tools. When it needs something, it searches. The API returns tool_reference blocks (up to five by default) and expands them into full definitions automatically. At least one tool must stay non-deferred, and it is normally the search tool itself.

There are two variants, and the choice is not arbitrary. Regex (tool_search_tool_regex_20251119) has the model construct patterns, which rewards the service-prefix naming convention from §6.10. For example, github_ matches everything GitHub in one query. BM25 (tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119) takes natural-language queries and matches them against descriptions, which rewards descriptions written for a reader and not for a matcher.
