If your tools are consistently namespaced, regex is sharper. If they are well described but inconsistently named, BM25 is.

AVG_TOOL_CHARS = 353       # measured over a real 7-tool surface
SEARCH_TOOL_CHARS = 420
TYPICAL_DISCOVERY = 2      # tools a given conversation actually needs
EXTRA_ROUND_TRIP_MS = 1_400


def approx_tokens(chars):
    return round(chars / 4)


searched = approx_tokens(SEARCH_TOOL_CHARS + TYPICAL_DISCOVERY * AVG_TOOL_CHARS)

print(f"{'tools':>7}{'eager':>10}{'with search':>14}{'saved':>10}")
for n in (7, 20, 40, 100, 400):
    eager = approx_tokens(n * AVG_TOOL_CHARS)
    print(f"{n:>7}{eager:>10,}{searched:>14,}{eager - searched:>+10,}")

print()
print(f"the search column never moves: {searched:,} tokens at every scale")
print(f"what it costs instead: one extra round trip (~{EXTRA_ROUND_TRIP_MS} ms)")
print("and a tool list that differs per conversation, so the cached prefix")
print("no longer matches (see 9.3)")

tools     eager   with search     saved
      7       618           282      +336
     20     1,765           282    +1,483
     40     3,530           282    +3,248
    100     8,825           282    +8,543
    400    35,300           282   +35,018

the search column never moves: 282 tokens at every scale
what it costs instead: one extra round trip (~1400 ms)
and a tool list that differs per conversation, so the cached prefix
no longer matches (see 9.3)

The flatness is the property, not the saving. The search column is the same 282 tokens whether the surface holds seven tools or four hundred, because the model only ever loads what it discovered. Eager loading grows linearly and is untenable well before the four-hundred mark.

So why did §6.9 say search earns its complexity only in the hundreds, when the table shows it winning on tokens even at seven? Because tokens are not what it costs. It costs an extra round trip before the first real tool call, around 1.4 seconds of latency on every conversation that needs a tool it has not already found. And it costs your prompt cache, because a tool list that expands differently per conversation is a prefix that differs per conversation (§9.3). At twenty tools, those two outweigh the 1,483 tokens saved without difficulty. At four hundred, 35,000 tokens a request is not something a round trip can outweigh.

7.6 Programmatic Tool Calling

This one solves a problem that looks like a context problem and is really a turn problem. Suppose the model needs to call get_order for 400 order ids and sum the totals. With ordinary tool use that is 400 tool calls, each returning a result into the context window, across many model turns.

Programmatic tool calling lets the model write code that calls your tools, and the code is executed inside the code execution sandbox (an isolated environment). The loop runs there, and only the final answer comes back.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    tools=[
        {"type": "code_execution_20260120", "name": "code_execution"},
        {"name": "get_order",
         "description": "Fetch one order by id. Returns total_cents and status.",
         "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                          "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
                          "required": ["order_id"]},
         # This is what makes the tool callable from inside code execution.
         "allowed_callers": ["code_execution_20260120"]},
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Total the 400 orders in orders.txt and give me the mean."}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print("answer     :", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

stop_reason: end_turn
answer     : The 400 orders total 1,712,400 cents; the mean is 42.81 EUR.

allowed_callers: ["code_execution_20260120"] is the whole switch. Without it the tool is callable only directly by the model, and with it the sandbox may call it too.

N_CALLS = 400
RESULT_TOKENS = 220          # one order record coming back
BASE_CONTEXT = 6_000
MODEL_TURN_MS = 1_400

# Ordinary tool use: results accumulate, and the conversation is resent each turn.
CALLS_PER_TURN = 8           # generous parallelism
turns = N_CALLS // CALLS_PER_TURN
ordinary_context = BASE_CONTEXT + N_CALLS * RESULT_TOKENS
ordinary_billed = sum(BASE_CONTEXT + t * CALLS_PER_TURN * RESULT_TOKENS
                      for t in range(1, turns + 1))

# Programmatic: the loop runs in the sandbox; one summary returns.
ptc_context = BASE_CONTEXT + 180
ptc_billed = BASE_CONTEXT * 2 + 180

print(f"{'':22}{'model turns':>12}{'peak context':>14}{'input billed':>14}")
print(f"{'ordinary tool use':<22}{turns:>12}{ordinary_context:>14,}"
      f"{ordinary_billed:>14,}")
print(f"{'programmatic':<22}{2:>12}{ptc_context:>14,}{ptc_billed:>14,}")
print()
print(f"latency from model turns: {turns * MODEL_TURN_MS / 1000:>6.1f}s  ->"
      f"{2 * MODEL_TURN_MS / 1000:>6.1f}s")
print(f"input tokens billed     : {ordinary_billed / ptc_billed:>6.0f}x fewer")

model turns  peak context  input billed
ordinary tool use               50        94,000     2,544,000
programmatic                     2         6,180        12,180

latency from model turns:   70.0s  ->   2.8s
input tokens billed     :    209x fewer

There are two constraints before you reach for it. It requires the code execution tool, which brings that tool's billing and its sandbox. And it is incompatible with strict: true (§6.8), so a tool you want schema-guaranteed cannot also be programmatically callable, and you have to decide which property matters more for that tool.

7.7 The MCP Connector

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for exposing tools to a model. Its usual shape is a client you run that speaks to a remote MCP server. The MCP connector removes the client: you name a remote MCP server in mcp_servers, and Anthropic's infrastructure connects to it and calls its tools.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    betas=["mcp-client-2025-11-20"],
    mcp_servers=[{
        "type": "url",
        "url": "https://mcp.example.com/sse",
        "name": "issue-tracker",
        "authorization_token": "OAUTH_TOKEN_HERE",
    }],
    tools=[{"type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "issue-tracker",
            "allowed_tools": ["search_issues", "get_issue"]}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is blocking the release?"}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print("answer     :", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

stop_reason: end_turn
answer     : Two issues are blocking: ENG-441 (auth migration) and ENG-455 (flaky deploy).

There are two components, and conflating them is the usual first mistake. mcp_servers declares the connection: URL, name and auth. A mcp_toolset entry in tools declares which of that server's tools are enabled, with allowed_tools as an allowlist. A server declared but never referenced by a toolset contributes nothing.

Two limitations to design around:

Only tool calls are supported. The MCP specification also covers resources, prompts and sampling, but the connector implements the tools portion. If your integration depends on MCP resources, the connector is not the mechanism.

A remote MCP server must be reachable over HTTP, using Streamable HTTP or SSE. A local STDIO server cannot be connected this way. That is how most MCP servers are developed and how Claude Code runs them, so the difference catches people moving a working local setup into an API integration.

And here is the consideration that outranks both: an MCP server is third-party code defining tools whose descriptions enter your model's context. A compromised or hostile server can describe a tool in terms designed to make the model call it with data from your conversation. allowed_tools is the control. Enumerate what you permit and do not accept whatever the server offers, so that a server that grows a new tool tomorrow does not silently acquire a place in your prompt.

7.8 Agent Skills

A Skill is not a tool. It is a directory of instructions, reference files and executable scripts that the model reads from a filesystem when it decides the task calls for it. The mechanism that makes this efficient has a name worth knowing: progressive disclosure, which means the model sees a short description first and loads more only when it needs it.

Level 1 — metadata
Always loaded, about 100 tokens per Skill. Just name and description from the YAML frontmatter. This is what the model matches your request against.
Level 2 — instructions
Loaded when the Skill triggers, under 5k tokens. The body of SKILL.md: workflows, conventions, gotchas.
Level 3 — resources
Nothing until read. Bundled files the instructions point at. Reference files cost tokens when opened; scripts run through bash, so only their output enters context, never their source.
SKILLS = [("pdf-processing", 104, 3_900, 12_000),
          ("brand-voice", 92, 2_100, 4_500),
          ("xlsx", 118, 4_400, 26_000),
          ("incident-review", 88, 3_200, 8_800),
          ("sql-conventions", 96, 2_800, 15_000)]

always = sum(meta for _, meta, _, _ in SKILLS)
if_all_loaded = sum(meta + body + res for _, meta, body, res in SKILLS)
one_triggered = always + SKILLS[0][2]        # metadata for all, body for one

print(f"{'skill':<18}{'metadata':>10}{'SKILL.md':>10}{'resources':>11}")
for name, meta, body, res in SKILLS:
    print(f"{name:<18}{meta:>10}{body:>10,}{res:>11,}")

print()
print(f"always in context (5 skills)      : {always:>7,} tokens")
print(f"one skill triggered, body loaded  : {one_triggered:>7,} tokens")
print(f"if everything were loaded eagerly : {if_all_loaded:>7,} tokens")
print(f"ratio                             : {if_all_loaded / always:>7.0f}x")

skill               metadata  SKILL.md  resources
pdf-processing           104     3,900     12,000
brand-voice               92     2,100      4,500
xlsx                     118     4,400     26,000
incident-review           88     3,200      8,800
sql-conventions           96     2,800     15,000

always in context (5 skills)      :     498 tokens
one skill triggered, body loaded  :   4,398 tokens
if everything were loaded eagerly :  83,198 tokens
ratio                             :     167x

Progressive disclosure is what lets you install many Skills, and the metadata cost is the whole of the argument. Five Skills cost about half a thousand tokens until one of them is needed. That is the entire architectural argument. It is also why the description is the most important line in a Skill: it is the only thing the model sees when deciding whether to look further, so it must say what the Skill does and when to use it, and not just what it is about.

In the API, Skills run inside code execution and are named in the container parameter.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    container={"skills": [{"type": "anthropic", "skill_id": "pptx",
                           "version": "latest"}]},
    tools=[{"type": "code_execution_20250825", "name": "code_execution"}],
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Make a five-slide deck on our Q3 incident trends."}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print("answer     :", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

stop_reason: end_turn
answer     : I have built a five-slide deck covering incident volume, mean time to recovery and the top three causes.

Skills require the code execution tool, because the filesystem they live on is that sandbox. You can use up to 20 Skills per request. The shape is identical for Anthropic-provided Skills (pptx, xlsx, docx, pdf) and custom ones you upload, and only type differs.

Pin the version in production. "version": "latest" is convenient, and it means the Skill's instructions can change underneath a prompt you evaluated last month. §13's regression suite cannot protect you from a dependency that updates itself. A regression suite compares your system against its own past behaviour, and it has no way to attribute a change to a Skill that silently updated.

7.9 Choosing Between Them

These mechanisms overlap enough that the choice is genuinely unclear in places. The question that resolves most cases is: what is the thing you actually have?

A function in your code
A client tool (§6). Add allowed_callers if it will be called in bulk; add strict if a bad argument is expensive. You cannot have both.
A capability Anthropic runs
A server tool. Bound it with max_uses and, where it reaches the network, with allowed_domains.
A service with an MCP server
The MCP connector, with allowed_tools enumerated. Saves you writing and maintaining an integration.
Knowledge, not an action
A Skill. "How we write incident reviews", "our SQL conventions", "the steps for a release". If the answer is a procedure rather than a call, a Skill is the shape.
Too many tools to load
Tool search, in the hundreds. Below that, consolidate instead (§6.10).

The distinction people most often get wrong is the fourth. A Skill is for knowledge, and a tool is for action. "Generate a PowerPoint" feels like a tool and is a Skill, because what the model needs is not a function to call but a procedure to follow plus a library to use. Conversely, "look up an order" feels like it could be documented as knowledge and is a tool, because it requires reaching a system only your code can reach.

Exercises

Exercise 7.1 — Bound a research agent. You are building an agent that answers questions about competitors using web search and web fetch. It handles 500 questions a day. Configure the tools, and compute the monthly cost of the server-tool fees alone.

Solution 
QUESTIONS_PER_DAY, DAYS = 500, 30
SEARCHES_PER_QUESTION = 4        # comparative questions, measured not guessed
FETCHES_PER_QUESTION = 2
SEARCH_FEE_PER_1000 = 10.00
FETCH_TOKENS_EACH = 25_000       # a large documentation page
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00

searches = QUESTIONS_PER_DAY * SEARCHES_PER_QUESTION * DAYS
search_fees = searches / 1000 * SEARCH_FEE_PER_1000

fetch_tokens = QUESTIONS_PER_DAY * FETCHES_PER_QUESTION * DAYS * FETCH_TOKENS_EACH
fetch_token_cost = fetch_tokens / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK

print(f"searches per month     : {searches:>12,}")
print(f"search fees            : {'$%.2f' % search_fees:>12}")
print(f"fetched tokens         : {fetch_tokens:>12,}")
print(f"cost of fetched tokens : {'$%.2f' % fetch_token_cost:>12}")
print(f"total                  : {'$%.2f' % (search_fees + fetch_token_cost):>12}")
print()
capped = QUESTIONS_PER_DAY * FETCHES_PER_QUESTION * DAYS * 4_000
print(f"with max_content_tokens=4000, fetched tokens: {capped:>10,}")
print(f"cost                                        : "
      f"{'$%.2f' % (capped / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>10}")
print(f"saving from one parameter                   : "
      f"{'$%.2f' % (fetch_token_cost - capped / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>10}")

searches per month     :       60,000
search fees            :      $600.00
fetched tokens         :  750,000,000
cost of fetched tokens :     $3750.00
total                  :     $4350.00

with max_content_tokens=4000, fetched tokens: 120,000,000
cost                                        :    $600.00
saving from one parameter                   :   $3150.00

The configuration.

TOOLS = [
    {"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search",
     "max_uses": 6,
     "blocked_domains": ["competitor-forum.example"]},
    {"type": "web_fetch_20250910", "name": "web_fetch",
     "max_uses": 3,
     "max_content_tokens": 4000},
]

The free tool is the expensive one, and that is the finding. Web search charges $10 per thousand searches and comes to $600 a month here. Web fetch charges nothing, and costs $3,750, more than six times as much, because 25,000 tokens of fetched page is 25,000 input tokens on that turn and on every turn after it. A cost model built from the published fee schedule alone would have got this exactly backwards.

max_content_tokens is the single highest-value parameter in the configuration. Capping fetched content at 4,000 tokens removes most of that spend for one line. The judgement call is what it costs you in answer quality, which is a §13 question and not a guess. Run the eval at 4,000, at 10,000 and uncapped, and buy the smallest cap that holds your accuracy.

Why blocked_domains and not allowed_domains here. Competitor research is open-ended, so an allowlist would have to enumerate the web. That makes this one of the few cases where a denylist is right. It also means the exfiltration argument in §7.4 applies with full force, so this agent must not be given access to anything confidential in the same conversation.

What I would add that the arithmetic does not show. A max_uses of 6 on search against a measured average of 4 leaves headroom for genuinely comparative questions while capping the tail. Measure the distribution before setting it. The mean is not the number that matters, and the p95 (the value that 95% of requests stay under) is.

Exercise 7.2 — Skill, tool, or MCP? Classify each and say why: (a) "format a number as currency in the user's locale"; (b) "look up a customer's subscription tier"; (c) "our team's code review checklist"; (d) "create and share a Linear issue"; (e) "convert this spreadsheet to a chart deck".

Solution 
ANSWERS = [
    ("a  format currency", "neither",
     "Deterministic, pure, no external state — write it in your own code and "
     "never involve the model. A tool call costs a round trip to do what a "
     "library does in microseconds."),
    ("b  look up subscription tier", "client tool",
     "Requires reaching a system only your code can reach, and the answer is "
     "an action's result rather than a procedure. Narrow schema, strict:true."),
    ("c  code review checklist", "Skill",
     "Knowledge, not action. Nothing to execute; the model needs a procedure "
     "to follow. Level-2 instructions, loaded when a review is happening."),
    ("d  create and share a Linear issue", "MCP connector",
     "A third party already publishes the integration. Writing and maintaining "
     "your own Linear tools is work the connector removes."),
    ("e  spreadsheet to chart deck", "Skill (+ code execution)",
     "Feels like a tool and is not: what is needed is a procedure plus "
     "libraries, running on a filesystem. This is exactly what pptx/xlsx are."),
]

for task, verdict, why in ANSWERS:
    print(f"{task:<36} -> {verdict}")
    print(f"{'':36}    {why}")

a  format currency                   -> neither
                                        Deterministic, pure, no external state — write it in your own code and never involve the model. A tool call costs a round trip to do what a library does in microseconds.
b  look up subscription tier         -> client tool
                                        Requires reaching a system only your code can reach, and the answer is an action's result rather than a procedure. Narrow schema, strict:true.
c  code review checklist             -> Skill
                                        Knowledge, not action. Nothing to execute; the model needs a procedure to follow. Level-2 instructions, loaded when a review is happening.
d  create and share a Linear issue   -> MCP connector
                                        A third party already publishes the integration. Writing and maintaining your own Linear tools is work the connector removes.
e  spreadsheet to chart deck         -> Skill (+ code execution)
                                        Feels like a tool and is not: what is needed is a procedure plus libraries, running on a filesystem. This is exactly what pptx/xlsx are.

(a) is the trap, and it is the most useful one in the list. "Format currency" is a perfectly plausible tool definition, and building it means every formatted number costs a model round trip and can be got wrong. If a task is deterministic and local, it does not belong to the model at all. The general rule is this: before asking which mechanism, ask whether the model should be involved.

(b) is a client tool and nothing else can be. No server tool reaches your subscription table, no MCP server exists for it, and no amount of instruction lets the model know the answer. This is the ordinary case, and it is most of production traffic.

(c) is the clearest Skill. There is nothing to execute. What the model lacks is your team's conventions: what you check, in what order, and what you always miss. Note that this could be a system prompt instead. The reason to prefer a Skill is §7.8's arithmetic: as knowledge it is only loaded when a review is actually happening, whereas a system prompt is present on every request forever.

(d) is MCP because the work is already done. You could write three client tools against Linear's REST API. The connector is the same capability without the maintenance, and allowed_tools lets you enable exactly create_issue and add_comment and not the server's whole surface.

(e) is the one that most often gets built wrong. The instinct is a make_presentation(data) tool, which means writing and maintaining slide-generation code and a schema rich enough to express a deck. The Skill approach gives the model the procedure and the library and lets it write the code in the sandbox. That is far more flexible, and it is already built.

The pattern. Ask what is missing. Missing reach into a system is a tool. Missing knowledge of how you do things is a Skill. Missing an integration someone else maintains is MCP. Missing nothing is a function call in your own code.

Exercise 7.3 — When does programmatic tool calling pay? Your agent calls get_customer in a loop. Find the number of calls at which programmatic tool calling beats ordinary parallel tool use, and name what the arithmetic leaves out.

Solution 
RESULT_TOKENS = 220
BASE_CONTEXT = 6_000
CALLS_PER_TURN = 8
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00
SANDBOX_OVERHEAD_TOKENS = 900      # the code the model writes, plus its output


def ordinary(n_calls):
    """Results accumulate in context, and the whole conversation is resent."""
    turns = max(1, -(-n_calls // CALLS_PER_TURN))
    return sum(BASE_CONTEXT + t * CALLS_PER_TURN * RESULT_TOKENS
               for t in range(1, turns + 1)), turns


def programmatic(n_calls):
    """One turn to write the code, one to read the summary."""
    return BASE_CONTEXT * 2 + SANDBOX_OVERHEAD_TOKENS, 2


print(f"{'calls':>7}{'ordinary tokens':>18}{'turns':>7}"
      f"{'ptc tokens':>13}{'turns':>7}{'winner':>12}")
crossover = None
for n in (2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 400):
    o_tokens, o_turns = ordinary(n)
    p_tokens, p_turns = programmatic(n)
    winner = "programmatic" if p_tokens < o_tokens else "ordinary"
    if crossover is None and p_tokens < o_tokens:
        crossover = n
    print(f"{n:>7}{o_tokens:>18,}{o_turns:>7}{p_tokens:>13,}{p_turns:>7}"
          f"  {winner:<12}")

print(f"\ncrossover is somewhere between "
      f"{[x for x in (2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 400) if x < crossover][-1]} "
      f"and {crossover} calls")
print(f"at 400 calls: {ordinary(400)[0] / programmatic(400)[0]:.0f}x fewer "
      f"input tokens, {ordinary(400)[1]} turns -> 2")

calls   ordinary tokens  turns   ptc tokens  turns      winner
      2             7,760      1       12,900      2  ordinary    
      5             7,760      1       12,900      2  ordinary    
     10            17,280      2       12,900      2  programmatic
     20            28,560      3       12,900      2  programmatic
     50            91,280      7       12,900      2  programmatic
    100           238,160     13       12,900      2  programmatic
    400         2,544,000     50       12,900      2  programmatic

crossover is somewhere between 5 and 10 calls
at 400 calls: 197x fewer input tokens, 50 turns -> 2

On tokens alone the crossover is startlingly low, between five and ten calls. The reason is §9.1's quadratic growth. Ordinary tool use does not merely accumulate results. It resends everything accumulated so far on every turn, so doubling the calls more than doubles the bill. By four hundred calls the gap is roughly two hundredfold.

Three things the arithmetic leaves out, and all three matter.

Programmatic tool calling requires code execution, which has its own billing. It is free when paired with web search or fetch, and otherwise billed by container time with a five-minute minimum. For a handful of calls, that minimum alone can dominate everything computed above, which pushes the real crossover higher than the token model suggests.

It is incompatible with strict: true. If get_customer is a read, that costs nothing. If the tool being looped over writes anything, you are choosing between schema guarantees and bulk efficiency, and for a write tool the guarantee usually wins.

The failure modes differ. With ordinary tool use, each call's result passes through the model, so a malformed record gets noticed. Inside the sandbox the loop either handles the error or throws, and what returns is a summary, so a systematic problem in row 200 can be silently averaged into an answer. That is an argument for having the generated code report counts and anomalies, and for §13.10's required-call assertions covering bulk operations too.

What I would actually do. Below roughly fifty calls, use ordinary parallel tool use, because it is simpler, more observable, and needs no extra tool. Above a few hundred, use programmatic calling. In between, measure, because the container minimum makes the token model optimistic.

SECTION 8

Multimodal, Files and Citations

Everything so far has been text in and text out. This section is about the other things a request can carry: images, PDFs and uploaded files. It is also about the mechanism that makes an answer drawn from them checkable, which is citations that point back at the exact passage.

One idea underneath all of it explains most of the costs and limits. Images are converted to tokens, and PDFs are processed as images. A page is not a cheap attachment. It is a few thousand tokens that occupy your context window and your bill. Every design decision here follows from that.

8.1 Images

An image block is a content block inside a user message. An image block can get its data from three sources, and the choice between them is about payload size and not capability.

import base64

PIXEL = base64.b64decode(
    "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mP8"
    "z8BQDwAEhQGAhKmMIQAAAABJRU5ErkJggg==")

by_base64 = {
    "type": "image",
    "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "image/png",
               "data": base64.standard_b64encode(PIXEL).decode()},
}
by_url = {
    "type": "image",
    "source": {"type": "url", "url": "https://example.com/diagram.png"},
}
by_file = {
    "type": "image",
    "source": {"type": "file", "file_id": "file_011CQ8s7Xk2b"},
}

for label, block in (("base64", by_base64), ("url", by_url), ("file", by_file)):
    payload = len(str(block))
    print(f"{label:<8} source type={block['source']['type']:<8} "
          f"block size {payload:>4} chars")

print()
print("base64 grows with the image; url and file_id do not")
print(f"a 4 MB photo base64-encodes to about "
      f"{round(4 * 1024 * 1024 * 4 / 3 / 1024):,} kB of request body")

base64   source type=base64   block size  182 chars
url      source type=url      block size   86 chars
file     source type=file     block size   77 chars

base64 grows with the image; url and file_id do not
a 4 MB photo base64-encodes to about 5,461 kB of request body

Base64 is the simplest and the one that fails first. Base64 is a way of writing binary data as plain text. The encoding inflates the data by about a third, and the request size limit is 32 MB for standard endpoints. Send several photos and you are there.

Formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP. Animations are not supported, and only the first frame is used, silently.

One capability worth naming, because it removes a design decision, is that multilingual input and output need no configuration. Text in any supported language goes in the same blocks as English, whether it is a French support ticket, a Japanese product description or a mixed-script document. The model answers in the language of the request unless told otherwise. What does change is the token count (§1.2). Non-Latin scripts run considerably denser, so a multilingual workload budgeted on English prose is under-budgeted.

The limits worth knowing before you design around them:

100 images per request
On models with a 200k window; 600 on models with a larger one. Request size usually binds first.
10 MB per image
Base64-encoded, on the Claude API. 5 MB on Bedrock and Google Cloud.
8000 × 8000 px
Maximum dimensions. Larger is rejected.
Over 20 images
A stricter per-image dimension limit applies to every image block in the request. Keep each under 2000 px, or keep the request to 20 blocks or fewer.

That last row is the one that surprises people, because the count includes images from earlier turns that you resend, and images nested inside tool_result content, such as screenshots returned to the computer use tool. An agent driving computer use accumulates them turn after turn, which is how a conversation crosses the threshold without any single request looking large. A conversation that accumulates screenshots crosses the threshold without any single request looking large.

8.2 What an Image Costs

The model views images in 28×28-pixel patches, and each patch is a visual token. So the cost is ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉, which you can compute exactly before you send anything.

import math

TIERS = {"standard": (1568, 1568), "high-resolution": (2576, 4784)}


def visual_tokens(width, height):
    return math.ceil(width / 28) * math.ceil(height / 28)


def after_downscale(width, height, tier):
    """Scaled to the largest size fitting both limits, preserving aspect ratio."""
    max_edge, max_tokens = TIERS[tier]
    scale = min(1.0, max_edge / max(width, height))
    w, h = width * scale, height * scale
    if visual_tokens(w, h) > max_tokens:
        scale *= math.sqrt(max_tokens / visual_tokens(w, h))
        w, h = width * scale, height * scale
    return round(w), round(h), min(visual_tokens(w, h), max_tokens)


SIZES = [(200, 200), (1000, 1000), (1920, 1080), (2000, 1500), (3840, 2160)]
print(f"{'image':<14}{'standard px':>14}{'tokens':>8}"
      f"{'high-res px':>14}{'tokens':>8}")
for width, height in SIZES:
    sw, sh, st = after_downscale(width, height, "standard")
    hw, hh, ht = after_downscale(width, height, "high-resolution")
    print(f"{f'{width}x{height}':<14}{f'{sw}x{sh}':>14}{st:>8}"
          f"{f'{hw}x{hh}':>14}{ht:>8}")

print()
OPUS_PER_MTOK = 5.00
for label, tokens in (("1000x1000 on Opus 5", 1296), ("4K on Opus 5", 4784)):
    print(f"{label:<24}{tokens:>6} tokens  "
          f"${tokens / 1e6 * OPUS_PER_MTOK * 1000:>6.2f} per thousand images")

image            standard px  tokens   high-res px  tokens
200x200              200x200      64       200x200      64
1000x1000          1000x1000    1296     1000x1000    1296
1920x1080           1467x825    1568     1920x1080    2691
2000x1500           1280x960    1568     2000x1500    3888
3840x2160           1467x825    1568     2576x1449    4784

1000x1000 on Opus 5       1296 tokens  $  6.48 per thousand images
4K on Opus 5              4784 tokens  $ 23.92 per thousand images

High resolution is automatic on Claude 4.7 and later. There is no header and no opt-in, and it costs up to roughly three times the visual tokens of the standard tier for the same image. That is a good trade for computer use, screenshot understanding and dense documents, and a poor one for a photo you only need described.

Downscale before uploading when you do not need the fidelity. It reduces tokens, latency and request size at once, and it is the single most effective lever here. It also simplifies any coordinate work, because the model reports coordinates relative to the image after resizing.

Two smaller notes have real consequences. Compressing to JPEG or WebP reduces latency by shrinking the request, but heavy compression makes small text unreadable, so check what you are actually sending. And an oversized image is silently downscaled by default. Setting the block's oversized_image to "error" makes it fail loudly instead, which is what you want in a coordinate workflow.

8.3 PDFs

A PDF is a document block, and it is processed by the same vision path: each page is rendered as an image and also extracted as text. A document block carries a source, an optional title, and an optional citations setting.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document",
         "source": {"type": "file", "file_id": "file_011CQ8s7Xk2b"},
         "title": "Q3 board pack",
         "citations": {"enabled": True}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "What was the reported churn rate?"},
    ]}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type != "text":
        continue
    print("answer:", block.text)
    for citation in (block.citations or []):
        print(f"  page {citation.start_page_number}"
              f"–{citation.end_page_number}: {citation.cited_text!r}")

print("input tokens:", response.usage.input_tokens)

answer: Reported churn was 3.1% for the quarter.
  page 14–15: 'Quarterly churn: 3.1% (down from 3.6%).'
input tokens: 48210

PDF support is available on every active model, and it needs no beta header. The requirements for PDF support are worth memorising because they are the ones you hit:

32 MB per request
The whole payload, not just the PDF.
600 pages
Per request — but 100 when the request's context window is under 1M tokens.
1,500–3,000 tokens/page
Typical, depending on density. No PDF surcharge; standard token pricing.
No encryption
Standard PDFs only. Password-protected files are rejected.
PAGES_PER_DOC = [("a 4-page invoice", 4), ("a 40-page contract", 40),
                 ("a 300-page annual report", 300)]
TOKENS_PER_PAGE_LOW, TOKENS_PER_PAGE_HIGH = 1_500, 3_000
WINDOW, INPUT_PER_MTOK = 200_000, 5.00

print(f"{'document':<28}{'pages':>7}{'tokens (low-high)':>22}"
      f"{'% of 200k window':>19}{'cost':>9}")
for name, pages in PAGES_PER_DOC:
    low, high = pages * TOKENS_PER_PAGE_LOW, pages * TOKENS_PER_PAGE_HIGH
    share = high / WINDOW
    print(f"{name:<28}{pages:>7}{f'{low:,}-{high:,}':>22}"
          f"{share:>18.0%}{'$%.3f' % (high / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>9}")

print()
print("the 300-page report does not fit a 200k window at all —")
print("the PAGE limit is 600, and the window binds long before that")

document                      pages     tokens (low-high)   % of 200k window     cost
a 4-page invoice                  4          6,000-12,000                6%   $0.060
a 40-page contract               40        60,000-120,000               60%   $0.600
a 300-page annual report        300       450,000-900,000              450%   $4.500

the 300-page report does not fit a 200k window at all —
the PAGE limit is 600, and the window binds long before that

Note the cited_text field on each citation. It carries the passage verbatim, so a check can compare cited_text against the source and not trust the page number alone (§8.5).

The page limit is almost never what stops you. A dense document fills the context window well before 600 pages, and the failure looks like a context error and not a document error. Split long documents into sections, or retrieve the relevant pages (§10) and do not send the whole thing.

Because PDF support runs on the vision path, it inherits every vision limitation. Accuracy degrades on low-quality scans, and the model should not be relied on for perfect precision without review.

8.4 The Files API

Uploading a file once and referencing it by file_id keeps request payloads small and avoids re-sending the same bytes on every turn of a conversation.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

uploaded = client.files.upload(
    file=("board-pack.pdf", b"%PDF-1.7 ...", "application/pdf"),
)

print("id           :", uploaded.id)
print("filename     :", uploaded.filename)
print("size (bytes) :", uploaded.size_bytes)
print("mime type    :", uploaded.mime_type)
print("downloadable :", uploaded.downloadable)

id           : file_011CQ8s7Xk2b
filename     : board-pack.pdf
size (bytes) : 2418877
mime type    : application/pdf
downloadable : False

The file_id then goes in a source of type "file", in an image block or a document block depending on what it is.

For an image, the file_id goes inside an image block's source, and for a PDF, inside a document block's. What this buys you is worth being precise about, because it is not a token saving. The content still enters the context window and is still billed as input tokens every turn. What you save is request payload, meaning the bytes crossing the wire. The upload is also done once and not per request. For a conversation that refers to the same 30-page PDF over ten turns, that is ten uploads avoided and the same token cost either way.

Files persist until deleted, and that is a data-retention surface: an uploaded customer document sits in your workspace until something removes it. Delete what you no longer need, and treat the file store the way you treat any other repository of customer content.

8.5 Citations

Citations turn an answer into something your code can check. Enable them on a document or search result, and each text block comes back with the exact passages it drew on.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

POLICY = ("Refunds are available within 30 days of delivery. "
          "Perishable goods are excluded. "
          "Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days.")

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document",
         "source": {"type": "text", "media_type": "text/plain", "data": POLICY},
         "title": "Refund policy",
         "citations": {"enabled": True}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "How long do refunds take, and are there exclusions?"},
    ]}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type != "text":
        continue
    marks = len(block.citations or [])
    print(f"[{marks} citation(s)] {block.text}")
    for citation in (block.citations or []):
        print(f"    chars {citation.start_char_index}-{citation.end_char_index}: "
              f"{citation.cited_text!r}")

[0 citation(s)] Here is what the policy says. 
[1 citation(s)] Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days, 
    chars 81-137: 'Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days.'
[1 citation(s)] and perishable goods are excluded.
    chars 51-81: 'Perishable goods are excluded.'

The granularity is character indices into your source. That is what makes the check mechanical and not a matter of judgement. You can verify that the cited span exists, that it says what the sentence claims, and, the useful one, that a sentence has no citation at all.

Three practical points.

Citations are off by default and enabled per block. Within one request, all search results must agree on the setting (§10.7), while documents are configured individually.

A text block with no citations is a claim resting on nothing in your sources. §10.7 built the grader, and this is where the data for it comes from. It is the cheapest faithfulness check available, and it needs no judge.

Not every uncited sentence is a defect. Connective prose such as "Here is what I found" legitimately cites nothing. The check to build is not "every block has a citation" but "every block making a factual claim has one". That is why §13.4's graders combine the citation check with a rubric and do not replace one with the other.

8.6 Designing a Multimodal Request

Putting it together, the decisions worth making deliberately.

SCENARIOS = [
    # (scenario, source, why)
    ("one screenshot, one turn", "base64",
     "simplest; payload is small and nothing is reused"),
    ("a 30-page PDF across 10 turns", "Files API",
     "upload once; the tokens recur either way but the bytes do not"),
    ("40 product photos to classify", "Files API + batch",
     "over the 20-image threshold, so resize to 2000px as well"),
    ("an image the user linked to", "url",
     "no upload, no payload — but the URL must stay reachable"),
    ("screenshots in an agent loop", "base64, resized",
     "they accumulate in context and count toward the 20-image threshold"),
]

print(f"{'scenario':<32}{'source':<22}{'why'}")
for scenario, source, why in SCENARIOS:
    print(f"{scenario:<32}{source:<22}{why}")

print()
print("the recurring trap: images from EARLIER turns still count")

scenario                        source                why
one screenshot, one turn        base64                simplest; payload is small and nothing is reused
a 30-page PDF across 10 turns   Files API             upload once; the tokens recur either way but the bytes do not
40 product photos to classify   Files API + batch     over the 20-image threshold, so resize to 2000px as well
an image the user linked to     url                   no upload, no payload — but the URL must stay reachable
screenshots in an agent loop    base64, resized       they accumulate in context and count toward the 20-image threshold

the recurring trap: images from EARLIER turns still count

And here are the limitations to design around and not discover. The model will not identify people in images and refuses to. Counting objects is approximate. Coordinate output is approximate. It cannot tell whether an image is AI-generated, and will be confidently wrong if asked. It is not a diagnostic tool for medical imaging. Each of these is a place where an application built on the assumption of precision will fail in a way its tests did not catch. So if your product depends on one of them, that is the case §13.3 needs in its edge-case bucket.

Exercises

Exercise 8.1 — Size a document pipeline. You process 2,000 scanned invoices a day, averaging 3 pages each, extracting line items as structured output. Compute the token cost, decide base64 versus Files API, and say what you would change to halve the bill.

Solution 
INVOICES_PER_DAY, PAGES_EACH, DAYS = 2_000, 3, 30
TOKENS_PER_PAGE = 2_200          # scans are dense; measure, do not assume
OUTPUT_TOKENS = 320              # a structured line-item extraction
IN_PER_MTOK, OUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 25.00
HAIKU_IN, HAIKU_OUT = 1.00, 5.00
BATCH_DISCOUNT = 0.50

pages = INVOICES_PER_DAY * PAGES_EACH * DAYS
input_tokens = pages * TOKENS_PER_PAGE
output_tokens = INVOICES_PER_DAY * DAYS * OUTPUT_TOKENS

opus = input_tokens / 1e6 * IN_PER_MTOK + output_tokens / 1e6 * OUT_PER_MTOK
haiku = input_tokens / 1e6 * HAIKU_IN + output_tokens / 1e6 * HAIKU_OUT

print(f"pages per month     : {pages:>12,}")
print(f"input tokens        : {input_tokens:>12,}")
print(f"output tokens       : {output_tokens:>12,}")
print()
print(f"{'configuration':<34}{'$/month':>12}{'vs baseline':>13}")
for label, cost in (("Opus 5, real time", opus),
                    ("Opus 5, Batch API", opus * BATCH_DISCOUNT),
                    ("Haiku 4.5, real time", haiku),
                    ("Haiku 4.5, Batch API", haiku * BATCH_DISCOUNT)):
    print(f"{label:<34}{'$' + format(cost, ',.0f'):>12}{cost / opus:>12.0%}")

print()
print(f"input is {input_tokens / (input_tokens + output_tokens):.0%} of all tokens:")
print("this is an INPUT-bound workload, so page count is the lever")

pages per month     :      180,000
input tokens        :  396,000,000
output tokens       :   19,200,000

configuration                          $/month  vs baseline
Opus 5, real time                       $2,460        100%
Opus 5, Batch API                       $1,230         50%
Haiku 4.5, real time                      $492         20%
Haiku 4.5, Batch API                      $246         10%

input is 95% of all tokens:
this is an INPUT-bound workload, so page count is the lever

Use the Files API, and be clear that it is not a cost decision. Base64 inflates the payload by a third, and a three-page scan is easily several megabytes, so at 2,000 a day you will meet the 32 MB request limit on the fat ones. But the token cost is identical either way, because the pages still enter the window. The Files API buys reliability and smaller requests, and not a smaller bill.

Batch processing halves it, and this workload is the ideal candidate. Invoices are not latency-sensitive, because nobody is waiting. That is a 50% saving for a scheduling change, and it is the first thing I would do.

Then reconsider the model. This is a structured-extraction task against a schema (§4), which is close to the definition of what a small model handles well. Haiku is a fifth of the price, and combined with batching it is a tenth of the baseline. The prerequisite is §13's eval: run both models over a few hundred labelled invoices and compare field-level accuracy. If Haiku holds, the saving is enormous. If it does not, you have learned that at the cost of an afternoon and not a quarter.

And the lever the arithmetic points at. Input is the overwhelming majority of tokens, so anything that reduces pages reduces the bill proportionally. Two things are worth checking. One is whether every page needs to go to the model at all, since a cover sheet and a terms-and-conditions page carry no line items. The other is whether the scans are being downscaled before upload. A 300 dpi scan of an A4 page is far past what is needed to read a table, and §8.2's arithmetic applies directly.

What I would measure first. The 2,200-tokens-per-page figure is an assumption, and everything above scales with it. count_tokens on a representative sample of real invoices costs nothing and turns this estimate into a number.

Exercise 8.2 — Build the citation check. Write a grader that flags unsupported claims in a cited answer, and say what it cannot catch.

Solution 
SOURCE = ("Refunds are available within 30 days of delivery. Perishable goods "
          "are excluded. Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days.")

# What the API returns: text blocks, each with zero or more citations.
BLOCKS = [
    ("Here is what the policy says.", []),
    ("Refunds are available within 30 days of delivery.",
     [(0, 49)]),
    ("Perishable goods are excluded.", [(50, 80)]),
    ("Processing takes 5 business days once approved.", [(81, 141)]),
    ("Most customers see the credit within a week.", []),
    ("Refunds are available within 60 days.", [(0, 49)]),
]

CLAIM_MARKERS = ("day", "week", "%", "excluded", "processed", "available")


def looks_factual(text):
    return any(marker in text.lower() for marker in CLAIM_MARKERS)


def grade(blocks, source):
    findings = []
    for text, spans in blocks:
        if not looks_factual(text):
            continue                      # connective prose cites nothing
        if not spans:
            findings.append(("UNCITED", text))
            continue
        for start, end in spans:
            cited = source[start:end]
            if cited not in source:
                findings.append(("BAD-SPAN", text))
    return findings


for kind, text in grade(BLOCKS, SOURCE):
    print(f"{kind:<10}{text}")

print()
total = sum(looks_factual(t) for t, _ in BLOCKS)
print(f"{total} factual claims, {len(grade(BLOCKS, SOURCE))} flagged")
print()
print("what it CANNOT catch:")
for miss in ("a claim that cites a real span which does not support it",
             "'60 days' citing the sentence that says 30 — the span is valid",
             "an omission: something true the answer left out"):
    print(f"  · {miss}")

UNCITED   Most customers see the credit within a week.

5 factual claims, 1 flagged

what it CANNOT catch:
  · a claim that cites a real span which does not support it
  · '60 days' citing the sentence that says 30 — the span is valid
  · an omission: something true the answer left out

What it catches is real and cheap. An uncited factual claim, such as "Most customers see the credit within a week", is flagged with no model call, no judge and no rubric. In a RAG system that is the most common hallucination shape, because the model is filling a gap the sources left.

What it misses is the more interesting half, and the last row is the demonstration. "Refunds are available within 60 days" cites character span 0–49, which is a genuine span of the source saying 30 days. The citation is structurally valid and semantically wrong. No span check can see that, because the mechanism only proves where the model looked and not that the sentence follows from it.

So the citation check is a filter, not a verifier, and it works together with §14's layers in the same way. Structural checks are free and catch the cheap failures at volume. A judge (§13.5) with a rubric that asks "is this claim supported by the cited text?" catches the expensive ones. You can afford to run it only on the blocks that carry citations, because the uncited ones were already caught for nothing.

The looks_factual heuristic is the weakest part, and I would replace it. Keyword matching to decide which sentences are claims will both over-fire and under-fire. It is here because it is honest about the shape of the problem. In production, the better design is to require citations on every block and treat the connective-prose exception as a rubric question for the judge.

One thing this cannot address at all: omission. An answer that cites everything it says and leaves out the exclusion for perishable goods scores perfectly. Faithfulness and completeness are different criteria, and §13.2's multidimensional table is where they get measured separately.

SECTION 9

Context Engineering

The model is stateless, which means it remembers nothing between requests. Every request carries the entire world it will see, and you resend that world on every turn. Section 6 built a loop that grows the conversation by two messages per tool call and then sends all of it again. This section is about what that costs, what it does to quality, and the four mechanisms the API gives you for controlling it.

The word engineering is doing real work in the title. Prompt engineering is about what you say. Context engineering is about what is present: what stays in the window, what gets cached, what gets cleared, what gets summarised, and what lives outside the window entirely and is fetched back on demand. In production systems this is where the money is and where the latency is. It is also, and people discover this last, where a surprising amount of the accuracy is, because a window stuffed with stale tool output is a window in which the relevant sentence is harder to find.

9.1 The Bill You Pay Every Turn

Start with the arithmetic, because it is unintuitive and it decides everything else.

SYSTEM_TOKENS = 1_200         # instructions, stable
TOOLS_TOKENS = 3_200          # 34 definitions, stable
USER_TOKENS = 60              # one question
ASSISTANT_TOKENS = 220        # one answer
TOOL_RESULT_TOKENS = 900      # one search result coming back

INPUT_PER_MTOK, OUTPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 25.00

print(f"{'turn':>4} {'input tokens':>13} {'cumulative in':>14} "
      f"{'cost this turn':>15} {'cumulative':>11}")
history = SYSTEM_TOKENS + TOOLS_TOKENS
cumulative_in = 0
cumulative_cost = 0.0
for turn in range(1, 11):
    history += USER_TOKENS + TOOL_RESULT_TOKENS + ASSISTANT_TOKENS
    cumulative_in += history
    cost = (history / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK
            + ASSISTANT_TOKENS / 1e6 * OUTPUT_PER_MTOK)
    cumulative_cost += cost
    if turn in (1, 2, 3, 5, 10):
        print(f"{turn:>4} {history:>13,} {cumulative_in:>14,} "
              f"{'$%.4f' % cost:>15} {'$%.4f' % cumulative_cost:>11}")

linear = 10 * (SYSTEM_TOKENS + TOOLS_TOKENS + USER_TOKENS
               + TOOL_RESULT_TOKENS + ASSISTANT_TOKENS)
print(f"\nif each turn were independent: {linear:,} input tokens")
print(f"because the conversation is resent: {cumulative_in:,} input tokens")
print(f"ratio: {cumulative_in / linear:.2f}x")

turn  input tokens  cumulative in  cost this turn  cumulative
   1         5,580          5,580         $0.0334     $0.0334
   2         6,760         12,340         $0.0393     $0.0727
   3         7,940         20,280         $0.0452     $0.1179
   5        10,300         39,700         $0.0570     $0.2260
  10        16,200        108,900         $0.0865     $0.5995

if each turn were independent: 55,800 input tokens
because the conversation is resent: 108,900 input tokens
ratio: 1.95x

A conversation costs a quadratic in its length, not a linear amount. Turn ten pays for turns one through nine again. That is why ten turns cost 108,900 input tokens and not the 55,800 they would cost if each stood alone, which is 1.95× already, and the multiplier keeps climbing. This is the single most important cost fact about the API, and it is invisible if you only ever test with two-turn conversations.

Three consequences follow, and each is a subsection below.

The stable part is resent unchanged every time, which means it can be cached and should be (§9.3). System prompts and tool definitions are the same bytes on turn ten as on turn one, so paying full price for them ten times is a choice and not a requirement.

The volatile part grows without bound, and most of the growth is tool results, at 900 tokens each here against 220 for the model's own answers. Those results were useful when the model read them and are mostly dead weight afterwards. §9.6 clears them.

Eventually the window fills. A 1M-token window is large, but an agent doing real work reaches it, and quality degrades before capacity does. §9.7 summarises instead of truncating (cutting off the oldest part).

9.2 Counting Before You Send

Guessing token counts is how people end up debugging a 400 in production. There is an endpoint for counting, it is free, and it accepts the same request shape you were going to send.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "search_docs",
    "description": "Full-text search over the internal handbook.",
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
                     "required": ["query"]},
}]

count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    system="You are a concise internal support assistant.",
    tools=TOOLS,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do I request unpaid leave?"}],
)

print("input tokens:", count.input_tokens)

input tokens: 168

Note what is being counted. tools and system are included, because they are part of the prompt. This is how you discover that a tool surface you thought was small is not.

Two facts about counting shape design decisions elsewhere in the course.

Tokens are not words and not characters. English prose runs roughly four characters per token, but code, JSON, non-Latin scripts and long identifiers all run denser. The ~chars/4 estimates used for back-of-envelope work in §6.9 are fine for deciding whether to investigate, and useless for deciding whether a request fits.

The tokeniser changed. Claude 4.7 and later use a newer tokeniser that produces roughly 30% more tokens for the same text than the one Sonnet 4.6 and earlier use. That is not a price rise, because per-token prices differ too. But it does mean that a token budget measured on an older model does not transfer. It also means that any hard-coded "this fits in 8,000 tokens" assertion inherited from an older codebase should be re-measured and not trusted.

9.3 Prompt Caching: The Prefix Rule

Caching is the highest-value change available in most LLM applications, and it hinges on one rule that is easy to state and easy to violate by accident.

The cache is a prefix match. The request is rendered in a fixed order (tools, then system, then messages), and a cache entry covers everything from the start up to a designated breakpoint. Any byte that changes anywhere in that prefix invalidates the entry and everything after it.

1. tools
Rendered first, so cached first. Change one tool description and every cache below it dies — tools, system and messages alike. A tool description is the highest-leverage text in the request in both directions: it decides tool selection (§6.2) and it gates the entire cache.
2. system
Second. A timestamp in the system prompt is the classic silent cache killer: it invalidates system and messages on every single request while looking completely harmless.
3. messages
Last, and the part that grows. In a conversation the breakpoint moves forward through this as turns accumulate.

The pricing is what makes it worth arranging your request around. A cache write costs 1.25× a normal input token, and a cache read costs 0.1×. So the break-even comes quickly:

BASE, WRITE_MULT, READ_MULT = 1.0, 1.25, 0.10

def cost(prefix_tokens, reads, cached):
    """Total cost in 'base input token' units for one write plus `reads` reuses."""
    if not cached:
        return prefix_tokens * BASE * (reads + 1)
    return prefix_tokens * WRITE_MULT + prefix_tokens * READ_MULT * reads


PREFIX = 20_000
print(f"{'reuses':>7} {'uncached':>10} {'cached':>10} {'saving':>8}")
for reads in (0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 50):
    a, b = cost(PREFIX, reads, False), cost(PREFIX, reads, True)
    print(f"{reads:>7} {a:>10,.0f} {b:>10,.0f} {(1 - b / a) * 100:>7.0f}%")

print("\nbreak-even is the first reuse: a single write costs "
      f"{WRITE_MULT}x, so one read at {READ_MULT}x already beats {2 * BASE}x.")

reuses   uncached     cached   saving
      0     20,000     25,000     -25%
      1     40,000     27,000      32%
      2     60,000     29,000      52%
      3     80,000     31,000      61%
      5    120,000     35,000      71%
     10    220,000     45,000      80%
     50  1,020,000    125,000      88%

break-even is the first reuse: a single write costs 1.25x, so one read at 0.1x already beats 2.0x.

One reuse pays for the write, and the first row is the only losing one. A prefix used exactly once costs 25% more cached than uncached, because you paid the write multiplier for a cache nobody read. Reuse it once and you are 32% ahead, and ten times and you are 80% ahead. Almost every real application has a repeated prefix, so there is essentially no scenario where caching is the wrong call. That is why the simplest form of it is a single top-level parameter.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

HANDBOOK = "…forty pages of policy text…"

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"},
    system=[{"type": "text", "text": f"Answer only from this handbook.\n\n{HANDBOOK}"}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do I request unpaid leave?"}],
)

u = response.usage
print("written to cache:", u.cache_creation_input_tokens)
print("read from cache :", u.cache_read_input_tokens)
print("uncached input  :", u.input_tokens)
print("total input     :", u.cache_creation_input_tokens
      + u.cache_read_input_tokens + u.input_tokens)

written to cache: 9840
read from cache : 0
uncached input  : 14
total input     : 9854

Automatic caching, which is that top-level cache_control, places the breakpoint at the last cacheable block for you and moves it forward as the conversation grows. Automatic caching consumes one of the four breakpoint slots, so it works alongside explicit ones and does not replace them. For most applications this is the right answer and the whole of your caching implementation.

Read the usage fields carefully, because their meaning is not the obvious one. input_tokens counts only the tokens after the last breakpoint, and not the total. The total is the sum of all three. A team tracking spend from input_tokens alone after enabling caching will see their numbers apparently collapse and conclude something is broken.

9.4 Placing Breakpoints by Hand

Explicit breakpoints, meaning cache_control on individual blocks, earn their complexity when different parts of your prompt change at different rates. You get four cache breakpoint slots, and the automatic breakpoint consumes one of the four if you use both. A cache breakpoint marks where a cached prefix ends, so its placement is the only decision that matters.

The design question is always the same: order your content from least to most volatile, and put the breakpoint at the boundary.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

POLICY = "…forty pages that change quarterly…"
ACCOUNT = "…this customer's plan, tier and open tickets…"

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[
        {"type": "text", "text": "You are a support assistant."},
        {"type": "text", "text": POLICY,
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}},
        {"type": "text", "text": ACCOUNT,
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Can I downgrade mid-cycle?"}],
)

print("stop_reason :", response.stop_reason)
print("cache writes:", response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens)

stop_reason : end_turn
cache writes: 11420

There are two breakpoints here, with two lifetimes. The policy is shared by every conversation in the system and changes quarterly, so it takes the 1-hour cache. The account block is shared by one customer's session, so it takes the default 5 minutes. The 1-hour cache costs 2× base input to write, against the 5-minute cache's 1.25×, so it pays for itself the moment it avoids one extra write.

Here is a constraint that will bite if you do not know it: entries with a longer TTL (time to live) must appear before shorter ones. A 1-hour breakpoint after a 5-minute breakpoint is rejected.

Here are some further mechanics worth having in your head and not in a doc:

There is a minimum cacheable prefix, and falling short of it fails silently. For Claude Opus 5 it is 512 tokens. For Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 it is 1,024, and for Opus 4.6 and Haiku 4.5 it is 4,096. Below the threshold you get no error and no cache, and both cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens come back zero. If your prefix is just short of the line, padding it to reach the threshold is usually worth it.

Breakpoints are free. You are billed for what is written and read, and not for how many markers you placed. There is no reason to be sparing with the four you have.

A cache entry becomes available only after the first response begins. Firing ten parallel requests against a cold cache writes it ten times. Warm it with one request first.

The 5-minute clock starts when the request starts, not when it ends. A response that streams for four minutes leaves about one minute of usable life. For agent turns that run long, that alone can be the argument for the 1-hour TTL.

9.5 What Invalidates a Cache, and How to Notice

Cache invalidation is the failure mode to understand here, and its defining property is that it is silent. The request succeeds, the answer is fine, and the bill is ten times what you expected. The only way to know is to look.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

SYSTEM = "…a long stable instruction block…"


def ask(question):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=256,
        cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"},
        system=[{"type": "text", "text": SYSTEM}],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    )
    u = response.usage
    total = u.cache_read_input_tokens + u.cache_creation_input_tokens + u.input_tokens
    hit_rate = u.cache_read_input_tokens / total if total else 0.0
    return u, hit_rate


for question in ("First question.", "Second question."):
    usage, rate = ask(question)
    print(f"{question:<18} write={usage.cache_creation_input_tokens:>5} "
          f"read={usage.cache_read_input_tokens:>5} "
          f"new={usage.input_tokens:>3}  hit rate={rate:>5.1%}")

First question.    write= 2410 read=    0 new=  8  hit rate= 0.0%
Second question.   write=    0 read= 2410 new=  8  hit rate=99.7%

If cache_read_input_tokens is zero across repeated requests, something in your prefix is changing. That is the whole diagnostic, and cache invalidation is the only explanation for it. Log the field, alert on it, and treat a drop as an incident and not as a curiosity.

The invalidators worth memorising, because each has caught someone out:

Anything in tools
Invalidates everything. Tools render first. A tool list built by iterating a set, or conditionally including a tool, re-orders or changes the prefix and kills the whole cache. Build the list deterministically and sort it.
A timestamp in system
Invalidates system and messages, every request. "Today's date is …" is the single most common cause of a zero hit rate. Put it in the user turn, after the breakpoint.
Toggling web search or citations
Invalidates system and messages. Both modify the constructed system prompt, so a request that conditionally enables one is two different prefixes alternating.
Changing effort or thinking config
Always invalidates messages, and on some models tools and system too. Setting effort explicitly to the model's default is the same as omitting it and does not invalidate.
Switching speed: "fast"
Invalidates system and messages. Fast mode has its own rate-limit pool, so falling back from fast mode to standard on a 429 costs a cache write as well as the retry — worth knowing before you write that fallback.
Unsorted JSON
Invalidates whatever it sits in. Serialising a dict whose key order varies between processes produces a different prefix on different machines. json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True).

One escape hatch is worth knowing about because it solves a problem that otherwise has no clean answer. A mid-conversation operator instruction can be added without invalidating anything. You do it by appending a {"role": "system"} entry to messages and not by editing the top-level system field. On Claude Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Fable 5 and Mythos 5 this preserves the cached prefix entirely, and it is not available on Sonnet 5. It is also the injection-safe channel for operator instructions, which §14.4 returns to.

9.6 Context Editing: Clearing Tool Results

Caching makes the stable part cheap. It does nothing about the part that grows, and in an agent that part is dominated by tool results such as file contents, search hits and page fetches. Those were valuable when the model read them and are mostly inert afterwards.

clear_tool_uses_20250919 deletes the oldest of them, server-side, once the prompt crosses a threshold.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{"name": "read_file",
          "description": "Read a file from the repository.",
          "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                           "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}},
                           "required": ["path"]}}]

response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    betas=["context-management-2025-06-27"],
    context_management={"edits": [{
        "type": "clear_tool_uses_20250919",
        "trigger": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 60000},
        "keep": {"type": "tool_uses", "value": 5},
        "clear_at_least": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 8000},
        "exclude_tools": ["read_file"],
    }]},
    tools=TOOLS,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise what you have found."}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print("text       :", response.content[0].text)

stop_reason: end_turn
text       : I read six files; the migration touches three modules.

Four parameters, and each exists to answer a real question.

trigger decides when clearing starts, and defaults to 100,000 input tokens. Below it, nothing happens.

keep decides how many recent tool use/result pairs survive, and defaults to 3. The oldest go first. This is the parameter to raise when the agent starts forgetting what it just read.

clear_at_least is the subtle one, and it exists because clearing invalidates your prompt cache. Content is being removed from the middle of the prefix, so everything after the removal has to be written again. If clearing 400 tokens costs a 40,000-token cache write, you have made things worse. clear_at_least says "do not bother unless it is worth it".

exclude_tools protects results you cannot afford to lose, such as a tool whose output is the task's working state and not a lookup.

Two properties of this mechanism are easy to get wrong.

It happens server-side, and your client keeps the full history. You do not mirror the edit, you do not remove anything locally, and you do not need to reconstruct what the model saw. Keep sending the whole conversation, and the API applies the strategy before the prompt reaches the model.

The model is told the result was removed, and is not left with a hole. Each cleared result is replaced by placeholder text, so the model knows it once had that information and does not conclude it never looked.

You can see exactly what happened in response.context_management.applied_edits, which reports cleared_tool_uses and cleared_input_tokens. Log those the way you log cache fields.

There is a sibling strategy, clear_thinking_20251015, for thinking blocks. Its default varies by model. Opus 4.5 and later keep all prior thinking, and older models keep only the last turn's. So if your code runs across model tiers, set keep explicitly and do not inherit a default that changes underneath you. Note that the caching interaction runs the opposite way here: keeping thinking blocks preserves the cache, and clearing them invalidates it at the clearing point.

9.7 Compaction: Summarising Instead of Deleting

Clearing is lossy in a blunt way, because the information is gone. Compaction replaces old context with a summary the model wrote, which is lossy in a much more useful way. It is the recommended default for long-running conversations. The reason to prefer it over clearing is not only capacity. Response quality degrades as context grows, so a shorter, denser context is often a better context.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    betas=["compact-2026-01-12"],
    context_management={"edits": [{
        "type": "compact_20260112",
        "trigger": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 150000},
    }]},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Continue the migration plan."}],
)

for block in response.content:
    print("block:", block.type)

print("top-level input :", response.usage.input_tokens)
for step in response.usage.iterations:
    print(f"  iteration {step.type:<10} in={step.input_tokens:>7,} "
          f"out={step.output_tokens:>6,}")

total_in = sum(s.input_tokens for s in response.usage.iterations)
print("billed input across all iterations:", f"{total_in:,}")

block: compaction
block: text
top-level input : 23000
  iteration compaction in=180,000 out= 3,500
  iteration message    in= 23,000 out= 1,000
billed input across all iterations: 203,000

The mechanism is this: when input tokens reach the trigger, the API generates a summary, emits it as a compaction block, and continues the response from the compacted context. On subsequent requests you append the response as usual, and the API drops every block before the compaction block automatically.

That last point is the one thing you must get right. Append response.content, not the extracted text. The compaction block lives in content. Pulling out block.text and appending a string throws it away, and the next request resends the full uncompacted history, silently, expensively, and with no error to tell you.

Three more things this example is showing.

Billing moved. Top-level input_tokens and output_tokens no longer cover everything, because they sum the non-compaction iterations only. The summarisation step is real work and is billed, and it appears as a compaction entry in usage.iterations. Any cost tracking that reads the top-level fields will under-report once compaction is on. Sum the iterations instead.

The trigger has a floor of 50,000 tokens and defaults to 150,000. Setting it low to "be safe" means summarising constantly, and each summarisation is a full pass over the conversation at the same model.

Compaction can fail when tools are defined. During the internal summarisation step the model occasionally calls a tool instead of writing a summary, and you get a compaction block with content: null. The fix is to supply instructions that forbid it explicitly — a prompt along the lines of "Summarise the transcript inside <summary> tags… Do not call any tools while writing this summary; respond with text only." If you use compaction with tools, write those instructions from the start rather than after the first null.

There is one limitation to plan around: the summary is written by the same model as the request. There is no option to summarise with something cheaper.

9.8 Memory: State That Outlives the Window

Caching, clearing and compaction all operate on the window. The memory tool operates outside it. It is a client-side tool, declared as {"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}, that lets the model read and write files in a store you control. What it writes survives the conversation ending.

The distinction that matters is what each mechanism does to information the model will need next week.

Clearing
Destroys it. Right for a file the agent has already summarised in its own words, wrong for a decision it will need to justify later.
Compaction
Compresses it, within this conversation. Survives the window filling; does not survive the conversation ending.
Memory
Persists it, outside any conversation. The model decides what is worth keeping and writes it down. Survives everything, including your process restarting.

The backend is yours to implement, and the directory it writes into is usually called a memory store. A memory store is a security boundary and not a formality. The memory tool supplies paths, and paths from a model are untrusted input. The model supplies paths, and §14.4 develops the argument. The short version is that a path from a model is untrusted input, and a memory backend that joins it onto a directory without normalising and re-checking is a directory traversal (a path like ../../etc escaping the intended folder) waiting to happen.

import os


class MemoryStore:
    """A memory backend confined to one directory. The confinement is the point."""

    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = os.path.realpath(root)

    def _resolve(self, path):
        candidate = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(self.root, path.lstrip("/")))
        if candidate != self.root and not candidate.startswith(self.root + os.sep):
            raise PermissionError(f"path escapes the memory root: {path!r}")
        return candidate

    def write(self, path, text):
        target = self._resolve(path)
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(target), exist_ok=True)
        with open(target, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            fh.write(text)
        return f"wrote {len(text)} chars"

    def read(self, path):
        with open(self._resolve(path), encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            return fh.read()


import tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    store = MemoryStore(tmp)
    print(store.write("/memories/customer_4471.md", "Prefers email. Gold tier."))
    print(store.read("/memories/customer_4471.md"))
    for hostile in ("../../../etc/passwd", "/memories/../../escape.txt"):
        try:
            store.write(hostile, "owned")
        except PermissionError as exc:
            print(f"blocked: {exc}")

wrote 25 chars
Prefers email. Gold tier.
blocked: path escapes the memory root: '../../../etc/passwd'
blocked: path escapes the memory root: '/memories/../../escape.txt'

os.path.realpath after the join is what does the work. It resolves .. and symlinks before the check, so a path that escapes is caught no matter how it is spelled. Checking the raw string for ".." is the version of this that gets bypassed.

9.9 Choosing Between Them

These four mechanisms are not alternatives. A production agent typically runs three of them at once, and they work together in a specific order.

Always
Caching. One parameter, pays for itself on the first reuse, no behavioural change. There is no application with a repeated prefix that should not have it.
Long conversations
Compaction. The default for anything that runs past a few tens of thousands of tokens. Handles the window filling without you writing summarisation code.
Heavy tool use
Context editing. Add it when tool results dominate the growth and are genuinely disposable. Set clear_at_least so it does not fight your cache.
Across sessions
Memory. Add it when the agent needs to know something next week that it learned today. Not a context-size mechanism at all — it solves a different problem that looks similar.

The one real tension is between clearing and caching, and it is worth stating plainly because it is the mistake this section exists to prevent. Clearing removes content from the middle of your prefix, which invalidates the cache from that point on. Aggressive clearing with a large cached prefix can cost more than not clearing at all. clear_at_least is the dial that resolves it, and the way to set it is to measure: clear enough that the tokens saved on subsequent turns exceed the write you just forced.

WRITE_MULT, READ_MULT = 1.25, 0.10
DOWNSTREAM = 12_000     # cached tokens after the clearing point, re-written once

# Clearing costs the DIFFERENCE between writing those tokens and reading them:
# they were going to be read at 0.10x anyway, and now cost 1.25x instead.
penalty = DOWNSTREAM * (WRITE_MULT - READ_MULT)

print(f"one-off penalty for re-writing {DOWNSTREAM:,} downstream tokens: "
      f"{penalty:,.0f}\n")
header = f"{'cleared':>9} {'saved/turn':>11}" + "".join(
    f"{str(t) + ' turns':>15}" for t in (2, 5, 10, 20))
print(header)
for cleared in (400, 2_000, 8_000, 20_000):
    saved_per_turn = cleared * READ_MULT
    cells = "".join(f"{saved_per_turn * t - penalty:>+15,.0f}"
                    for t in (2, 5, 10, 20))
    print(f"{cleared:>9,} {saved_per_turn:>11,.0f}{cells}")

print("\nbreak-even, in turns that must still remain:")
for cleared in (400, 2_000, 8_000, 20_000):
    print(f"  clear {cleared:>6,} tokens -> "
          f"{penalty / (cleared * READ_MULT):>6.0f} more turns")

one-off penalty for re-writing 12,000 downstream tokens: 13,800

  cleared  saved/turn        2 turns        5 turns       10 turns       20 turns
      400          40        -13,720        -13,600        -13,400        -13,000
    2,000         200        -13,400        -12,800        -11,800         -9,800
    8,000         800        -12,200         -9,800         -5,800         +2,200
   20,000       2,000         -9,800         -3,800         +6,200        +26,200

break-even, in turns that must still remain:
  clear    400 tokens ->    345 more turns
  clear  2,000 tokens ->     69 more turns
  clear  8,000 tokens ->     17 more turns
  clear 20,000 tokens ->      7 more turns

Read the sign and not the size. The units are "base input tokens", so the comparison is honest even though the absolute numbers are abstract. Two things fall straight out of the table, and neither is obvious.
