Clearing a small amount is never worth it, at any conversation length. Four hundred tokens saves forty a turn against a one-off penalty of nearly fourteen thousand, so it would need hundreds of remaining turns. That is what clear_at_least exists to prevent, and why its sensible value is not zero.

Clearing a large amount is worth it only if the conversation continues afterwards. Even dropping 20,000 tokens is still under water at five remaining turns. Clearing near the end of a session is pure cost. That is an argument for leaving the trigger high and not tuning it down out of caution, and for thinking about clearing in terms of turns remaining and not tokens accumulated.

Exercises

Exercise 9.1 — Find the cache killers. This request handler has a cache hit rate of zero and nobody knows why. Find every reason, and rewrite it.

import datetime
import json

def build_request(user_question, enabled_tools, customer):
    return {
        "model": "claude-opus-5",
        "max_tokens": 1024,
        "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
        "tools": [TOOL_REGISTRY[name] for name in enabled_tools],
        "system": [{
            "type": "text",
            "text": (
                f"You are a support assistant. Today is "
                f"{datetime.datetime.now().isoformat()}.\n"
                f"Customer profile: {json.dumps(customer)}\n"
                f"{HANDBOOK}"
            ),
        }],
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": user_question}],
    }
Solution

There are four independent causes, and they invalidate at three different levels.

import datetime
import json

TOOL_REGISTRY = {"search": {"name": "search", "description": "Search the handbook.",
                            "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {}}},
                 "escalate": {"name": "escalate", "description": "Escalate a ticket.",
                              "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {}}}}
HANDBOOK = "…forty pages…"


def build_request(user_question, enabled_tools, customer, now=None):
    now = now or datetime.datetime(2026, 8, 25, 9, 0, 0)
    return {
        "model": "claude-opus-5",
        "max_tokens": 1024,
        # 1. every request offers the same tools, in a fixed order
        "tools": [TOOL_REGISTRY[name] for name in sorted(TOOL_REGISTRY)],
        "system": [
            # 2. stable instructions and the handbook, cached for an hour
            {"type": "text",
             "text": f"You are a support assistant.\n{HANDBOOK}",
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}},
            # 3. per-customer block, cached for the session's five minutes
            {"type": "text",
             "text": "Customer profile: "
                     + json.dumps(customer, sort_keys=True),
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
        ],
        # 4. the volatile date moves after the last breakpoint
        "messages": [{"role": "user",
                      "content": f"Today is {now.date().isoformat()}.\n"
                                 f"{user_question}"}],
    }


a = build_request("Can I downgrade?", ["search"], {"tier": "gold", "id": 4471})
b = build_request("What about refunds?", ["escalate"], {"id": 4471, "tier": "gold"})

print("tool order identical  :", [t["name"] for t in a["tools"]]
      == [t["name"] for t in b["tools"]])
print("system prefix identical:", a["system"][0] == b["system"][0])
print("customer block identical:", a["system"][1] == b["system"][1])
print("breakpoints            :", sum("cache_control" in blk for blk in a["system"]))
print("ttl order (long first) :",
      [blk["cache_control"].get("ttl", "5m") for blk in a["system"]])

tool order identical  : True
system prefix identical: True
customer block identical: True
breakpoints            : 2
ttl order (long first) : ['1h', '5m']

1. enabled_tools varies per request. Tools render first, so any change to the array invalidates tools, system and messages, which is the entire cache, every time the caller passes a different subset. This is the most damaging of the four because it is total. Two fixes are available: send the full registry every time in a fixed order (chosen here), or accept the invalidation and cache nothing above the tools. Sorting matters even when the set is constant, because a set or dict iteration order that varies between processes produces different bytes.

2. datetime.now() in the system prompt. This changes on every request, invalidating system and messages. It is the single most common cause of a zero hit rate in the wild, because it looks like context and not like a variable. Moving it into the user turn, after every breakpoint, keeps the model informed and the prefix stable.

3. The customer profile sits above the handbook. Even with the timestamp gone, putting per-customer data before forty pages of shared policy means the shared part can never be cached across customers. It is not a prefix. It is a suffix of something volatile. Reordering to stable → less stable → volatile is the whole discipline, and here it is what lets the handbook be cached once for everybody.

4. json.dumps without sort_keys. Python dicts preserve insertion order, so the same profile built by two different code paths serialises differently. The check above proves it: the two calls pass the same customer with the keys in a different order, and the blocks still compare equal only because sort_keys=True is set.

One judgement call worth naming. Splitting the system prompt gives two breakpoints where the original had one, and costs nothing, because breakpoints are free and you are billed only for what is written and read. The 1-hour TTL on the handbook is chosen because it is shared across all customers and therefore refreshed constantly by someone. The customer block gets the default five minutes because it is only reused within one session. And the long TTL must come first, which is why the ordering is not merely tidy but required.

Exercise 9.2 — Should this agent clear or compact? An agent reads source files to answer questions about a codebase. A typical session: 40 turns, a 4,000-token system prompt, 12 tools totalling 3,500 tokens, and 30 read_file results averaging 2,500 tokens each. Decide what to enable, and show the arithmetic that justifies it.

Solution 
SYSTEM, TOOLS = 4_000, 3_500
N_READS, READ_TOKENS = 30, 2_500
TURNS = 40
CHAT_TOKENS_PER_TURN = 300        # the question and the model's prose reply

stable = SYSTEM + TOOLS
tool_results = N_READS * READ_TOKENS
chat = TURNS * CHAT_TOKENS_PER_TURN
final = stable + tool_results + chat

print(f"stable prefix (system + tools) : {stable:>8,} tokens")
print(f"tool results                   : {tool_results:>8,} tokens")
print(f"conversation prose             : {chat:>8,} tokens")
print(f"context at the final turn      : {final:>8,} tokens")
print(f"tool results as a share         : {tool_results / final:>8.0%}")
print()

# What each mechanism addresses.
print(f"caching can make cheap         : {stable:>8,} tokens ({stable / final:.0%})")
print(f"clearing can remove up to      : "
      f"{(N_READS - 5) * READ_TOKENS:>8,} tokens (keeping the last 5)")
print(f"compaction triggers at         :  150,000 tokens — "
      f"{'reached' if final > 150_000 else 'NEVER reached in this session'}")

stable prefix (system + tools) :    7,500 tokens
tool results                   :   75,000 tokens
conversation prose             :   12,000 tokens
context at the final turn      :   94,500 tokens
tool results as a share         :      79%

caching can make cheap         :    7,500 tokens (8%)
clearing can remove up to      :   62,500 tokens (keeping the last 5)
compaction triggers at         :  150,000 tokens — NEVER reached in this session

Enable caching and context editing. Do not enable compaction.

Caching first, and it is not the interesting part of the answer. The stable prefix is 7,500 tokens, which is a small share of the final context but is present on all 40 turns. So it is the part that is resent most often and the cheapest to fix. It takes one parameter.

Context editing is the mechanism that matches this workload. Tool results are around 80% of the context, and they are the disposable kind. Once the agent has read a file and answered a question about it, the full text is dead weight. keep: 5 retains enough for follow-up questions about recent files, and exclude_tools is not needed here because every result is the same kind of thing.

Compaction would never fire, because the session ends well below the 150,000-token trigger and the floor for the trigger is 50,000. You could lower the trigger to 50,000 and it would fire once near the end. But compaction costs a full summarisation pass at the same model, which for a session this size is worse than simply clearing results the agent no longer needs. Compaction earns its cost when the conversation itself is the thing that has grown too long, and not when a few large results have.

Set clear_at_least deliberately. A clearing event forces everything downstream of the clearing point to be written to cache again, at 1.25× instead of the 0.10× it would otherwise have been read at. Clearing a single 2,500-token result saves only 250 token-equivalents per future turn, which is far too little to repay that, as §9.9's table shows. Set clear_at_least to several results' worth, around 8,000–10,000 tokens, so that clearing happens in a few large batches and not continuously.

What I would measure before shipping. I would look at the applied_edits field, to confirm clearing is actually firing and how much it removes. I would also look at the cache hit rate immediately after each clearing event, to confirm the re-write is being amortised and not repeated. If the hit rate never recovers between clears, clear_at_least is too low.

Exercise 9.3 — The cost of a naive loop. Take the agent from §6.4 and give it 15 tool-using turns, a 2,000-token system prompt, 3,000 tokens of tool definitions, 700-token tool results and 200-token replies. Compute the input-token bill three ways: naive, cached, and cached with clearing after turn 8 (keeping the last 3 results). Say which change you would make first.

Solution 
SYSTEM, TOOLS, RESULT, REPLY, QUESTION = 2_000, 3_000, 700, 200, 50
TURNS = 15
WRITE_MULT, READ_MULT = 1.25, 0.10

stable = SYSTEM + TOOLS


def naive():
    total, history = 0, stable
    for _ in range(TURNS):
        history += QUESTION + RESULT + REPLY
        total += history
    return total


def cached():
    """The stable prefix is written on the first turn and read on every later one."""
    billed, volatile = 0, 0
    for turn in range(TURNS):
        volatile += QUESTION + RESULT + REPLY
        billed += stable * (WRITE_MULT if turn == 0 else READ_MULT) + volatile
    return billed


def cached_with_clearing(clear_after=8, keep=3):
    billed, volatile, results_held = 0, 0, 0
    for turn in range(1, TURNS + 1):
        volatile += QUESTION + RESULT + REPLY
        results_held += 1
        rate = WRITE_MULT if turn == 1 else READ_MULT
        if turn == clear_after:
            dropped = results_held - keep
            volatile -= dropped * RESULT
            results_held = keep
            rate = WRITE_MULT                    # clearing re-writes the prefix
        billed += stable * rate + volatile
    return billed


base = naive()
for label, value in (("naive", base), ("cached", cached()),
                     ("cached + clearing", cached_with_clearing())):
    print(f"{label:<20} {value:>10,.0f} token-equivalents  "
          f"{value / base:>5.2f}x  ${value / 1e6 * 5:>6.3f}")

naive                   189,000 token-equivalents   1.00x  $ 0.945
cached                  127,250 token-equivalents   0.67x  $ 0.636
cached + clearing       105,000 token-equivalents   0.56x  $ 0.525

Caching is the change to make first, and it is not close. It is one parameter, it changes no behaviour, and it removes most of the repeated cost of the 5,000-token stable prefix across 15 turns.

Clearing adds a further saving, and the number is smaller than intuition suggests. It fires once, drops five results, and pays a cache re-write for the privilege. Over the seven remaining turns the saving is real but modest. That is exactly the arithmetic clear_at_least exists to force you to do. Clearing early in a short session is close to break-even, and clearing in a 60-turn session is transformative. The mechanism has not changed, and only the number of turns over which the re-write is amortised has.

What the model does not tell you is that the naive figure is also the quality figure. By turn 15 the naive context holds fourteen stale tool results, and the model is choosing which of fifteen file contents is relevant. Clearing improves that, and no cost model captures it. This is the argument for enabling context editing even in sessions where the arithmetic is neutral. It is also the reason §13 measures answer quality against context length and does not assume more context is better.

SECTION 10

Retrieval

A model knows what was in its training data and what is in its context window. Everything else has to be put there, by you, at the moment it is needed. That includes your handbook, your tickets, your codebase, and anything written since the model's training cutoff. That is retrieval, and the pattern built on it is retrieval-augmented generation, usually shortened to RAG: find the relevant passages, put them in the window, and answer from them.

RAG has a reputation as a solved, almost trivial pattern: embed everything, search by cosine similarity, and stuff the top five results into the prompt. (An embedding is a list of numbers that captures meaning, and cosine similarity measures how close two of them are.) That pipeline works well enough to demo and badly enough to be the most common source of disappointing LLM products. Every stage of it has a decision in it that changes the answer. This section is about those decisions: how you split the documents, how you find them, how you rank what you found, and how you make the answer checkable afterwards.

10.1 When Retrieval Is the Wrong Answer

Start here, because context windows are large now, and the reflex to build a pipeline is often wrong.

CORPUS_SIZES = [("a product FAQ", 40, 600),
                ("an employee handbook", 220, 900),
                ("one year of engineering docs", 3_400, 1_100),
                ("a support ticket archive", 210_000, 400)]

WINDOW = 200_000
INPUT_PER_MTOK, CACHE_READ_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 0.50

print(f"{'corpus':<30}{'docs':>9}{'tokens':>12}{'fits?':>8}{'cached/query':>14}")
for name, docs, tokens_each in CORPUS_SIZES:
    total = docs * tokens_each
    fits = total < WINDOW
    cached = total / 1e6 * CACHE_READ_PER_MTOK if fits else None
    print(f"{name:<30}{docs:>9,}{total:>12,}{('yes' if fits else 'NO'):>8}"
          f"{('$%.4f' % cached) if fits else '—':>14}")

print("\nif it fits and it is stable, cache it and skip retrieval entirely")

corpus                             docs      tokens   fits?  cached/query
a product FAQ                        40      24,000     yes       $0.0120
an employee handbook                220     198,000     yes       $0.0990
one year of engineering docs      3,400   3,740,000      NO             —
a support ticket archive        210,000  84,000,000      NO             —

if it fits and it is stable, cache it and skip retrieval entirely

If the whole corpus fits in the window and changes rarely, put all of it in and cache it. There is no chunker, no vector store, no embedding pipeline to keep in sync, and no retrieval failure, because the model sees everything and the answer to "did we retrieve the right passage?" is always yes. At a cache-read rate this is startlingly cheap, and the engineering saved is substantial.

Retrieval earns its complexity when one of three things is true:

The corpus does not fit. This is the obvious case, and the honest one.

The corpus changes constantly. A cache write per change is fine at daily granularity and untenable at per-minute. Retrieval reads current state at query time.

Most of the corpus is irrelevant to any given query, and its presence hurts. This is the subtle one, and §9 already made the argument. A window stuffed with material the model must sift is a window in which the relevant sentence is harder to use. Beyond some size, retrieval improves accuracy and not just cost.

The failure to avoid is building a pipeline for a 40-document FAQ because RAG is what one builds.

10.2 Chunking

If you do retrieve, the first real decision is how to split documents, and it is more consequential than the choice of embedding model. You retrieve chunks, so a chunk is the unit of what the model gets to see. Split badly, and the sentence that answers the question is separated from the context that makes it meaningful.

DOC = """# Refund Policy

## Standard refunds
Customers may request a refund within 30 days of delivery. Refunds are
issued to the original payment method.

## Exceptions
Perishable goods are not refundable. Custom orders are not refundable
once production has begun.

## Processing time
Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval. The customer's
bank may take a further 3 to 5 days to post the credit."""


def fixed_size(text, size, overlap=0):
    """Split by character count. Fast, structure-blind."""
    step = size - overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]


def by_heading(text):
    """Split on markdown headings. Structure-aware, variable size."""
    chunks, current = [], []
    for line in text.split("\n"):
        if line.startswith("## ") and current:
            chunks.append("\n".join(current).strip())
            current = []
        current.append(line)
    if current:
        chunks.append("\n".join(current).strip())
    return chunks


for label, chunks in (("fixed 180, no overlap", fixed_size(DOC, 180)),
                      ("fixed 180, overlap 40", fixed_size(DOC, 180, 40)),
                      ("by heading", by_heading(DOC))):
    print(f"{label}  ->  {len(chunks)} chunks, "
          f"sizes {[len(c) for c in chunks]}")

print()
print("the question: 'are custom orders refundable?'")
print()
import re

for label, chunks in (("fixed 180", fixed_size(DOC, 180)),
                      ("by heading", by_heading(DOC))):
    hit = next((c for c in chunks if "Custom orders" in c), None)
    headings = re.findall(r"^#+ (.+)$", hit, re.M)
    print(f"{label}: the chunk containing the answer reads —")
    print(f"  {hit!r}")
    print(f"  headings inside it : {headings or 'NONE'}")
    print(f"  the rule belongs to: 'Exceptions'")
    print(f"  correctly labelled : {headings == ['Exceptions']}")
    print()

fixed 180, no overlap  ->  3 chunks, sizes [180, 180, 47]
fixed 180, overlap 40  ->  3 chunks, sizes [180, 180, 127]
by heading  ->  4 chunks, sizes [15, 129, 110, 147]

the question: 'are custom orders refundable?'

fixed 180: the chunk containing the answer reads —
  "re not refundable. Custom orders are not refundable\nonce production has begun.\n\n## Processing time\nRefunds are processed within 5 business days of approval. The customer's\nbank may"
  headings inside it : ['Processing time']
  the rule belongs to: 'Exceptions'
  correctly labelled : False

by heading: the chunk containing the answer reads —
  '## Exceptions\nPerishable goods are not refundable. Custom orders are not refundable\nonce production has begun.'
  headings inside it : ['Exceptions']
  the rule belongs to: 'Exceptions'
  correctly labelled : True

Read the last comparison, and note that the fixed-size chunk did not merely lose its heading. It acquired the wrong one. The rule about custom orders belongs under Exceptions, and the only heading inside that chunk is Processing time, because the 180-character window straddled a section boundary. A model retrieving it sees a prohibition filed under a heading about timescales.

That is worse than losing the heading, and it is the characteristic failure of structure-blind chunking. Boundaries fall in the middle of sections, so chunks end up carrying a neighbour's label. The heading-based split gets it right by construction, because its boundaries are the section boundaries.

Four strategies, and the ordering is a genuine recommendation:

Structural chunking, wherever structure exists. Split on headings, sections, functions and ticket boundaries. Chunks land where a human would split, and each carries its own context. This is the default, and it is right far more often than it is used.

Fixed size with overlap, when there is no structure, such as plain prose, transcripts and OCR output. A chunk overlap of 10–20% means a sentence cut at a boundary appears whole in one of the two neighbouring chunks. Without chunk overlap, boundary sentences are unretrievable in one piece, and the block below prices what that overlap costs in storage.

Contextual retrieval, where each chunk is prefixed with a short generated description of where it came from before being embedded. It costs one pass over the corpus with a cheap model, and it fixes the heading problem above directly. The chunk about custom orders arrives carrying the sentence "This is from the Exceptions section of the refund policy", so it matches a refund query and is intelligible when retrieved alone. Where a corpus has no usable structure, contextual retrieval is the technique that recovers most of what structural chunking would have given you.

Whole documents, when they are small. A 400-token FAQ entry is a chunk. Splitting it gains nothing and can only lose context.

DOC_TOKENS, CHUNK_TOKENS = 1_400, 220

for overlap_pct in (0, 10, 20, 40):
    step = CHUNK_TOKENS * (1 - overlap_pct / 100)
    n_chunks = max(1, round(DOC_TOKENS / step))
    stored = n_chunks * CHUNK_TOKENS
    print(f"overlap {overlap_pct:>2}%  ->  {n_chunks:>2} chunks  "
          f"{stored:>6,} tokens stored  "
          f"{stored / DOC_TOKENS:>4.2f}x the document")

print("\noverlap is duplication: it is bought with storage and embedding cost")

overlap  0%  ->   6 chunks   1,320 tokens stored  0.94x the document
overlap 10%  ->   7 chunks   1,540 tokens stored  1.10x the document
overlap 20%  ->   8 chunks   1,760 tokens stored  1.26x the document
overlap 40%  ->  11 chunks   2,420 tokens stored  1.73x the document

overlap is duplication: it is bought with storage and embedding cost

10.3 Keyword Search: BM25

The instinct is to reach for embeddings first. Start with keyword search instead, because it is cheap, needs no model, and is better than semantic search at exactly the queries users actually type: identifiers, error codes, product names, and anything rare.

BM25 is the standard scoring function for keyword search: a formula that ranks documents by how well their words match the query. It is worth building once to understand what it rewards.

import math
import re
from collections import Counter

DOCS = {
    "d1": "Refunds are issued within 30 days of delivery to the original card.",
    "d2": "Perishable goods and custom orders are not refundable.",
    "d3": "Error ERR_4471 means the payment gateway rejected the refund.",
    "d4": "Our returns process: pack the item, print the label, post it.",
    "d5": "Refund processing takes 5 business days after approval.",
}


def tokenise(text):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower())


class BM25:
    """The standard ranking function. k1 damps term frequency, b damps length."""

    def __init__(self, docs, k1=1.5, b=0.75):
        self.k1, self.b = k1, b
        self.docs = {i: tokenise(t) for i, t in docs.items()}
        self.avg_len = sum(len(t) for t in self.docs.values()) / len(self.docs)
        self.df = Counter()
        for tokens in self.docs.values():
            self.df.update(set(tokens))
        self.n = len(self.docs)

    def idf(self, term):
        # Rare terms score high; a term in every document scores near zero.
        return math.log(1 + (self.n - self.df[term] + 0.5) / (self.df[term] + 0.5))

    def score(self, query, doc_id):
        tokens = self.docs[doc_id]
        counts = Counter(tokens)
        total = 0.0
        for term in tokenise(query):
            if term not in counts:
                continue
            tf = counts[term]
            norm = 1 - self.b + self.b * len(tokens) / self.avg_len
            total += self.idf(term) * tf * (self.k1 + 1) / (tf + self.k1 * norm)
        return total

    def search(self, query, k=3):
        ranked = sorted(self.docs, key=lambda d: -self.score(query, d))
        return [(d, round(self.score(query, d), 3)) for d in ranked[:k]]


index = BM25(DOCS)
for query in ("refund", "ERR_4471", "can I return a cake"):
    print(f"{query!r:<24} -> {index.search(query)}")

print()
print("idf, most to least selective:")
for term in ("err_4471", "perishable", "refund", "the"):
    print(f"  {term:<12} {index.idf(term):>6.3f}  "
          f"(appears in {index.df[term]} of {index.n} docs)")

'refund'                 -> [('d5', 0.946), ('d3', 0.901), ('d1', 0.0)]
'ERR_4471'               -> [('d3', 1.426), ('d1', 0.0), ('d2', 0.0)]
'can I return a cake'    -> [('d1', 0.0), ('d2', 0.0), ('d3', 0.0)]

idf, most to least selective:
  err_4471      1.386  (appears in 1 of 5 docs)
  perishable    1.386  (appears in 1 of 5 docs)
  refund        0.875  (appears in 2 of 5 docs)
  the           0.539  (appears in 3 of 5 docs)

ERR_4471 is where keyword search wins outright. It appears in one document, its IDF (a score that rewards rare words) is high, and it ranks first with certainty. An embedding of that string is a point in space near other alphanumeric noise, and semantic similarity has nothing useful to say about it. Every corpus has terms like this, including SKUs, error codes, function names and customer identifiers, and they are disproportionately what people search for.

The refund query shows the classic keyword-search defect, and it is worth catching here. d1 begins "Refunds are issued…" and scores exactly zero, because this tokeniser produces refunds and the query produces refund, and those are different strings. Real keyword search applies a stemmer, which reduces words to a common root, so that both become refund. Leave it out and your search silently misses every plural, every tense and every inflected form, which in an English corpus is a large fraction of everything. It is also a good illustration of why hybrid search (§10.5) is worth having, because a vector retriever has no such blind spot.

"can I return a cake" is where it loses, and the last row shows why. Not one word of the query appears in the document about perishable goods. Keyword search cannot bridge cake to perishable. That is the gap embeddings fill.

10.4 Embeddings and Semantic Search

An embedding maps text to a vector (a list of numbers) such that similar meanings land near each other. Similarity is then the cosine similarity, which is the cosine of the angle between two vectors. It is 1.0 for identical directions and 0.0 for orthogonal (unrelated) ones.

Anthropic does not offer an embedding model. The Claude API has no embeddings endpoint, and any example claiming otherwise is wrong. The documented recommendation is Voyage AI, whose current generation is voyage-4 and variants (32,000-token context, 1024 dimensions by default, with 256, 512 and 2048 also available), plus domain-specific models for code, finance and law. Choosing a provider is a real decision with real lock-in, because re-embedding a large corpus is expensive, so it deserves more thought than the default.

The mechanics are worth building once, because the arithmetic explains several practical constraints.

import math

# Toy 4-dimensional "embeddings", hand-placed so the geometry is visible.
VECTORS = {
    "refund policy":    [0.90, 0.10, 0.05, 0.20],
    "return an item":   [0.85, 0.15, 0.10, 0.25],
    "perishable goods": [0.60, 0.55, 0.10, 0.15],
    "server latency":   [0.05, 0.10, 0.95, 0.30],
    "payment gateway":  [0.30, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80],
}


def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    return dot / (math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b)))


query = VECTORS["return an item"]
ranked = sorted(((cosine(query, v), name) for name, v in VECTORS.items()),
                reverse=True)
print("query: 'return an item'")
for score, name in ranked:
    bar = "#" * round(score * 40)
    print(f"  {score:>6.3f}  {name:<18} {bar}")

print()
DIMENSIONS = [(256, 4), (512, 4), (1024, 4), (2048, 4)]
CHUNKS = 500_000
print(f"{'dims':>6}{'bytes/vector':>14}{'500k chunks':>14}")
for dims, bytes_per in DIMENSIONS:
    per_vector = dims * bytes_per
    print(f"{dims:>6}{per_vector:>14,}{per_vector * CHUNKS / 1e9:>12.2f} GB")

query: 'return an item'
   1.000  return an item     ########################################
   0.994  refund policy      ########################################
   0.849  perishable goods   ##################################
   0.602  payment gateway    ########################
   0.251  server latency     ##########

  dims  bytes/vector   500k chunks
   256         1,024        0.51 GB
   512         2,048        1.02 GB
  1024         4,096        2.05 GB
  2048         8,192        4.10 GB

Three facts that follow from the geometry.

Cosine similarity is bounded and comparable within one model, and meaningless across models. A score of 0.83 from one embedding model and 0.83 from another are not the same quantity. Similarity thresholds must be tuned per model and re-tuned when you change it.

Dimension is a cost knob with a quality trade-off. Storing 500,000 chunks at 1024 dimensions is a couple of gigabytes. At 256 it is a quarter of that, and search is proportionally faster. Models that support several output dimensions let you pick the point on that curve and do not force one on you.

Nothing here is exact search. At production scale, a vector database stores these vectors and searches them with an approximate nearest-neighbour index, which trades recall for speed. That trade is a knob on the vector database, and a badly tuned index silently fails to return documents that exist. That failure mode looks exactly like the model being unhelpful.

10.5 Hybrid Search

Keyword search wins on rare terms, and semantic search wins on paraphrase. Real queries contain both, so run both and fuse the results. The standard fusion method is reciprocal rank fusion, which combines rankings and not scores. That is the point, since the two scores are not on a comparable scale.

BM25_RANKING = ["d3", "d1", "d5", "d2", "d4"]        # rare terms, exact matches
VECTOR_RANKING = ["d2", "d1", "d4", "d5", "d3"]      # paraphrase, meaning


def rrf(rankings, k=60):
    """Reciprocal rank fusion: sum 1/(k + rank) across every ranking."""
    scores = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[doc] = scores.get(doc, 0.0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])


fused = rrf([BM25_RANKING, VECTOR_RANKING])
print("bm25   :", BM25_RANKING)
print("vector :", VECTOR_RANKING)
print("fused  :", [doc for doc, _ in fused])
print()
for doc, score in fused:
    b = BM25_RANKING.index(doc) + 1
    v = VECTOR_RANKING.index(doc) + 1
    print(f"  {doc}  bm25 #{b}  vector #{v}  fused {score:.5f}")

print()
print("d1 is second in both and wins: agreement beats a single first place")

bm25   : ['d3', 'd1', 'd5', 'd2', 'd4']
vector : ['d2', 'd1', 'd4', 'd5', 'd3']
fused  : ['d1', 'd2', 'd3', 'd5', 'd4']

  d1  bm25 #2  vector #2  fused 0.03226
  d2  bm25 #4  vector #1  fused 0.03202
  d3  bm25 #1  vector #5  fused 0.03178
  d5  bm25 #3  vector #4  fused 0.03150
  d4  bm25 #5  vector #3  fused 0.03126

d1 is second in both and wins: agreement beats a single first place

Fusion rewards agreement. d1 is not first in either ranking and comes out on top, because both retrievers rank it highly, which is a better signal than one retriever being confident. d3 and d2 are each first in one ranking and low in the other, and they land below it.

The k constant (conventionally 60) damps the influence of top ranks. Lower it and first places dominate, and raise it and the fusion flattens toward counting appearances.

Hybrid is the default worth starting from, and not an optimisation to add later. It is a handful of lines on top of two retrievers you were going to build anyway, and it removes the single biggest failure mode of pure vector search, which is that exact identifiers become unfindable.

10.6 Reranking

Retrieval optimises for recall, meaning it tries to get the right chunk into the top fifty. Ranking the top fifty well is a different problem, and a reranker is much better at it. A reranker is a model that scores query and document pairs directly and does not compare pre-computed vectors.

The reason is structural. An embedding is computed without knowing the query, so it has to be a general-purpose summary of the chunk. A reranker sees the query and the document together and can judge this document against this question. That costs a model call per candidate, which is why it runs over fifty candidates and not over the whole corpus.

# Scores a reranker returned for one query over ten retrieved candidates,
# alongside the retrieval order that produced them.
RETRIEVED = [
    ("c1", 0.81, 0.12), ("c2", 0.79, 0.94), ("c3", 0.78, 0.31),
    ("c4", 0.77, 0.88), ("c5", 0.76, 0.09), ("c6", 0.75, 0.71),
    ("c7", 0.74, 0.05), ("c8", 0.73, 0.97), ("c9", 0.72, 0.22),
    ("c10", 0.71, 0.14),
]
RELEVANT = {"c2", "c4", "c8"}


def precision_at_k(order, k):
    return sum(c in RELEVANT for c in order[:k]) / k


by_retrieval = [c for c, _, _ in RETRIEVED]
by_rerank = [c for c, _, _ in sorted(RETRIEVED, key=lambda r: -r[2])]

print("retrieval order:", by_retrieval)
print("reranked order :", by_rerank)
print()
for k in (1, 3, 5):
    print(f"precision@{k}  retrieval {precision_at_k(by_retrieval, k):>5.0%}"
          f"   reranked {precision_at_k(by_rerank, k):>5.0%}")

print()
sent_without = 5
sent_with = 3
CHUNK_TOKENS = 240
print(f"send top {sent_without} unreranked: {sent_without * CHUNK_TOKENS:>5,} tokens, "
      f"{sum(c in RELEVANT for c in by_retrieval[:sent_without])} of 3 relevant")
print(f"send top {sent_with} reranked   : {sent_with * CHUNK_TOKENS:>5,} tokens, "
      f"{sum(c in RELEVANT for c in by_rerank[:sent_with])} of 3 relevant")

retrieval order: ['c1', 'c2', 'c3', 'c4', 'c5', 'c6', 'c7', 'c8', 'c9', 'c10']
reranked order : ['c8', 'c2', 'c4', 'c6', 'c3', 'c9', 'c10', 'c1', 'c5', 'c7']

precision@1  retrieval    0%   reranked  100%
precision@3  retrieval   33%   reranked  100%
precision@5  retrieval   40%   reranked   60%

send top 5 unreranked: 1,200 tokens, 2 of 3 relevant
send top 3 reranked   :   720 tokens, 3 of 3 relevant

Reranking lets you send fewer chunks and get better ones. That is the whole value proposition, and it compounds. Fewer chunks means fewer tokens, lower latency and, per §9, a context in which the relevant passage is easier for the model to use.

Notice that the retrieval scores in that data are all between 0.71 and 0.81. Vector similarity is poor at fine-grained ordering, because those scores are nearly indistinguishable and the differences are noise. Retrieval is a coarse filter that is very good at its job, and treating its ordering as a ranking is asking it for something it does not provide.

The practical shape is to retrieve 50 with hybrid search, rerank to 5, and send those. Voyage's rerank-2.5 and rerank-2.5-lite are the models the documentation points at.

10.7 Grounding the Answer

Retrieval puts passages in the window. Nothing so far makes the model use them, or makes its use checkable. Two features do, and they are the difference between a RAG system you can audit and one you have to trust.

Search result blocks carry a source and a title alongside the text, and Claude cites them automatically.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

RESULTS = [
    {"type": "search_result",
     "source": "kb://refund-policy",
     "title": "Refund Policy",
     "content": [{"type": "text",
                  "text": "Customers may request a refund within 30 days of "
                          "delivery. Perishable goods are not refundable."}],
     "citations": {"enabled": True}},
    {"type": "search_result",
     "source": "kb://processing-times",
     "title": "Processing Times",
     "content": [{"type": "text",
                  "text": "Refunds are processed within 5 business days of "
                          "approval."}],
     "citations": {"enabled": True}},
]

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": [*RESULTS,
                           {"type": "text",
                            "text": "How long does a refund take?"}]}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type != "text":
        continue
    print("text:", block.text)
    for citation in (block.citations or []):
        print(f"  cited: {citation.source} — {citation.cited_text!r}")

text: Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval.
  cited: kb://processing-times — 'Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval.'

source can be any stable string. It can be a URL or an internal identifier like kb://article-1234. It does not have to resolve to anything, because it is the handle your application uses to link back.

Citations are off by default and must be enabled per result, and all search results in one request must agree. Mixing enabled and disabled is rejected.

Search results hold text only. No images inside the content array.

What this buys you is mechanical. Every text block carries the passages it drew on, so a claim with no citation is detectable by code. That is §13's faithfulness check without needing a judge, and it is the strongest anti-hallucination measure available in a RAG system.

# The check that becomes possible once every claim carries its source.
BLOCKS = [
    ("Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval.",
     ["kb://processing-times"]),
    ("Your bank may take a further week to post the credit.", []),
    ("Perishable goods are not refundable.", ["kb://refund-policy"]),
]

uncited = [text for text, cites in BLOCKS if not cites]
print(f"{'cited?':<8}{'claim'}")
for text, cites in BLOCKS:
    print(f"{('yes' if cites else 'NO'):<8}{text}")
print(f"\n{len(uncited)} of {len(BLOCKS)} claims rest on nothing in the sources:")
for text in uncited:
    print(f"  {text}")
print("\nthat is a code-based grader, not a judge (13.4)")

cited?  claim
yes     Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval.
NO      Your bank may take a further week to post the credit.
yes     Perishable goods are not refundable.

1 of 3 claims rest on nothing in the sources:
  Your bank may take a further week to post the credit.

that is a code-based grader, not a judge (13.4)

10.8 Evaluating a Retrieval Pipeline

A RAG system has two failure modes, and they need separate measurement because the fixes are unrelated. Retrieval failure: the answer was not in the retrieved chunks. Generation failure: it was, and the model did not use it or used it wrongly.

Conflating them is how teams spend a month tuning a prompt to fix a chunker.

CASES = [
    # (id, gold chunk, retrieved chunks, answer was correct)
    ("q1", "c2", ["c2", "c7", "c9"], True),
    ("q2", "c4", ["c1", "c3", "c8"], False),
    ("q3", "c5", ["c5", "c2", "c1"], False),
    ("q4", "c1", ["c1", "c4", "c6"], True),
    ("q5", "c9", ["c3", "c7", "c2"], False),
    ("q6", "c3", ["c3", "c9", "c5"], True),
]

retrieved_ok = [c for c in CASES if c[1] in c[2]]
answered_ok = [c for c in CASES if c[3]]
retrieval_failures = [c[0] for c in CASES if c[1] not in c[2]]
generation_failures = [c[0] for c in CASES if c[1] in c[2] and not c[3]]

print(f"recall@3 (gold chunk retrieved) : "
      f"{len(retrieved_ok)}/{len(CASES)} = {len(retrieved_ok) / len(CASES):.0%}")
print(f"end-to-end answer accuracy      : "
      f"{len(answered_ok)}/{len(CASES)} = {len(answered_ok) / len(CASES):.0%}")
print()
print(f"retrieval failures  {retrieval_failures}  -> fix chunking or search")
print(f"generation failures {generation_failures}  -> fix the prompt or the model")
print()
ceiling = len(retrieved_ok) / len(CASES)
print(f"answer accuracy can never exceed recall: ceiling is {ceiling:.0%}")
print("no prompt change moves a case whose answer was never in the window")

recall@3 (gold chunk retrieved) : 4/6 = 67%
end-to-end answer accuracy      : 3/6 = 50%

retrieval failures  ['q2', 'q5']  -> fix chunking or search
generation failures ['q3']  -> fix the prompt or the model

answer accuracy can never exceed recall: ceiling is 67%
no prompt change moves a case whose answer was never in the window

Recall is a ceiling on end-to-end accuracy, and that single fact tells you where to work. If recall@k is 67% and accuracy is 50%, the largest available gain is in retrieval, because no amount of prompt engineering reaches a passage that was never retrieved. (Recall@k is the share of questions where the right chunk appears in the top k results.)

Measure recall@k, not precision, at the retrieval stage. Getting the gold chunk (the correct answer's source) into the candidate set is the job, and ordering it is the reranker's (§10.6). A retriever tuned for precision@3 will discard candidates a reranker would have promoted.

Building the gold set is the expensive part, and there is a shortcut. For each chunk, have a model generate a question that chunk answers, and the chunk is then the gold label for that question. It produces a large synthetic set for the cost of one pass over the corpus. It is biased, because the questions are phrased like the chunk, so it flatters semantic search and understates the paraphrase gap. So pair it with a smaller hand-written set drawn from real user queries. §13.3's rule about edge cases coming from people who saw the system fail applies exactly here.

Exercises

Exercise 10.1 — Diagnose four failures. A RAG assistant over an engineering handbook produces these. For each, say which stage is at fault and what you would change.

(a) Asked "what is our on-call escalation path?", it answers about incident severity levels — a real section, wrong one. (b) Asked "what does ERR_4471 mean?", it says the handbook does not cover it. It does. (c) Asked "can contractors approve deploys?", it retrieves the right section and answers "yes", where the section says contractors may approve deploys to staging. (d) Asked about a policy changed last week, it gives the old answer.

Solution 
DIAGNOSES = [
    ("a  wrong-but-related section", "retrieval: ranking",
     "The right chunk was probably retrieved and ranked below a plausible "
     "neighbour. Add a reranker (10.6) before touching anything else."),
    ("b  exact identifier not found", "retrieval: no keyword search",
     "ERR_4471 is a rare token. Pure vector search cannot find it. Add BM25 "
     "and fuse (10.3, 10.5) — this is the single most common RAG defect."),
    ("c  right chunk, wrong answer", "generation, or chunking",
     "The qualifier was either split off by the chunker or present and "
     "ignored. Look at the retrieved chunk first: it decides which."),
    ("d  stale answer", "indexing, not retrieval at all",
     "The pipeline is working perfectly on an index that is out of date. "
     "Nothing in the retrieval stack can fix it."),
]

for case, stage, action in DIAGNOSES:
    print(f"{case:<32} {stage}")
    print(f"{'':32} {action}")

a  wrong-but-related section     retrieval: ranking
                                 The right chunk was probably retrieved and ranked below a plausible neighbour. Add a reranker (10.6) before touching anything else.
b  exact identifier not found    retrieval: no keyword search
                                 ERR_4471 is a rare token. Pure vector search cannot find it. Add BM25 and fuse (10.3, 10.5) — this is the single most common RAG defect.
c  right chunk, wrong answer     generation, or chunking
                                 The qualifier was either split off by the chunker or present and ignored. Look at the retrieved chunk first: it decides which.
d  stale answer                  indexing, not retrieval at all
                                 The pipeline is working perfectly on an index that is out of date. Nothing in the retrieval stack can fix it.

(a) is a ranking failure, and the tell is that the retrieved section is related. Incident severity and on-call escalation sit near each other in embedding space, and cosine similarity is poor at fine-grained ordering (§10.6), so the scores for the two are probably within a few hundredths. A reranker sees the query and the candidate together and separates them easily. Before that, confirm the right chunk was in the candidate set at all. If recall@50 already contains it, this is a reranking job. If not, it is a chunking or search job, and reranking will not help.

(b) is the textbook argument for hybrid search. ERR_4471 is one rare token whose embedding carries almost no usable meaning, while its BM25 IDF is as high as it gets. A pure vector pipeline finds it by accident or not at all. Add keyword search and fuse with RRF (reciprocal rank fusion). This failure is common enough that "our RAG cannot find error codes" is close to a diagnosis on its own.

(c) needs the retrieved chunk before you can diagnose it, and that is the point of the exercise. Two very different bugs look identical from outside. If the chunk contains "contractors may approve deploys to staging", the model dropped a qualifier, and the fix is on the generation side: a prompt that requires quoting the passage (§14.5), or a judge in the eval that checks qualifiers survive. If the chunk contains only "contractors may approve deploys" with the qualifier in an adjacent chunk, the chunker split a sentence from its condition, and the fix is structural chunking (§10.2). Always look at the retrieved text before theorising about the model.

(d) is not a retrieval problem at all, and it is the one most likely to waste a week. Every stage did its job, and the index is stale. The fixes are operational: re-index on write and not on a schedule, or record an updated_at per chunk and surface it so the model can say how current its source is. It is worth adding a case like this to the eval set precisely because it is invisible to every retrieval metric. Recall@k is 100% against an index that is a week out of date.

Exercise 10.2 — Size a pipeline. 200,000 documents averaging 1,800 tokens. Chunk at 300 tokens with 15% overlap. Compute the chunk count, storage at 1024 dimensions, and decide whether to embed the whole corpus. Then compute what a hybrid + rerank query costs against a pure vector one.

Solution 
DOCS, DOC_TOKENS = 200_000, 1_800
CHUNK, OVERLAP_PCT, DIMS, BYTES = 300, 15, 1024, 4

step = CHUNK * (1 - OVERLAP_PCT / 100)
chunks_per_doc = max(1, round(DOC_TOKENS / step))
chunks = DOCS * chunks_per_doc
stored_tokens = chunks * CHUNK
raw_tokens = DOCS * DOC_TOKENS

print(f"chunks per document : {chunks_per_doc:>12,}")
print(f"total chunks        : {chunks:>12,}")
print(f"tokens embedded     : {stored_tokens:>12,}  "
      f"({stored_tokens / raw_tokens:.2f}x the corpus, from overlap)")
print(f"vector storage      : {chunks * DIMS * BYTES / 1e9:>12.2f} GB")
print(f"  at 256 dimensions : {chunks * 256 * BYTES / 1e9:>12.2f} GB")
print()

# Per query, in model calls and added latency.
CANDIDATES, FINAL = 50, 5
RERANK_MS, SEARCH_MS = 180, 40
CHUNK_TOKENS_SENT = {"vector only": 10 * CHUNK, "hybrid + rerank": FINAL * CHUNK}
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00

print(f"{'pipeline':<20}{'chunks sent':>13}{'tokens':>9}"
      f"{'added latency':>15}{'cost/query':>12}")
for name, tokens in CHUNK_TOKENS_SENT.items():
    latency = SEARCH_MS if name == "vector only" else SEARCH_MS * 2 + RERANK_MS
    print(f"{name:<20}{tokens // CHUNK:>13}{tokens:>9,}{str(latency) + ' ms':>15}"
          f"{'$%.5f' % (tokens / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>12}")

print()
print(f"reranking costs ~{RERANK_MS + SEARCH_MS} ms and saves "
      f"{(10 - FINAL) * CHUNK:,} tokens per query")

chunks per document :            7
total chunks        :    1,400,000
tokens embedded     :  420,000,000  (1.17x the corpus, from overlap)
vector storage      :         5.73 GB
  at 256 dimensions :         1.43 GB

pipeline              chunks sent   tokens  added latency  cost/query
vector only                    10    3,000          40 ms    $0.01500
hybrid + rerank                 5    1,500         260 ms    $0.00750

reranking costs ~220 ms and saves 1,500 tokens per query

Yes, embed it. The corpus is far past the point where retrieval is optional. 360 million tokens does not fit in any context window, so §10.1's question answers itself. The storage is unremarkable by database standards, and the 256-dimension row is worth noting: if quality holds, it is a four-fold saving in storage and a proportional speed-up in search. Measure it with §10.8's recall@k and do not assume.

The overlap costs 17% more embedding and storage than the raw corpus, and that is the honest price of not cutting sentences at boundaries. It is usually worth paying. If it were not, the alternative is structural chunking, which needs no overlap because it splits where a human would.

Reranking looks expensive per query and is not. It adds roughly 220 ms and one model call, and it halves the tokens sent to the main model. The token saving alone roughly pays for it, and the accuracy gain (§10.6) is the actual reason to do it. Against a 1,400 ms model turn, 220 ms is a fraction of the total the user perceives.

What the arithmetic leaves out, and it is the expensive part. Embedding 360 million tokens once is a batch job with a real invoice, and, more importantly, the corpus changes. The recurring cost is re-embedding what changed, and the recurring engineering cost is keeping the index in step with the source of truth. Exercise 10.1(d) is what happens when that slips. Budget for the pipeline, and not just for the query.

One decision I would revisit. 300-token chunks with 15% overlap is a reasonable default for prose and a poor one for a corpus with structure. Before accepting it, check whether these documents have headings or sections. If they do, structural chunking (§10.2) will beat this on both recall and cost, because it needs no overlap at all.

SECTION 11

Building Agents

Section 6 built a loop and pointed out that it has no stop condition. Section 9 explained why its context grows and what to do about that. This section turns the loop into something you would let near production. It has to be bounded, observable and recoverable. It also has to be scoped to a job it can actually do, and that part takes judgement and not code.

It starts with the question most projects skip.

11.1 Should This Be an Agent?

An agent is a loop in which the model decides what happens next. That degree of autonomy is the definition, and it is also the entire cost. You have given up control of the control flow (which step runs next), and every later design decision is about bounding what that autonomy can reach. Everything that makes agents attractive and everything that makes them expensive comes from that one trade.

Most tasks do not need it. There is a ladder, and the right answer is usually the lowest rung that works.

One call
Classification, extraction, summarisation, a question with an answer. One request, one response, predictable cost, testable with §13's machinery. Most production LLM traffic is this and should be.
A chain
Several calls in an order you decide. Extract, then validate, then draft. The control flow is yours; the model fills in steps. Debuggable, cheap, and covers far more than people expect.
A workflow with tools
A loop you drive, over a small fixed tool set, with a shape you know. "Look up the order, then answer." The model chooses arguments, not the plan.
An agent
The model chooses the plan. Open-ended, variable cost, variable latency, and only testable through §13.10's trajectory evaluation. Correct when the task genuinely cannot be specified in advance.

Four questions decide whether the last rung is justified, and a "no" to any one of them means stop.

Complexity. Is the task genuinely hard to specify in advance? "Turn this design document into a pull request" is. "Extract the title from this PDF" is not. If you can write the steps down, write them down, because a chain of three calls beats an agent that rediscovers your process every run.

Value. Does the outcome justify a variable bill and variable latency? An agent that takes 40 seconds and $0.30 to do something a single call does in 2 seconds for $0.004 has to be much better to be worth it.

Viability. Is the model actually good at this task? An agent amplifies capability and does not create it. If a single call cannot do a step, a loop that calls it eleven times will not either. It will just be wrong at greater length.

Cost of error. Can mistakes be caught and undone? This is the one people weigh last and should weigh first. An agent that writes code you review is safe because the review is a gate. An agent that issues refunds is safe only if you built the gate. §11.6 builds it.

CANDIDATES = [
    # (task, specifiable, value, viable, recoverable)
    ("extract invoice totals from PDFs",      True,  "high",   True,  True),
    ("negotiate with a supplier by email",    False, "high",   False, False),
    ("reconcile unmatched payments",          False, "high",   True,  False),
    ("tidy variable names across the repo",   False, "low",    True,  True),
    ("investigate a failing test and fix it", False, "high",   True,  True),
]

print(f"{'task':<40}{'verdict'}")
for task, specifiable, value, viable, recoverable in CANDIDATES:
    if not viable:
        verdict = "no — the model cannot do the underlying job"
    elif specifiable:
        verdict = "no — write the steps down; use a chain or a workflow"
    elif not recoverable:
        verdict = "only with a human gate on every irreversible step"
    elif value == "low":
        verdict = "no — the value does not justify the variance"
    else:
        verdict = "YES — this is what agents are for"
    print(f"{task:<40}{verdict}")

task                                    verdict
extract invoice totals from PDFs        no — write the steps down; use a chain or a workflow
negotiate with a supplier by email      no — the model cannot do the underlying job
reconcile unmatched payments            only with a human gate on every irreversible step
tidy variable names across the repo     no — the value does not justify the variance
investigate a failing test and fix it   YES — this is what agents are for

Each row fails on a different question, which is the useful part. A "no" arrives for four distinct reasons, and only the last row survives all four. That ratio is roughly right in practice too.

11.2 The Harness

An agent is a loop plus the scaffolding that makes the loop safe. That scaffolding has a name, the agent harness, and it is the part you actually write. The model is a component, and the agent harness is the system. Everything that makes an agent trustworthy lives in the harness and not in the model.

Budget
Turns, tokens, wall-clock, money. Every one of them bounded, and every bound producing a defined outcome rather than an exception. §11.3.
Execution
Dispatch, authorisation, error shaping. The only place with the session, the permissions and the real world. §6.5 and §6.10 built most of this.
Context policy
What is cached, cleared, compacted, remembered. §9, applied rather than discussed.
Gates
What requires a human. Not a nice-to-have on anything irreversible. §11.6.
Observability
A record of every turn, every call, every argument. Without it, an agent that misbehaves once is not debuggable at all. §11.7.

The mistake worth naming early is treating the system prompt as the harness. Instructions like "never refund more than €100 without approval" are guidance to a component that produces text. They are not a control. The €100 check belongs in create_refund, where it is code, and where no amount of clever input can talk it out of firing.

11.3 Bounding the Loop

Here is §6.4's loop with the missing half. Every bound is explicit, and, the part that matters, every bound has a defined outcome.

import time


class Budget:
    """Turns, tokens, seconds and money, each with a defined outcome when hit."""

    def __init__(self, max_turns, max_tokens, max_seconds, max_cost,
                 now=lambda: 0.0):
        self.max_turns, self.max_tokens = max_turns, max_tokens
        self.max_seconds, self.max_cost = max_seconds, max_cost
        self.turns = self.tokens = 0
        self.cost = 0.0
        self._now = now
        self.started = now()

    def spend(self, input_tokens, output_tokens):
        self.turns += 1
        self.tokens += input_tokens + output_tokens
        self.cost += input_tokens / 1e6 * 5.0 + output_tokens / 1e6 * 25.0

    def exhausted(self):
        if self.turns >= self.max_turns:
            return "turn_limit"
        if self.tokens >= self.max_tokens:
            return "token_limit"
        if self._now() - self.started >= self.max_seconds:
            return "time_limit"
        if self.cost >= self.max_cost:
            return "cost_limit"
        return None


clock = {"t": 0.0}
budget = Budget(max_turns=20, max_tokens=200_000, max_seconds=120, max_cost=1.00,
                now=lambda: clock["t"])

TURN_COST = [(4_000, 300), (9_000, 450), (16_000, 380), (30_000, 900),
             (52_000, 700), (61_000, 1_200), (74_000, 600)]

for input_tokens, output_tokens in TURN_COST:
    stop = budget.exhausted()
    if stop:
        print(f"stopped after {budget.turns} turns: {stop}")
        break
    budget.spend(input_tokens, output_tokens)
    clock["t"] += 9.5
    print(f"turn {budget.turns:>2}  tokens {budget.tokens:>7,}  "
          f"cost ${budget.cost:>5.3f}  elapsed {clock['t']:>5.1f}s")
else:
    print(f"finished normally after {budget.turns} turns "
          f"(${budget.cost:.3f}, {budget.tokens:,} tokens)")

turn  1  tokens   4,300  cost $0.028  elapsed   9.5s
turn  2  tokens  13,750  cost $0.084  elapsed  19.0s
turn  3  tokens  30,130  cost $0.173  elapsed  28.5s
turn  4  tokens  61,030  cost $0.346  elapsed  38.0s
turn  5  tokens 113,730  cost $0.623  elapsed  47.5s
turn  6  tokens 175,930  cost $0.958  elapsed  57.0s
turn  7  tokens 250,530  cost $1.343  elapsed  66.5s
finished normally after 7 turns ($1.343, 250,530 tokens)

Four bounds, not one, because they fail in different ways. A turn cap does not stop one turn that reads a 400,000-token file. A token cap does not stop an agent waiting on a slow tool. A time cap does not stop something cheap and fast that loops forever within budget. Money is the one your finance team cares about and the one nobody adds until an incident.

A bound must produce an outcome, not an exception. stopped: turn_limit is a state your caller can handle: show partial results, escalate to a human, or resume with a raised budget. A raised RuntimeError in the middle of a loop that has already issued a refund is not a state. It is a mess.

Inject the clock. The now parameter is what makes this testable and what makes the output above identical on every run. §13 cannot evaluate an agent whose time limit depends on how busy the machine was.

There is a related feature worth knowing about, and it solves a different problem: task budgets. A task budget differs from every bound above in one respect that changes how it behaves. A task_budget inside output_config tells the model how many tokens it has for the whole job, so it paces itself and finishes gracefully and is not cut off mid-thought. It is advisory, and it complements the hard bounds above and does not replace them.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

with client.beta.messages.stream(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=64000,
    betas=["task-budgets-2026-03-13"],
    output_config={"effort": "high",
                   "task_budget": {"type": "tokens", "total": 40000}},
    tools=[{"name": "read_file",
            "description": "Read a file from the repository.",
            "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                             "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}},
                             "required": ["path"]}}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Audit the auth module for bugs."}],
) as stream:
    response = stream.get_final_message()

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print("output tokens:", response.usage.output_tokens)

stop_reason: end_turn
output tokens: 11840

Note the streaming. A max_tokens that large on a non-streaming request risks an HTTP timeout, which is why the budget example uses .stream() and get_final_message() and not create().

max_tokens and task_budget are not the same thing, and the difference matters. max_tokens is a hard ceiling on one response that the model does not know about, so hitting it gives you a sentence cut in half. task_budget is a figure the model can see and pace against across the whole loop. Use both: the task budget so the model lands the plane, and the ceiling so it cannot run away.

11.4 Designing the Tool Surface for an Agent

§6.10 covered tool design in general. Agents add one question that single-call systems never face: how much of the world should this loop be able to touch?

The instinct is to give the agent everything it might need. The better instinct is the opposite, and there is a concrete rule that captures it.

An agent's blast radius is everything all its tools together can do. (Blast radius is a term borrowed from explosives: how much damage spreads if something goes wrong.) It should be sized to the worst plausible sequence and not the intended one. A tool set of read_file, write_file and run_shell is, whatever the system prompt says, an agent that can do anything to that machine.

TOOLSETS = {
    "reader": ["search_docs", "read_file"],
    "support": ["get_order", "check_refund_policy", "create_refund",
                "send_email"],
    "dev": ["read_file", "write_file", "run_tests", "run_shell"],
}

CAPABILITY = {
    "search_docs": ("read", "public"), "read_file": ("read", "repo"),
    "get_order": ("read", "customer"), "check_refund_policy": ("read", "public"),
    "create_refund": ("write", "money"), "send_email": ("write", "outbound"),
    "write_file": ("write", "repo"), "run_tests": ("execute", "sandbox"),
    "run_shell": ("execute", "host"),
}

for name, tools in TOOLSETS.items():
    kinds = {CAPABILITY[t][0] for t in tools}
    reach = sorted({CAPABILITY[t][1] for t in tools})
    irreversible = [t for t in tools
                    if CAPABILITY[t] in (("write", "money"), ("write", "outbound"),
                                         ("execute", "host"))]
    print(f"{name:<9} kinds={','.join(sorted(kinds)):<20} reach={','.join(reach)}")
    print(f"{'':9} needs a gate: {irreversible or 'nothing — safe to run unattended'}")

reader    kinds=read                 reach=public,repo
          needs a gate: nothing — safe to run unattended
support   kinds=read,write           reach=customer,money,outbound,public
          needs a gate: ['create_refund', 'send_email']
dev       kinds=execute,read,write   reach=host,repo,sandbox
          needs a gate: ['run_shell']

The reader agent can be run unattended on a schedule, and nobody needs to think about it again. The other two cannot, and the reason is visible in one line and not buried in a system prompt.

Two agent-specific tool design rules follow.

Split read from write, and make the write tools narrow. A single update_order(fields) tool that accepts arbitrary fields has a much larger blast radius than cancel_order(id) and change_address(id, address). Narrow tools are also easier for the model to call correctly, so this is not purely a safety trade.

Give the agent a way to finish. An explicit done(summary) tool is often better than relying on the model to stop calling tools, because it makes completion an observable event you can log, gate and evaluate. Without it, "the agent finished" and "the agent gave up" look identical from outside.

11.5 A Complete Harness

Here is the whole thing, assembled. It is longer than the loop in §6.4 by roughly the amount of scaffolding a production system needs, which is the point.

class Halt(Exception):
    """Raised by the executor when a call must not proceed. Never reaches the model."""


class Agent:
    def __init__(self, tools, implementations, *, max_turns=12,
                 gate=None, on_event=None):
        self.tools = tools
        self.implementations = implementations
        self.max_turns = max_turns
        self.gate = gate or (lambda name, args: True)
        self.on_event = on_event or (lambda *a: None)
        self.trace = []

    def _execute(self, name, args):
        if name not in self.implementations:
            return f"No such tool: {name}", True
        if not self.gate(name, args):
            return (f"The call to {name} was declined by policy and was not "
                    f"executed. Ask the user to approve it, or choose another "
                    f"approach."), True
        try:
            return str(self.implementations[name](**args)), False
        except Halt as exc:
            return f"Refused: {exc}", True
        except Exception as exc:
            return f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", True

    def run(self, turns_of_calls):
        """`turns_of_calls` stands in for the model: each entry is what the model
        asks for on that turn. Substituting the API here changes nothing else."""
        for turn, calls in enumerate(turns_of_calls, 1):
            if turn > self.max_turns:
                self.on_event("halted", {"reason": "turn_limit"})
                return "turn_limit"
            if calls == "done":
                self.on_event("finished", {"turns": turn})
                return "finished"
            results = []
            for name, args in calls:
                content, is_error = self._execute(name, args)
                self.on_event("tool", {"turn": turn, "name": name, "args": args,
                                       "error": is_error, "result": content})
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "content": content,
                                "is_error": is_error})
            self.trace.append(results)
        self.on_event("halted", {"reason": "ran_out_of_plan"})
        return "ran_out_of_plan"


REFUNDED = {}


def create_refund(order_id, amount_cents):
    if amount_cents > 10_000:
        raise Halt("refunds above 100.00 require a supervisor")
    REFUNDED[order_id] = amount_cents
    return f"refunded {amount_cents} on {order_id}"


def get_order(order_id):
    return {"id": order_id, "total_cents": 4250, "status": "delivered"}


events = []
agent = Agent(
    tools=[],
    implementations={"get_order": get_order, "create_refund": create_refund},
    max_turns=6,
    # The gate owns the "needs approval" band. The hard ceiling is not its job.
    gate=lambda name, args: not (name == "create_refund"
                                 and 5_000 < args.get("amount_cents", 0) <= 10_000),
    on_event=lambda kind, data: events.append((kind, data)),
)

outcome = agent.run([
    [("get_order", {"order_id": "ord_1"})],
    [("create_refund", {"order_id": "ord_1", "amount_cents": 4250})],
    [("create_refund", {"order_id": "ord_2", "amount_cents": 7500})],
    [("create_refund", {"order_id": "ord_3", "amount_cents": 25000})],
    [("delete_everything", {})],
    "done",
])

for kind, data in events:
    if kind == "tool":
        status = "ERROR" if data["error"] else "ok   "
        print(f"turn {data['turn']}  {status} {data['name']:<18} "
              f"{str(data['result'])[:56]}")
    else:
        print(f"        {kind}: {data}")

print("\noutcome:", outcome)
print("refunds actually made:", REFUNDED)

turn 1  ok    get_order          {'id': 'ord_1', 'total_cents': 4250, 'status': 'delivere
turn 2  ok    create_refund      refunded 4250 on ord_1
turn 3  ERROR create_refund      The call to create_refund was declined by policy and was
turn 4  ERROR create_refund      Refused: refunds above 100.00 require a supervisor
turn 5  ERROR delete_everything  No such tool: delete_everything
        finished: {'turns': 6}

outcome: finished
refunds actually made: {'ord_1': 4250}

Read what each of the four create_refund attempts did.

The first succeeded, because it was under both limits.

The second was declined by the gate, because it was over €50 and under the hard limit. The model is told, in a sentence it can act on, that the call was not executed and what to do next. It is not told "error". It is told the shape of the constraint.

The third hit Halt inside the implementation. This is the layer that matters, because it fires whether or not the gate exists, whether or not the system prompt said anything, and whether or not the model was persuaded by something it read in a tool result. The gate is policy, and Halt is the law.

The fourth was a tool that does not exist, which is returned as an error and does not crash the loop. Models occasionally invent tool names, especially with large surfaces, and a harness that dies on one is a harness that dies in production.

And the whole run is in events, which is §11.7's subject.

11.6 Human Gates

Human in the loop is the name for what §11.5's gate implements. The gate there is a function returning a boolean. In a real system it is a workflow, and the design question is where the approval gate goes and not whether there is one.

Before the loop
Approve the plan. Ask the model what it intends, show it, get a yes. Cheap and popular, and it protects less than it appears to — plans drift once tool results start arriving.
At the call
Approve this specific action with these specific arguments. The strongest form of human in the loop, and the only approval gate that sees the actual amount, the actual recipient, the actual file. Use it for anything irreversible.
After the fact
Review what happened. Adequate when the action is reversible and the review is real. This is what makes coding agents workable: the pull request is the gate.
Never
Correct for read-only agents whose entire tool surface is reads within a boundary. Gating those trains people to click approve, which is worse than not gating.

That last row is the one teams get wrong in the safe direction and pay for anyway. An approval gate that fires on everything is an approval gate nobody reads, and human in the loop stops meaning review the moment that happens. Approval fatigue is a real failure mode. After the fortieth approval prompt for a file read, the forty-first, the one asking to delete a directory, gets the same reflexive yes. Gate the irreversible, and log the rest.

POLICY = [
    # (tool, condition, decision)
    ("read_file",     lambda a: True,                          "allow"),
    ("write_file",    lambda a: a["path"].startswith("src/"),   "allow"),
    ("write_file",    lambda a: True,                           "ask"),
    ("create_refund", lambda a: a["amount_cents"] <= 2_000,     "allow"),
    ("create_refund", lambda a: a["amount_cents"] <= 10_000,    "ask"),
    ("create_refund", lambda a: True,                           "deny"),
    ("run_shell",     lambda a: True,                           "deny"),
]


def decide(tool, args):
    """First matching rule wins, so order encodes precedence. Default is deny."""
    for name, condition, decision in POLICY:
        if name == tool and condition(args):
            return decision
    return "deny"


ATTEMPTS = [
    ("read_file", {"path": "src/auth.py"}),
    ("write_file", {"path": "src/auth.py"}),
    ("write_file", {"path": "/etc/hosts"}),
    ("create_refund", {"amount_cents": 1500}),
    ("create_refund", {"amount_cents": 4250}),
    ("create_refund", {"amount_cents": 90000}),
    ("run_shell", {"cmd": "rm -rf /"}),
    ("send_email", {"to": "everyone@"}),
]

for tool, args in ATTEMPTS:
    decision = decide(tool, args)
    marker = {"allow": "  ", "ask": "? ", "deny": "! "}[decision]
    print(f"{marker}{decision:<6} {tool:<14} {args}")

asks = sum(decide(t, a) == "ask" for t, a in ATTEMPTS)
print(f"\n{asks} of {len(ATTEMPTS)} attempts interrupt a human")

allow  read_file      {'path': 'src/auth.py'}
  allow  write_file     {'path': 'src/auth.py'}
? ask    write_file     {'path': '/etc/hosts'}
  allow  create_refund  {'amount_cents': 1500}
? ask    create_refund  {'amount_cents': 4250}
! deny   create_refund  {'amount_cents': 90000}
! deny   run_shell      {'cmd': 'rm -rf /'}
! deny   send_email     {'to': 'everyone@'}

2 of 8 attempts interrupt a human

The default is deny, and send_email proves it. A tool with no policy entry is refused and not allowed, so adding a tool without thinking about its policy fails closed. Reversing that default is how an agent acquires a capability nobody reviewed.

Ordering encodes precedence. The three create_refund rules read as a ladder, where small amounts pass, medium ones ask and large ones are refused, because the first match wins. Written in the other order, everything would be denied.

Two of eight attempts interrupt a human. That ratio is the thing to tune. If it approaches one in two, people stop reading. If it is zero on an agent that spends money, you have no gate at all.

11.7 Observability

An agent that misbehaves once and cannot be reconstructed is an agent you cannot fix. The record (the trace) has to be complete enough to answer why did it do that, which means capturing the inputs to the decision and not only the decision.

import json

TRACE = [
    {"turn": 1, "kind": "request", "in_tokens": 4210, "tools_offered": 6},
    {"turn": 1, "kind": "tool_use", "name": "get_order",
     "args": {"order_id": "ord_1"}, "id": "toolu_a"},
    {"turn": 1, "kind": "tool_result", "id": "toolu_a", "ms": 42,
     "error": False, "bytes": 180},
    {"turn": 2, "kind": "request", "in_tokens": 4980, "tools_offered": 6},
    {"turn": 2, "kind": "tool_use", "name": "create_refund",
     "args": {"order_id": "ord_1", "amount_cents": 4250}, "id": "toolu_b"},
    {"turn": 2, "kind": "gate", "id": "toolu_b", "decision": "ask",
     "approved_by": "ana@example.com", "ms": 41_200},
    {"turn": 2, "kind": "tool_result", "id": "toolu_b", "ms": 310,
     "error": False, "bytes": 34},
    {"turn": 3, "kind": "request", "in_tokens": 5310, "tools_offered": 6},
    {"turn": 3, "kind": "finished", "reason": "end_turn"},
]

turns = max(e["turn"] for e in TRACE)
tool_calls = sum(e["kind"] == "tool_use" for e in TRACE)
errors = sum(e.get("error") is True for e in TRACE)
model_ms = sum(e.get("ms", 0) for e in TRACE if e["kind"] == "tool_result")
gate_ms = sum(e.get("ms", 0) for e in TRACE if e["kind"] == "gate")
peak_in = max(e["in_tokens"] for e in TRACE if e["kind"] == "request")

print(f"turns              : {turns}")
print(f"tool calls         : {tool_calls}  ({errors} errors)")
print(f"peak input tokens  : {peak_in:,}")
print(f"tool execution time: {model_ms:,} ms")
print(f"waiting on a human : {gate_ms:,} ms  "
      f"({gate_ms / (gate_ms + model_ms):.0%} of measured latency)")
print()
print("the one line an incident review needs:")
print(json.dumps(next(e for e in TRACE if e["kind"] == "gate")))

turns              : 3
tool calls         : 2  (0 errors)
peak input tokens  : 5,310
tool execution time: 352 ms
waiting on a human : 41,200 ms  (99% of measured latency)

the one line an incident review needs:
{"turn": 2, "kind": "gate", "id": "toolu_b", "decision": "ask", "approved_by": "ana@example.com", "ms": 41200}

Human approval dominates the latency, and it is invisible to any measurement that only times the API. That is worth knowing before somebody spends a week optimising model latency in a system whose real bottleneck is a person's inbox.

Five fields make a trace usable, and each is missing from somebody's production system right now:

The arguments, in full. "Called create_refund" tells you nothing. "Called create_refund(ord_1, 4250)" is the incident report.

The tool result, or at least its size and a hash. Results are often large and sometimes sensitive. Log the size and a digest at minimum, because "the model did something strange after this call" needs the call's output to explain it.

The gate decision and who made it. This is the audit trail. If a refund is disputed, approved_by is the answer.

Token counts per turn. Growth in in_tokens is how you notice a context problem before the bill does.

A correlation id across turns. It is omitted above for brevity and is mandatory in practice, because without it you cannot reconstruct a single run out of a log containing thousands.

One caution: traces contain everything the model saw, which means everything the user typed and everything your tools returned. That is a data-protection surface, and it deserves the same retention and redaction rules as any other log of customer content.

11.8 Multiple Agents

Once one agent works, the temptation is several. Sometimes that is right, but more often it is a way to turn one debuggable system into three that communicate by prose.

The case for splitting is context, not specialisation. A single agent that must read forty documents and then reason about them fills its window with reading. Handing each document to a sub-agent that returns a paragraph keeps the orchestrator's context small and its reasoning sharp. (The orchestrator is the main agent that hands out the work.) That is a real architectural gain, and it is the main one.

The case against is that every hand-off is lossy. Sub-agents communicate in natural language, so the orchestrator receives a summary and not the evidence, and errors compound quietly.

DOCUMENTS = [("d1", 8200), ("d2", 12400), ("d3", 6100), ("d4", 19800),
             ("d5", 9300), ("d6", 15200)]
SUMMARY_TOKENS = 320
ORCHESTRATOR_BASE = 2_400

single = ORCHESTRATOR_BASE + sum(size for _, size in DOCUMENTS)
fanned = ORCHESTRATOR_BASE + SUMMARY_TOKENS * len(DOCUMENTS)

print(f"one agent reads everything : {single:>7,} tokens in one window")
print(f"orchestrator + 6 workers   : {fanned:>7,} tokens in the orchestrator")
print(f"reduction                  : {1 - fanned / single:>7.0%}")
print()

# The work does not disappear; it moves, and it is billed at each worker.
worker_total = sum(size + SUMMARY_TOKENS for _, size in DOCUMENTS)
print(f"total tokens billed, single : {single:>7,}")
print(f"total tokens billed, fanned : {fanned + worker_total:>7,}")
print(f"extra tokens for the fan-out: {fanned + worker_total - single:>+7,}")
print()
print("the orchestrator's window shrinks 94%; the total bill grows 5%")

one agent reads everything :  73,400 tokens in one window
orchestrator + 6 workers   :   4,320 tokens in the orchestrator
reduction                  :     94%

total tokens billed, single :  73,400
total tokens billed, fanned :  77,240
extra tokens for the fan-out:  +3,840

the orchestrator's window shrinks 94%; the total bill grows 5%

Fan-out trades a little money for a great deal of context. The orchestrator's window drops by 94% while the total token spend rises by only 5%. Every document is still read, and each summary is written once and read once, which is nearly free next to the documents themselves. That is a much better trade than the framing "multi-agent costs more" suggests, and the parallelism usually buys latency back as well.
